en: The *Seo-jeong seok-dip nu* (Preface to the Path of Stone-Dripping Milk) was compiled by Master In-gong; it is a record of the profound origins of the lineage of the Way.
The work was nearly completed when Master In-gong passed away, whereupon his dharma-heir, Master Seokwon Un-gong, took it up and finalized the transcription.
This was done to manifest the legacy of his ancestors and to recount the entirety of the patriarchal lineage.
The compilation began with Mount Jing and drew from the works of the three gentlemen Cao Shicang, Tan Sa’an, and Qian Mucai, during the Wanli, Qianlong, and Tianqi eras.
Throughout the world, everyone knows how to read Buddhist scriptures; yet, those who can trace back the branches to their source are few, and among them, these three gentlemen are the most thorough.
These three gentlemen were indeed those who personally beheld the lineage chart (yuanliu) written by Linji at Mount Jing.
At that time, those who struck the lion’s string were as numerous as a forest, yet Yuan Liaofan received the secret teachings of Yungu, and Master Han [Zhixu] spoke of himself as follows:

Having personally received the master’s hammer and tongs, he comprehensively mastered the scriptural teachings. His transverse and vertical wondrous applications were like a dream journey through echoes and shadows;
there was no scripture he had not fully extracted and brought forth. Thus, he offered special prayers to Master Zhuan of Yunju.

Whether it was the Vinaya for the cultivation of the person or the Teachings for the exposition of meaning, why must one always raise the fist and say, "This is the Tathāgata’s true and wondrous [Dharma]?"
How profoundly this meaning has been revealed! One does not know that the secret, true mechanism had already been entrusted to the successor and hidden in the snowy valley long ago;
there was no need for further disclosure. Truly, this is a matter for those who observe the world from afar to look up to with reverence.
Because I read Master Yun’s "Dripping Milk on the Path Stone," I was moved to a deep realization regarding the ancients. Yangqi occupied the seat of Linji—
The Orthodox Lineage: Ying’an ascended to the true pulse of the Golden Wheel. At its inception, such individuals were truly rare, and the thread of the lineage hung by a slender cord;

it was only Chaozong who obtained it. How could there ever have been a case where the floorboards shook and a thousand bowls rang out together, or where the bells struck and a cloud of fingers descended?
To harvest the trees of Mount Denglin would not suffice to provide for his staffs, and to exterminate the species of the female elk would leave nothing behind.
Can it not suffice to sweep away the dust? This compilation may not necessarily equal the milk of the snow-mountain ox, nor may its carvings necessarily fill the rafters of the cloud-patterned hall;
yet upon reading a single phrase, it is as if a thunderbolt were to shake the gates of heaven.
To recognize his virtuous conduct is as swift as six horses galloping down a level slope; his upright mind is manifest, and the ultimate truth is clearly present.
Were it not for this book, how could the spiritual brilliance of the Great Mirror and the secret teachings of Linji have been brought to light?

Truly, it should be stored in a fragrant pouch and inscribed upon birch bark, so that one may feel as if personally beholding Duquan Bridge and receiving instruction face-to-face from Jingshan, free from all doubt.
This is a matter of duplicity. Were it not for having inherited the direct lineage of the Master’s breast-milk, how could one be capable of such things?

It is because I have attained realization through my connection with the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. Long ago, in the city of Vaiśālī, there were a thousand young boys who took up bows and staves to bring disorder to the kingdom.
The King was distressed by this, and the junior queen, becoming aware of it, called the thousand boys to her from atop the eastern tower and fed them from her own breast.
Milk flowed from her left breast in five hundred streams, and from her right breast likewise in five hundred streams.

The thousand children were each satisfied, and all knew their own mother. Since the junior concubines were not the true mothers of these children, how could milk have issued from those thousand streams for all of them?
It was only because each of the thousand children knew his own mother that each was satisfied with milk, and only then did the milk from the thousand streams [flow].
This is indeed the true essence. Among those in the world who propagate the Dharma at the seat of teaching, how could there be only a thousand children?
They all have yet to find the Mother; they have not yet obtained the true milk. To her left are five hundred paths, and to her right are five hundred paths, situated within the Eastern Tower.
At that time, there was indeed a tower in the eastern city. The Lady suspended two breasts there to await the thousand children.

My child! If you can, at the point where the lights of the mirrors intersect, receive a single touch upon the crown of your head and thereby enter samādhi, then I know that at the moment the stone drips with milk, the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) and the *Luohu yelu* (Record of the Wild Lake) will manifest the "invisible-peak" mark (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*) within this world of Zhendan.
This is because Master Shanduo is the true successor of the Dharma gate. — Stone Source.
Master Yun’s role as a teacher was like the true dripping of breast-milk; only those with the discerning eye will recognize it for themselves.
Written on the sixth day of the tenth month in the twenty-first year of the Kangxi era by the student from Guangji, Chu, Shu Fengji. Kāṅ.
The Reverend Bashi inscribed this at Huangniu Yuan on Dongchong.

Regarding the *Jingshan Diru Ji* (Collection of the Dripping Milk of Jingshan), these are the general rules for the work compiled by our late Master Donglin. It is based upon the various regional lamp records concerning Linji.
In the orthodox lineage following Duanqiao, various patriarchs have appeared, sometimes in concealment and sometimes in manifestation.

Many of them survive only with their verses on the transmission of the Dharma, while their recorded teachings and encounters are largely missing. Consequently, I conducted extensive research into the ancestral records and consulted various biographies to compile this complete work.
Before the collection was finished, my late teacher passed away, and more than half of the surviving drafts were lost. (Yun) followed his [teacher's]...
I, Zhi, have traveled extensively to exhaustively seek out [the teachings]. Whenever I encountered even a single word or half-phrase that revealed the perfect clarity of the patriarchal eye,

I did not fail to promptly collect and include it, so as to fulfill the unfulfilled wishes of my late teacher and, moreover, to slightly discharge my duty as a junior successor in continuing his legacy.
Lamps are used to transmit the Way; lineages are used to continue the pulse. That the Way is not clarified and the lineage is not rectified was the concern of the former sages.
Our former teacher, seeing that the Dharma-gate had become subject to monopolization, felt a profound sorrow and far-reaching anxiety;

thus he compiled this book, truly capturing the intent of following the constitutional precedents of the patriarchs. Now, I have deleted the redundant and extracted the essentials, harmonizing the detailed with the concise.
The same. This is intended so that future scholars, upon opening this volume, may gain realization.
The *Dilu Ji* (Collection of Droplets of Milk) records exclusively the lineage of Master Lun.

Because various regional lamp records do not prioritize the direct transmission of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' life-force of wisdom (*hui-ming*), but instead focus on personal preferences and private standards of selection and rejection, they have caused the various patriarchs...

The records of their teachings that have circulated in the world are not numerous, and those for whom woodblocks were carved are likewise rare. Now, having carefully selected and supplemented these, they are included here to remedy the omissions and deficiencies of the various lineages.
This book is fundamentally intended for the circulation of the Eye of the School; however, the two masters Zhenji and [the other] each elucidated their respective regions and eras.

It is difficult to compile these completely. Let those who obtain them first record them first; those who obtain them later shall record them later; and those not yet obtained shall await future supplementation.
The various records include the *Wujinding* (Inexhaustible Lamp), *Funiu*, *Liyi*, *Fengtan*, *Huanji*, *Tinghan*, *Shanqing*, and others.
Regarding those whose lineages were previously unknown, we have not yet fully attained the truth concerning them.

Now, by examining the sources and lineages of these various masters, we include them under their respective founding teachers, so that it may be known where their spiritual succession resides and they do not fall into oblivion.
Xingkong’s lineage descended to Yue Tan Cheng; Cheng to Jianfu Kai; Kai to Huashan Wen; Wen to Tianmu Ding;
Ding to Fushan Zhi; and Zhi to Miaofeng Li. His descendants have long been prominent in Yun and Gui provinces, though they have not yet been collected here and await supplementation.
There were various writings by Huangbo, but they have not been fully cataloged; only Hongjue appended [his records] under Daixiu Long.
(Yun) Upon reading the Record of Daixiu, I saw a public preface which states: "The Master entered nirvana in the twenty-first year of the Jiajing era."
Two years later, I was born; eighteen years after that, I finally began my pilgrimage (*fang-chang*).

It was not until I reached the age of forty-five that I was able to open the eyes of my dream, and so forth. According to this account, although this master had received the great seal of the mind (*daxiu xin-yin*), they had in fact never met in person.
Consequently, this record is likewise classified among the "unknown" and has not been dared to be included in the orthodox lineage.
This is because it disrupts the lineage.

The *Record of the Mind-Lamp of Guo’u* records this without sufficient detail; however, the recorded机缘 (kaiyuan—circumstances of enlightenment) therein accords with those found within the *Lanfeng Huashan Record*.
Based on this, the master-disciple succession is clearly established. How can it be said that [the lineage] is "not detailed"? It is merely...

Pō’ān served as the First Seat at Lingyin Monastery. The Master (Zhaozhou) followed him there once more.

One day, while they were strolling together at Shishun Monastery, a practitioner requested instruction, saying, “I cannot catch this monkey; I beg the Master for a skillful means. Pō’ān said, “What need is there to catch it?”
"Just as wind blowing over water naturally forms ripples," at which the Master attained great enlightenment while standing by his side.

Muyun Men’s Verse says: When the city gate catches fire, the stench and smoke spread abroad; The calamity reaches the fish in the pond, their tails scorched to ash.
Nowhere else can one seek even three feet of water; One must watch well as they shake their manes and ascend the blue clouds.
Nanjian asked for a verse, which was given as follows: The breath drinks the long rainbow and has already devoured the ox; Blood flows across the earth, its light making people sorrowful.
With the wind, the fire is fanned without much effort; Spring fills the imperial capital and its four hundred prefectures.
Nanyue Ji’s verse says: A frost-sword between the brows leans against the cold heavens; Try unfolding its edge, as vast as the sea.
On the path by the Stone笋 (Shisun), one encounters a wine shop; With three cups and two goblets, the face of sorrow is broken.
Shimen’s Verse on the Clouds says: Frost flies in the sixth month, bringing calamity to my private gate; The disaster reaches the common people, who are like overturned basins.
North, south, east, and west—there is nowhere to go; With a single blow of the fist, the Iron Kunlun is shattered.
The verse for the transmission of the Dharma to Pò'ān says: "If I do not see it, you should see that which is not seen.
This seeing of seeing is not one's own mind; one's own mind is ever-manifest. Shortly thereafter, Pò'ān went to Tiāntóng to sweep the pagoda, and the Master accompanied him.

He further invited Yuè Shíxī to travel together through Tái and Yàn. Upon reaching Ruìyán Yúnniáo, he requested the Master to occupy the seat of division (fēnzuò). That night, he had a dream of a majestic figure...

The person wearing official robes and cap presented him with a bundle of *máo* grass. The following day, a special envoy from Qingliang in Mingzhou arrived. The Master accepted the invitation and entered the monastery.
Upon seeing the shrine of the local deity, he found that its surname was *Máo* and that its attire was no different from what he had dreamed of in the past.
He ascended the seat to expound the Dharma, offering a single incense stick to Pò'ān. After three years, he moved to Jiaoshan; after one year, he moved to Xuedou. Another three...

In his [seventh] year, by imperial decree, he was transferred to the Yuyang Monastery. Three years later, after concluding the retreat at Shaolin on Mount Song, the Emperor appointed him to succeed to the abbacy at Jing Mountain.
The following year, the temple was destroyed by fire; the Master had anticipated this event and remained unmoved in countenance, maintaining his composure.

In the tenth month of winter that year, an edict was issued summoning him into the inner court. The Emperor received him in the Xiuzheng Hall, where the Master’s responses were detailed and clear. The Emperor...
Moved by his virtuous appearance, [the Emperor] bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe and summoned him to enter the Ciming Hall, where he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor listened from behind a curtain and was greatly pleased; he conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Fojian. Three years later, the temple was completed.

After six years, it was again destroyed by fire, yet with the arrival of many helpers like clouds, it was restored to its former splendor within a few years. Forty *li* from the temple, he built a residence.
There were one hundred pillars, where travelers from all quarters were received; the plaque above the gate read "Ten Thousand Years of Righteous Continuity" (Wànnián Zhèngxù).

Several hundred paces to the west of Zhèngxù, a hermitage was constructed as a repository for sacred treasures. A multi-storied pavilion was erected above it to house the imperial calligraphies bestowed upon the monastery throughout its history.

To the east and west of the spacious hall, altars were established to honor the ancestral patriarchs and the spirits of former generations. On the anniversary of the founder’s birthday, a Buddhist service of feeding the Sangha was performed.

To augment their posthumous merit, the ancestral sacrifices of the milk-masters of Shu had consequently been discontinued; [the Emperor] established a shrine to honor them, thereby manifesting filial devotion and longing. Upon hearing of this, the Sovereign sighed with admiration.
Entering the hall, he said: "Name cannot be grasped, form cannot be grasped, taking is impossible, letting go is impossible—only thus can it be attained. But tell me, what is it that is attained?
"What is this? Three people have taken a tortoise and turned it into a soft-shelled turtle.
Regarding this, Shicheng’s verse says: "The rolling red pearls are not blood from the eyes; paper ashes are dyed to become flower-butterflies."
Since the dream ended and consciousness was severed like that of Zhuang Zhou, scattered jinnian coins have drifted like yellow leaves.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "If one discusses this matter, it is truly simple and easy to understand; it is mostly people who themselves create difficulties."
This creates an obstacle for oneself. Thus, when I usually see people on the east or west corridors bowing and greeting me, I simply lower my head to receive them;
there is truly nothing else to it. It is simply that I want everyone to recognize that this old monk is a native of Longqing Prefecture in Xichuan.
If you recognize me, I shall speak some of our local dialect with you and tell you some stories.
Local dialect. For now, let us not speak of your recognition of the Elder. First, each of you must know your own native place.
Do you know it? Mingzhou has six counties; Fenghua has eight districts.
Ascending the hall: Under the gate of Wufeng, there is not a single thing of the hundred kinds. The meditation seat is cramped; the offerings in the hall are meager.
What you step upon with your feet is nothing but broken bricks and shattered tiles. What you run straight into before your face is Wang Gela and Li Mahu.
With such meager merit as I have, I dwell in the mountains; I truly bring shame upon the sages of old. (After a long silence) Nevertheless, let me clarify this further.
He ascended the hall and said: "The summer retreat is now complete; there is nothing left undone. Thus, we have bowls from Suifu and porcelain cups from Gongzhou."
In the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era, the Master built a dwelling by the Moonlight Pond and inscribed it with the name "Retiring from Plow.

He requested retirement from the court, but his chronic illness happened to flare up. On the first day of the third month of the Jiyou year, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "This mountain monk is both old and ill;
I lack the strength to engage in idle chatter with you all here and there. Today, I have exerted myself to come forth to speak once more of what has been said before."
"It cannot be reached. I shall now fully shake it out for all of you. He then rose from his seat, shook his robe, and asked, "How much is there?
Thereupon, he returned to the abbot’s quarters.
On the fifteenth day, he assembled the community to arrange his final affairs. He personally wrote several dozen posthumous petitions and letters, speaking and laughing as usual.
When his disciples requested a parting verse, the Master took up his brush and wrote: "When coming, empty and desolate; when departing, bare and naked.
If you wish to ask for the ultimate point, there is the Stone Bridge at Tiantai. Having finished the verse, he passed away within a short while.
Donglin’s verse says: The battle ended, he leans on the tower with a heroic laugh; Head and tail of the tiger are both brought under control.
People of this age do not recognize the colors of wind and clouds; When struck on the back of the head, who can know shame?

The First Generation of Jingshan (the Seventeenth Generation under Linji):
Chan Master Duangqiao Miaolun of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai in Taizhou, successor to Chan Master Jingshan Fan. His secular surname was Xu; he was a native of Huangyan in Taizhou.
Her mother, Lady Liu, became pregnant after dreaming of the moon. At the age of eighteen, she received the tonsure at the Guangci Monastery in Yongjia. There she met Guyuan at Ruiyan;
hearing the "three pounds of flax" koan, she harbored doubts. One day, she visited Yunju and happened to see Shantang reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage that says, "Even mosquitoes, gnats, and ants have no speech, yet they are able to perform their tasks," she attained sudden enlightenment.
The Master went to Xuedou to study under Fojian. Fojian asked him, "Why does a dog have karmic consciousness?
and had the Master offer responses thirty times; none were in accord with the truth. The Master said, "Is there no expedient means? Fojian cited a verse by Zhenjing:
"To say 'karmic consciousness remains' / Who would say the meaning is not profound? / When the ocean dries up, its bottom is finally seen; / When a person dies, their mind is not known. The Master...
He stood motionless for a long while. Suddenly, he heard a voice from his own mouth, and sweat poured down his entire body.
Thereupon, he attained a sudden realization. Jing Shan offered this verse: "A leaking roof meets with rain through the night; Adding further sorrow, mist locks the thatched gate."
Suddenly the clouds vanish and the solitary orb surges forth; layered green mountains thrust toward the distant heights.
A verse by Yichu says: A single blow to the crown of the head, sweat like oil; The old Zhaozhou of those days was caught and defeated.
Thus, the Yellow River is exhausted down to its very bottom; With every sudden rain, there is another wave of sorrow.
Tianyan composed this eulogy, saying: Exhausting every mechanism, one seeks to reach the limit; A single strike of the sounding board opens the crown of the head.
Pushing open the azure void, a thousand fathoms of pines appear; Releasing the golden crow, crimson at the hour of midnight.
Lotus Hermit Yan’s verse says: In the third month of spring, orioles warble amidst the green thickets; The father of Huan (Yin Xi) strolls leisurely to the east of the Wei River.
After all, there are those who covet the fragrant bait; Henceforth, I shall rejoice that my efforts are not spent in vain.
Longmen’s Verse on Nature says: The battle clouds gather at dawn as the wind howls in rage; The ant-hill pierces through the pearl, the combat grows ever higher.
Seeking to flee, the thief has nowhere to go; With a single leap of his horse, he breaks through to the heavens.

The *Duo-song* (Bell-Praise) for Protecting the Nation says: A young lord in brocade robes, intoxicated at a rustic farmstead, leans upon the railing and opens his chest to gaze at the setting clouds.
Suddenly, the wind turns and the lotus leaves stir; in the heart of the pond, a single flower-bud alone is revealed.
Shimen’s Cloud Verse says: Meeting face-to-face, we hold hands and stroll through the imperial street; The springtime splendor spreads across four hundred prefectures.
From tail to head of the lightning-flash, a single thread runs through; The black wind turns over the fishing boat.
Fojian presented his master with this verse of dharma-transmission: "The Absolute Truth is as straight as a string; What need is there for speech, and what need for silence?

I now entrust it well to you; The mind’s essence is fundamentally unattainable. Fujian then moved to Yuyang Monastery, where the Master shared the seat with him. Later, they moved from Jetavana to Ruiyan.
Later, he resided at Jingci Monastery. In his quarters, he would occasionally test his students by using the phrase "The myriad dharmas return to the One.
If anyone’s response did not accord with the truth, he would immediately drive them out; it was here that he caused them to lose their "eyes."
Jingshan Jin said: "Old man Duqiao was certainly well-intentioned, yet he cannot avoid ruining the sons and daughters of others' families.
Although Fengge lost his eyes, his kindness remains difficult to repay. Jinding wishes to ask:"
"Great Assembly, what is 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'? Where does the One return? "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind. Donglin said:
"The ancient Buddhas bestowed their compassion; every fragment of their blood-stained hearts is revealed, like Ciming setting down his sword, or Bimozhi [brandishing his staff]."
Holding up a staff, Linji would shout as soon as someone entered the gate; Deshan would strike with his staff as soon as someone entered the gate.
Through such various expedients, he sought to have people exhaust their thieving minds and fall into no path of escape. Ruiyan was adept at setting tiger traps to ensnare all under heaven.
Gao Feng thus lost his eyes; it was much like stumbling upon a prize on level ground. Yet, fundamentally, he did not recognize that "the myriad dharmas return to the One.
Jing Shan’s extensive verse says: "Going out at dawn, returning at evening; Barefoot and with disheveled hair, his face covered in ash."
Boiling rice-less porridge in a bottomless cauldron; the stench of smoke billows as the flame-tip blows.
Entering the hall: Deshan bows his head; Jiaxian nods his head; Jueyi raises a finger; Xuansha strikes and breaks off his own toe. Holding up his staff, he says:
"All of these do not go beyond the tip of this mountain monk’s staff. How do you see it?"
He obtained it. Holding up his staff, Zhuo said, "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the whole world.
Xijue Rui said, "Deshan bowing his head is like marking the boat to find the sword. Jia Shan nodding his head is like gouging out flesh to create a sore.
Juzhi raising a finger is like branding a cow by planting horns on it. Xuansha striking and breaking his own toe..."
By what cause is this attained? Does the Great Assembly truly understand the teaching of loyalty at the tip of the staff?
When the solitary moon shines upon the mountains and peaks, how many people can find rest within this?
Master Mu’s eulogy says: "The extraordinary and the hundred wonders / Are found within a single hair-tip. / Cast away the hair-tip and look:
/ Frost-flakes in the sixth month’s cold. His praise for Master Jun says:
"How many painted pavilions and jade towers? / How many flower-strewn streets and willow-lined alleys? / From beginning to end..."
He spoke this to a traveler; it was generally circulated throughout the streets of Chang’an.
Ji Bei Hong Song said: "The west wind arrived last night at the wutong trees; The famous gardens have fallen into decay, yet my thoughts remain unrefined."
The bridegroom and his wife have not yet been permitted to return; the curtains and blinds lean against the red *liǎo'é* flowers.
The *Lóngmén Yuān* praises this, saying: "Under fine rain and slanting wind, a single-leaf boat; that fellow displays his cleverness, knowing no rest."
A single sound of a shepherd’s flute echoes through the secluded valley; from before the marshy banks of red *liǎo* flowers, white gulls take flight.
Ascending the hall, he cites the occasion for Yunmen’s address to the assembly: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
He offers this verse: Faintly, from the smoke-filled village, the barking of dogs is heard; Seeking to find it, one sees no person.
At home, he suddenly encountered a place where the bridge was broken and the stream receded, from which three or four blossoms of a green peach flowed out.
He ascended the hall and cited the karmic occasion of Ciming’s practice room, wherein a single sword, a pair of straw sandals, and a basin of water were placed.
The verse says: Amidst a thicket of a hundred flowers, he gallops past on his whip; how much brilliance and elegance there is!
When a scholar who has not yet passed the examinations looks upon this with his own eyes, his breast is filled with an old sorrow that he can do nothing to dispel.

Ascending the hall, he said: "In the Jingshan Mountains there is jade, yet those who obtain it do not find it within the mountains themselves. In the Red Waters there is a pearl, yet those who pick it up do not find it within the waters themselves.
Zen monks possess the 'True Person of No Rank,' yet those who realize it find its entrance and exit through the gate of the face.
He suddenly took up his staff and asked, "Do you understand? A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangtze River in Youzhou."

Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Daguan Ying’s instruction to the assembly: "The Seven Buddhas are the subjects of one's nature; the myriad dharmas are the slaves of one's mind. But tell me, where is the master?
He then gave a shout himself, saying, "From the Seven Buddhas downward, all have shown their heads! Then he nodded himself, saying, "Each shall attend to his own duties.
The Master said, "To call the Seven Buddhas 'subjects of one's nature' and to point to the myriad dharmas as 'slaves of the mind'—this is Daguan himself."
This refers to having a path that leads out of the body, as well as responding with "yes" and "no" in a natural and straightforward manner. Furthermore, these are matters pertaining to a slave;
when has the master ever even dreamed of them? Do you all wish to see? With his whisk, he made a single sweep and said:
"At dawn, a spring breeze stirs, and throughout the gardens, a hundred varieties of flowers bloom."
Yuet-tang Yin went to consult with the Master. The Master asked, "Is it true that Linji received three severe blows from Huangbo? He replied, "Yes.
The Master said, "Why then did he punch Da-yu in the ribs three times? He replied, "When one receives an ox from another, one returns a horse to them.
The Master nodded in approval. Yin bowed.
One day, when the Master entered the hall, he saw Yuan sitting upright and motionless. The Master blew upon his ear;
Yuan opened his eyes wide and looked at the Master, intending to speak. The Master let out a thunderous shout. Later, Yuan said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter.
In the past, when I was struck by a single shout from Jingci, my soul was scattered and my spirit dispersed."

As he approached his death, he gathered the assembly and entered his room. He wrote a letter bidding farewell to the various monasteries and the Duke of Wei. When the Duke sent medicine as a gift, he would not accept it.

The Duke again dispatched a messenger to ask, "The Master was born at Tiantai; why have you died at Jingci? The Master replied, "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. He then composed a verse and passed away.
Kim Myeong-uk said, "If Jingci answers the question in such a manner, he cannot avoid being seen through by the secular official.
Yi Lin Nengbie said, "If one does not answer in such a manner, one is likewise seen through by the secular official."
Chan Master Fāngshān Bǎo of Ruìyán in Tàizhōu,
the second-generation successor of Chan Master Tiāntái Lún of Jìngshān, was the son of the Gè clan of Tányáng. While traveling with his father on official duty, one day—

While providing alms for the monastic community at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou, he happened to read the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*. It felt as though it were something he had practiced in the past.

He then recounted the karmic conditions regarding the robe and bowl of Huangmei and asked Chan Master Gong: "Since he did not understand the Buddha-dharma, why did he succeed to the patriarchal seat?"
Gong said, "Not only the Patriarch; there are many who do not understand the Buddha-dharma yet still succeed to the Patriarchal seat.
The Master asked, "Does the Abbot also succeed to the Patriarchal seat? Gong replied, "If one succeeds to the Patriarchal seat, then one understands the Buddha-dharma."
Huanglong Wushang Lingshang said, "How great and small is Jingci! His answers to questions are never finished.
Jiansou Shi said, "Jingci is much like one who, though wealthy, complains that a thousand mouths are too few; or one who, though poor, laments that he has too many bodies."
Fojian was residing at Mount Jing by imperial decree. The Master, together with Tianjie Ri and others, formed a group to go and study under him, and they all attained his essential instructions.
One day, a doubt suddenly arose regarding Xinghua’s saying, "Coming from the four quarters and the eight directions. He then requested further instruction from Fojian, who said:
"The old monk cannot explain it for you; you must look for it yourself. The Master requested further instruction up to two times, but he was never told anything.
He was directed to visit Shiqiao. Following these instructions, the Master went there and exhausted all his mental faculties and methods, yet Shiqiao refused him every time.

The Master investigated with fierce determination, requesting further instruction eleven times. One evening, sitting upright in meditation, he suddenly beheld a lamp light before him, and his mind opened up in a flash of clarity.

The next morning, they entered the abbot’s quarters. Bridge said, "You have caught the thief. The Master prostrated and said, "The thief has already been apprehended; I ask the Abbot to inspect the stolen goods.
Bridge raised the phrase, "All dharmas return to One," but the Master’s answer was not accepted either. After the midday meal, there was a communal work assignment (*fǔqǐng*).
The Master had forgotten what he was holding in his hand. Jiaomeng picked up a radish root and showed it to him, saying, "What is this? Thereupon, the Master attained great enlightenment.

Later, when Yuan Tong finished his retreat and entered the hall for formal instruction, he raised the karmic incident of Jiaomeng picking up the radish root that led Fangshan to his great enlightenment.
He asked, "Furthermore, tell me: where did you find your strength? Yuan Tong replied, "Fangshan was in the Buddha."
The mirror attains its substance; the stone bridge attains its function. Like wind blowing over water, ripples form naturally.
If one were to say that awakening lies in the roots of the *xian* plant, one would bury the predecessors of old. Deep inquiry leads to true assent.
Jingshan submitted this verse: "Plucking up the root of amaranth, the hair on one's skin stands on end; Needlessly seeking a scar from cauterization upon healthy flesh.
Having realized the true secret of the single transmission, Before the wind, everything is a life-giving elixir."
Donglin’s verse says: To the very end he clings to his saddle, refusing to rest; On the open plain he seizes the drum, seeking to become a marquis.
The moment he picks up the medicinal herbs by the roadside, He transforms into an immortal and ascends to the wine tower.
Shimen’s Cloud Verse says: Washing clean the common bones, leaping through the Dragon Gate; Shaking the mane and raising the tail, surging at the vital ford.
Beyond that shore, one does not dwell in formless images; Let the precious treasury remain as it is, content in its own poverty.
The verse of Master Qiaofu on the Dharma states: "Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; delusion and awakening are sought within oneself.

Remembering my youth, I now realize I have grown old without even noticing. He succeeded to the seat of Master Qiao. Whenever a monk entered his room, he would generally raise his whisk and ask, "What is this?
If the monk hesitated, he would strike him out directly. For twenty years, few were able to grasp his vital point.
Master Yijian Ji of Huangyan said: "The gateways of the ancients were established in such a manner;
nowadays, people wag their tails and beg for pity, fearing only that the ants will not perceive the stench or the flies will not come to the filth."
Shimen Yun said, "As for the teachers and monks, once they have recognized the whisk, what then? After a long silence, he snapped his fingers once.
Jinming Xu commented on Shimen’s words: "Having recognized the whisk, one buys straw sandals and sets out on pilgrimage."
Wujingdeng entered for an interview. The Master held up his whisk and asked, "What is this? Wujingdeng also said, "What is this?
The Master said, "Remove the four great elements for me and speak another phrase. Wujingdeng walked from east to west. The Master extended his left foot;
Wujingdeng walked from west to east. The Master extended his right foot. Wujingdeng stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. The Master then took his whisk and—

"What has ever been lacking? They all replied, "Since nothing is lacking, why did Shen Guang stand in the snow and cut off his arm?
The Master said, "He did so only to ruin his family and exhaust his wealth. At these words, they all attained great enlightenment.
A monk asked, "The waters of Caoxi flow stream after stream toward the east; why does the water at Ruiyan flow toward the west? The Master said, "You, Senior, do not recognize good from evil.

The monk said, "I have been asking about water; why do you say I do not recognize good from evil? The Master said, "You blind fellow truly do not recognize it! and struck him. Another asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "A fugitive committing a crime at night. Another asked. The Master said, "A fugitive committing a crime at night. [End of excerpt]
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "You have precisely seized upon my itchy spot.
A monk asked, "What is the essence of *prajñā*? The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone. The monk asked, "What is the function of *prajñā*?
The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone rolling through empty space."
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: fanning fierce flames within the great chiliocosm, a single snowflake falls directly before us;
wielding tongs and hammers within the wondrous and secret arena, iron is transmuted into gold therein. Upon the red sand dunes, amidst the mountains of Staff Grove.
Every single one of you eats arsenic and drinks lethal poison; you walk upon jagged ice and tread upon the edge of a sword.
As it is said, "In the boiling cauldron, there is no place that is cold. You all cling to withered paulownia wood and guard over dead ashes; when will the beans ever burst?
Today, Xianan adds charcoal to the furnace for you all—put forth your best effort!

Ascending the hall, he held his staff horizontally across his chest and looked at the assembly, saying, "This and that—this and that. He then descended from the seat. Ascending the hall again, he said:
"The sentiments of the various sages remain; the net of views is difficult to penetrate. No stages are established; for vast eons there has been no gate.
The wisdom of Prajñā is ever-luminous, and the essence of True Suchness is uniquely revealed. Yet scholars everywhere have minds that are not clear, all because—"
Devious teachers muddle the teachings like silkworms weaving cocoons or snakes clinging to their burrows; they claim to have reached the destination and refuse to meet others.
Among them, there are those with clever intellects who engage in speculative reasoning, taking a vague approximation for true suchness and a hazy semblance for buddha-nature—truly pitiable!

The Master resided at Ruiyan and constantly posed three questions to test his students, saying: "Those who are truly outstanding and of the highest caliber are like fine horses that gallop upon seeing the shadow of a whip;

A person who steers an iron boat across the bottom of the sea—why do they cry out in distress within the eye of a needle?
Master Heng of Jizhu Xiao-yue composed this verse: The Yellow River stretches far into the white clouds;

Obscured by grime, I happened to pass through the golden palace; my body stretched across, trailing the incense smoke from the imperial burner.

Chan Master Juexiang’s Verse on Dongshan’s “Not at Ease”: Dongshan has a path leading through Yunyan; At the point of total severance, it is difficult for one to pass through.
When a living road is opened at the tip of the staff, One then knows there is not a hair’s breadth of separation.
Chan Master Zhuyu Jian’s Verse on “Mount Gu’s Holy Arrow”: The young lad with double reins makes his jade steed neigh; His pale white spring robe is encircled by a green sash.
Returning at midnight beneath the flowers under the moon, He strikes with his golden whip, and scattered red petals fly.
Chan Master Zangshi Huizhen composed a verse on Dongshan’s parting from Yunyan: He dug up a single grave in Lantian; Coral and agate were used to adorn it.
Let the donkeys and horses carry it away—do not call it a treasure; Calamity will reach the descendants until the entire clan is extinguished.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'a fire burning the mountains in the twelfth lunar month'? The Master said, "Searching everywhere, not a single blade of grass is found.
Cen Gui Chan Master of Zhushan was exceptionally unconventional. One day, while visiting Foyan, he heard the sound of wind chimes on the corner of the hall;
leaning on his staff, he passed away. Upon cremation, countless śarīras were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa to the west of Foyan.
Chan Master Wujian Xiandou of Tiantai in Taizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ruoyan Bao, the third patriarch of the Jing Mountain lineage.
He was a native of the Ye family in Xianju, Tai prefecture, during the Song dynasty. The *Xian*... [text continues]
Chun was born on the sixth day of the fifth month in the year of Yichou. From his youth, he possessed a sharp and brilliant disposition and was fond of reading;
he could recite a day’s worth of texts by the end of that very day. One day, his father met with the śramaṇa Śānagong, who passed by and recognized him, saying, "This is a vessel of the Dharma.

You should not let him remain stagnant in the local village. His father, filled with reverence and faith, agreed to this. By the time Chun reached the age of twenty, he followed the Venerable Hǒu of Gūtán to receive the tonsure and become a monk.

At Tianning Monastery in the commandery, he ascended the high seat and appointed [the Master] to serve as an attendant. Morning and evening, he advanced in this Way, and later attended Fangan at Xianan.
The Master asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Fangan opened his mouth and thrust out his tongue to show him.
The Master was at a loss for what to do. Xishan drove him out with his staff. He went to visit Tianfeng Zhen; before he had even finished recounting the previous dialogue, Zhen also struck him.
He returned to Xishan’s West Hermitage. On the road, while holding onto a slippery surface, he attained realization.
Upon meeting Xishan, Xishan asked, "Why have you returned so quickly? The Master said, "At that time, you could not strike me, Reverend. Xishan asked, "What did Tianfeng tell you?"
"Ma! The Master recounted the circumstances from his journey on the road, and Mount Shan struck him again.
Weifan Qi said, "Fangshan’s way of holding up the teaching can truly be called brilliant throughout ancient and modern times.
Had it not been for Huading being a descendant of Linji, he would have nearly broken through Caizhou."
Shimen’s Verse on the Clouds says: The first arrow has sunk to the west; the situation is already perilous. Adding another arrow breaks the heavy siege.
How many have been captured alive with a mere twitch? Yet they still hold the bow-end as they accompany their wine cups.
The Master built a dwelling on Mount Huading and exhorted himself with rigorous asceticism. While engaged in manual labor, his doubts were suddenly and completely resolved.

He went to the Western Hermitage to present his realization. Upon seeing him, Mountain [Shishuang Qingzhu] was immediately in accord with him and bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "This mind is infinitely vast; Even empty space cannot be compared to it.
This Way is exactly like this: Receive and uphold it; cease seeking elsewhere."
The Verse on Harmonizing Reality says: The ninefold elixir of immortality still transforms into cinnabar; Purple mists enshroud the walls as the myriad stars cluster together.
Splitting open the golden cauldron, flames erupt; Pouring it out makes heaven and earth shiver with cold.
Wanfeng Wei had long served at the Master’s seat. The Master asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?
Wei stepped forward, paid his respects, and stood with his hands joined. The Master asked, "What is the Way? Wei replied, "The Way is not something that can be spoken of. The Master said:
[The Master] said, "I do not say 'it exists. What do you say? Weiyue replied, "I am precisely wanting the Master to have doubts.
The Master said, "To have doubts is an error. Weiyue said, "To have no doubts is also an error. The Master then gave a shout; Weiyue also gave a shout. The Master said, "A word has no second echo."
Weiyi shook his sleeves and departed.
He addressed the assembly: "The wind is cold and crisp; the sun is bright and clear. The *campaka* flowers bloom, their fragrance filling the road; in a single night, spring grass grows in the pond.
How pitiable and yet how laughable is Old Gautama! For forty-nine years he said nothing that could reach it. A-he-he! He struck [the meditation seat].
A single strike upon the meditation seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, the Buddhas of the three periods and the entire Great Canon of teachings cannot fully explain it;

the elder monks throughout the land cannot lift it up. Even if one possessed the eloquence that overturns the ocean and the spiritual mechanism that topples the mountains, not even a single speck [of it could be grasped]."
It is of no use. O worthy ones! When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; when hot, seek the cool; when cold, face the fire. Each is truly genuine;

each is luminously wondrous. If you can take a step forward, then discussing Zen and discussing the Way will be like mistaking fish eyes for pearls or misidentifying orange peel as fire. Have you not heard it said: "The great capacity must penetrate"?
"Chè! Great function must be direct. Not knowing Old Confucius of the Eastern House, you instead seek ritual and music in another land.
He struck the ground with his staff and said, "Wrong! He then raised the case of Layman Pang asking Master Mazu: "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single mouth; then I will tell you."
The Master said, "The Way! A man of cultivation has an awakening. He then offered this verse: "To swallow up the Western River in a single gulp, The partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers.
Even if one were to directly accept it at once, It would still be more than ten thousand miles away from the white clouds."
Small Sermon: The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate. It is like seeking a form in a dream or grasping at the moon in water.
The Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter perfect luminosity. It is like catching a mouse and breaking an oil jar.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very Dharma. Since they themselves have no wounds, do not injure them. Within the state beyond calculation—

It is turned into calculation. Within that which has no path, it is turned into a path. Little do they realize that the slaughterhouse and the wine shop fully manifest the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas;
the bustling marketplace and the red dust reveal the very core of the Patriarchs. If you can bring this up, one clarifies three;
with eyes attuned to the subtlest weight, how could it be anything less than ten thousand miles of white clouds? *Sha!* Flowers bloom and fall, left to the wind. By oneself—
A fragrant scent filled the heavens and the earth. He showed it to Xu Zhigong.
During the long summer, we were able to dwell together; amidst the crags and beneath the pines, whether speaking a word or remaining silent, our joy was beyond measure.
Now tell me: is this the same as, or different from, the ancients who during the summer did not hear the two characters "zhengyin" (the true cause)? Please speak.
If Zhigong utters a single turning word, you must look before the pivot; otherwise, you are not yet among the elite.
In the past, Fenyang consulted over seventy virtuous teachers, but it was only after meeting Shoushan that he asked: "What is the meaning behind Baizhang’s folding of the mat? Shoushan replied:
"The dragon’s sleeve sweeps it open, and the whole body is revealed. Fengyan asked again, "What is your meaning, Master? Shishuang said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox.
At these words, Fengyang attained great enlightenment. Rising from his prostrations, he said: "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool."
Only after repeated searching and probing did he finally come to understand. A monk standing nearby asked, "What principle have you seen that you have thus come to accept it yourself?
Wufeng said, "This is precisely where I let go of my body and relinquish my life. He continued, "Look at the ancients; they never consented to ending their practice prematurely.

Even if one has some realization while studying Chan, if one does not seek out a teacher, it is called 'deluded Chan. If the traces of awakening are not eliminated," [the practice remains incomplete].

It becomes a cage and a trap; everywhere it acts as a restriction. Though one sits within the realm of supreme excellence, those of former generations called this the "falcon-scented cloth shirt," which is most difficult to cast off. You should examine this with utmost care:
first, you must not make your livelihood within the ghost-cave beneath Black Mountain; second, you must not play with a ball upon a rushing torrent. The four dignified postures—
Within the ritual practice, apply yourself with urgency and diligence. Suddenly, when you break through the gateway of the face, you will realize it is simply the person of old;
there is not a single thread or speck of dust that acts as an obstruction or hindrance. Words are many, yet the Way is far—strive on!
Testament on the First Day of the Fifth Month in the Year of Jiashu (1334), Yuan Tong: "You who have left the household life must practice the conduct of those who have left the household life.
You must reflect upon the four debts of gratitude that are difficult to repay, and the offerings of the faithful that are difficult to digest. Strive with all your might to hold the Way as paramount;

do not let your time pass in vain. Regarding the property of the Sangha throughout the ten directions, for the sake of the elderly and the infirm, you must not engage in competition or harbor the notions of self and other, thereby increasing [afflictions]."
Ignorance breeds contention and disputes over right and wrong. Guard against this; be cautious! Tomorrow, trouble the assembly to perform the cremation early.
There is no need to shave the head, nor is it necessary to bathe. A single brazier of fierce fire will suffice for a thousand times over.

The verse he spoke on the second day of the second month when bidding farewell to the world reads: "The phrase of immediate realization is not hindered by being brought forth; as the void collapses, Mount Sumeru dances.
He passed away suddenly at the age of seventy and with fifty years of monastic seniority (*kṣaṇa*). On the ninth day after his death, his body was cremated, and his relics were collected.
A stupa was erected to the west of the monastery, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Miaoming Zhenjue. The stupa was named...
Jiguang. Chan Master Ling of Yiyuan at Fengshan in Hangzhou studied under Fangshan at Ruiyan and served as the Hall Superintendent (*tangsi*).

One day, while entering the master’s room for instruction, he requested clarification on the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman and attained realization. Later, while presiding over the assembly at Fengshan, he ascended the hall and spoke, citing the world...
The Case of the Venerable One Ascending the Seat and Mañjuśrī Striking the Gavel. The Master said: "The World-Honored One has already spoken erroneously;
Mañjuśrī has already transmitted erroneously; I, Xinfengshan, today have already raised this erroneously. Do you understand? 'When a character is transcribed three times, it becomes a horse.'"
Chan Master Yuanzhan of Songyan in Mingzhou had long studied under Juexiang. Later, he visited Fangshan and attained the essential meaning [of the Dharma].
While traveling, he happened upon Songyan in Mingzhou; captivated by its purity and excellence, he could not bear to leave.

He then sat cross-legged upon a rock, whereupon two tigers suddenly appeared, crouching at his side as if to guard him. The Master commanded them to lie down and leaned back against their backs to sleep soundly.

The mountain folk marveled at this; they established a monastery on that very spot to house him. The Master did not involve himself in worldly affairs, remaining as tranquil and indifferent as possible beyond his Dharma-giving.
When he was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly and, approaching his coffin, spoke this verse: "Bathing and donning robes, the funeral rites are complete;
Sitting cross-legged in peaceful meditation, I enter the coffin to be concealed. Flowers bloom upon the iron tree, the clay ox bellows; A single moon shines eternally in the heavens."

The light from the ground then manifested again, and he said to the assembly, "Fifteen years hence, this temple shall be consumed by fire; if you open the reliquary chamber, the fire may be extinguished.
When the appointed time arrived, it was indeed so. The assembly collectively opened the chamber; the Master’s countenance and spirit were as if alive, and his nails and hair had grown long.
Zen Master Wujin Zudeng of Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Wang family of Siming.
He studied under Master Rixi Yong at Tianning Temple and asked about the great matter of birth and death and the swiftness of impermanence, requesting instruction.

Rixi said, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, investigate this closely and secretly. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again. The Master raised his voice and said, "There is none!"
He was always swift. "The matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, Xī gave a shout. The Master immediately prostrated.
Xī asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself thus? The Master replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Xī nodded his head in approval.
Subsequently, the Master traveled to Fāngshān, where he received the Dharma. He planted his staff atop Yúnfēng Mountain and did not venture beyond the mountains for fifty years.

On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested slight illness. When it was nearly midnight, he looked toward his attendants and asked, "Is the sky beginning to brighten?
They replied, "Not yet. Someone asked, "What will you do at such a time, O Master? The Master broke into a smile and said:
Formerly, when Deshan was sitting in illness, a monk asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? Deshan said, "There is. The monk asked, "Who is this one who does not fall ill?
Deshan said, "A-ye, a-ye. The Master [Linji] remained silent for a long while and then said, "Can such a thing as this be called being ill?"
The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "The physical body is impermanent; seek realization early. The time has come; I am about to depart.
The attendant held up paper and requested a verse. The Master said, "Is it that one cannot die unless there is a verse? When the attendant’s request was insistent, the Master then wrote this verse:
"Arising and ceasing, coming and going, Are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. I have toppled the five Sumerus."
Suddenly, he became vast and empty, with no sense of front or back. He set down his writing brush, sat upright, and passed away.
Layman Ding had long practiced the craft of acupuncture under Master Fangshan, hoping to clarify his fundamental nature.
However, Fangshan did nothing but strike east and west, occasionally reviling those from other quarters; whatever he said was that "this old monk" was merely a vulgar fellow of common custom.
"I do not wish to strike you with evil poison. On the first day of the fourth month, Dingliu attained realization. He wrote a verse and presented it to Shanshan:
"Lift it up! Lift it up! Let it go! Let it go! This point of radiance illuminates heaven and earth.
Shanshan rejoiced in his pure and simple practice and thus granted him formal approval (*inka*).

The Fourth Generation Dharma Heir of Jing Mountain under Chan Master Tian Tai Du was Chan Master Baiyun Zhidu of Fulin Monastery in Chuzhou. His surname was Wu; he was a native of Lishui in that commandery. At the age of fifteen—

He received the tonsure from the provisional Chan Master [Jingqing Daofu] and practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) deeply. He traveled extensively to consult various masters, yet none could satisfy his mind.
He returned once more to Baiyun in his native village, where he built a dwelling on the old site of Chan Master Cheng and resided there. Later, he visited Xifeng at Jingci Temple.
Neither [of these] was in accord. Later, while attending Wu Jian, the Master asked, "I do not yet understand the secret intent of the West;
how is it? Jian said, "Wait until Mount Śāla nods its head, and I will tell you. As the Master gestured with his hand as if about to answer, Jian gave a shout. The Master said:
At the summit of Mount Sāla, white waves surged to the heavens. Flowers bloomed after芒種 (Mangzhong), and leaves fell before立秋 (Liqiu).
[Zhao]jian said, "In my house, there is no leftover soup or stale rice. The Master said, "What else could this be but leftover soup and stale rice?
Jian nodded his head. The Master prostrated himself.

Yilin Neng said: "On that day, there was no one to see the Patriarch topple Mount Hua and crush three hundred and eighty-four families of the Central Kingdom (Zhixian Shenzhou), leaving even the Great Spirit (Juling) unable to raise his hands in protest.
Now, in upholding the essential principles of Linji and the core tenets of the Stone Bridge, he causes hundreds of thousands of millions of Śāla peaks to..."
He nodded his head. Yet he had not yet granted him permission. Why? "To change the bones and wash the entrails, one must reorganize;
though the whole body is eyes, one must still investigate.
Shimen Yun’s verse says: "Zhang Qian trampled the summit of Mount Kunlun; clouds lock the hanging river, and ice freezes the ferry."
Fortunately, the long winds beyond the kalpas still exist; in one moment they blow the spring of Shanglin Park into full bloom.
Jin Mingxu’s verse says: Weeping as he sets out on his desperate journey, he encounters a sudden rain; clinging to his saddle, he reaches Chang’an at the cost of his life.
At Longtou, the songs of victory resound in the Hall of the Divine; the mountains and rivers of the myriad nations are seen as a single unified realm.
He presented the Master with a verse, saying: "The ultimate greatness is this mind; the ultimate sagehood is this Dharma. Lamp after lamp, their light does not err."

Having realized this mind, Daoshi took his leave. As he was departing, [Nanyue] instructed him, saying: "In the past, Nanyue received the prediction and transmission from Dajian; later, he obtained the mind-dharma from Mazu.
Their meeting was like a needle meeting its eye—there was no need for many words. Do not wag your three-inch tongue to deceive people;
you must possess true and correct insight and manifest it in your conduct. Only then will you be able to repay the profound kindness of the Buddha. Daoshi received these instructions with reverence.
After a long time, he went again to Changsha to visit Fangpu at Yunju and paid his respects to Xiaoyin Da. In the Jiamu year of the Zhizheng era, he returned to Folin.

He subsequently presided over Longquan Puci and was later transferred to Wufeng. The Prefectural Governor, He Mian, came to consult him. The Master recounted how Baiyun had said to the Fifth Patriarch:
"There were several Chan practitioners who came from Mount Lu; they all possessed realization. When I asked them to speak about it..."
It is also said that there is a source for this. When he presents the causal conditions and questions him, the student also understands clearly;

he is taught to descend into awakening and he indeed succeeds in descending. Yet, it is simply not yet complete. Since there is already an entry into awakening, why is it not yet complete? The Hermit smiled.
The Master said, "The Fifth Patriarch said, 'Because of this, I broke into a cold sweat all over my body and thereby understood the clear breeze that descends in a cart. How about you?"
Miaoyan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Layman, be careful. Miaoyan did not look back.
[The Master] then asked Yuantong, "Baiyun says, 'Carrying a pure breeze on my shoulder,' and Miaoyan shakes his sleeves and departs—what is the meaning of this?
Yuantong said, "How do you understand it? [The Master] said, "Is it not the place where he relinquishes his life?"
Mo Tong said, "So it is, so it is. Bashi offered this verse in praise:
"Having found the Peach Blossom Spring, one might well avoid Qin; Unexpectedly, however, rebels come to invade.
Now, as a lone horse passes before the stream, The regret for the ruined state and fallen house grows ever deeper."
Donglin’s verse says: A single melody on the level sands spreads as the wild geese settle; The "Yangchun" and "Baixue" are ultimately difficult to harmonize.
Since Ziqi has departed, there is no one who understands; How much resentment must this withered paulownia endure?

In the *jǐyǒu* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued summoning eminent monks from throughout the realm to convene a Dharma assembly at Mount Jiangshan. The Master responded to the summons;

once the affairs of the assembly were concluded, he traveled from Jingkou to Huqiu, where he paid homage at the stupa of Patriarch Daolun. Continuing his journey, he arrived in Hangzhou, where the local people invited him to reside at Hupao.
In the autumn, he proceeded to Mount Huading. In the spring of the *gēngxū* year, he manifested a slight illness and returned once more to Folin Monastery, where he bathed and changed his robes.

He donned his robes, took up a brush, and wrote a verse: "There is no world from which to take leave; there is only the assembly from whom one parts. Within the great void, why must one drive in a stake?
Having cast down the brush, he passed away. His cremation yielded relics of five colors, which were enshrined in a stupa to the west of the monastery.
He was sixty-seven years of age and fifty-three years of seniority.
Zen Master Zhedù of Píng hú, a successor of the ancient Zen Master Jìngtáng, ascended the hall and said: "Since the commencement of the retreat, it has been forty days of overcast skies.

Today the weather is clear and bright, a fine day for drying things in the sun. Nevertheless, even though one’s own arm does not bend outward, you must still examine yourselves within your own sphere."
Clearly so. Ascending the hall, he said: Autumn waters are pure, autumn clouds are white; autumn arrives at the wutong trees as the wind whistles. On the river, the hibiscus sheds its crimson petals.
How many have their dreams severed, recognizing the butterfly of Zhuangzi?
Chan Master Jinling Tianjie Guzhuo Jun was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Baiyun Du,
the fifth patriarch of the Jing Mountain lineage. A native of Songling, he possessed divine intelligence from his youth and could memorize a thousand words a day.

Having exhaustively searched through the myriad classics, he declared: "The ritual protocols of our Confucian tradition and the transformative arts of Laozi and Zhuangzi are surpassed only by the ocean-like depth of the Buddha’s nature, meaning, and principle;
of this I am truly not in error. Yet, if one wishes to exhaust all profound dialectics and attain the wondrous awakening to the True宗 (zong), nothing compares to the Way of Chan.
At the age of twenty, he went to Rizhou Temple in Yuezhou to shave his head and traveled everywhere to seek instruction from various masters.

Unable to attain liberation, he eventually joined a companion and returned to his hometown. He established a limit for himself to practice *bìguān* (wall-contemplation) for nine years, burning one finger every three years until all three were consumed.

One day, he suddenly attained sudden enlightenment (*piédì*). Hearing that Master Báiyún’s teaching style was solitary and austere, and that few students could enter his chamber, the Master joyfully went to visit him.
Upon seeing him, Báiyún recognized his potential and immediately appointed him as the head of the assembly.
One day, the Master requested instruction on the fundamental tenets of the predecessors. Yunshu ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One held up a flower—a heap of bones on level ground.
Kāśyapa smiled—an inability to restrain one's brilliance. Both together turn into something quite extraordinary. At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
Wuwei shook his hand and said, "Stop, stop! Yunmen threw down his whisk and descended from his seat. The Master followed him into the abbot’s quarters.
Yunmen questioned him, saying, "What did you just see that you acted like this? The Master replied, "If there were anything to be seen, I would have failed the Master. Yunmen deeply approved.
Donglin Zai said: "With a sword leveled at the gate, the forms of demons and Buddhas vanish; with a single strike of the poisonous drum, the courage of devas and humans fails.
Those who do not die upon hearing its sound were originally not counted among the many.

As for Fengxue’s ascent to the hall, he raised the occasion when the World-Honored One, with his blue-lotus eyes, looked out over the great assembly and said: "Right at this very moment... [The karmic conditions of] Shoushan.
In a mere flash of insight, one attains self-conviction. Furthermore, when Guishan stirred the fire and Dongshan beheld the shadow, both were instantly struck dumb upon hearing the sound.

When Guzhuo first inquired about the fundamental tenets of the ancestors, Baiyun merely tapped him lightly with his staff—the "poisonous drum"—and he immediately understood how to manifest himself throughout the myriad lands of the universe.
Is this not the nine-times refined elixir of immortality?
Shimen Yun’s Verse says: From the Crystal Palace emerges crystal water; The Taiye Pond tosses its Taiye waves.
A night of fine wind is not enough to satisfy; At daybreak, one can do nothing about the depth of the snow.
Yingji’s *Easily Recited Ode* says: After many years, we suddenly meet again; We indulge our spirits by ascending the tower to speak of our shared sorrows.
The most difficult thing of all to tell is this: Tears fall like pearls, soaking through my heart until it turns crimson.
Baibyun presented the verse of entrustment for the Dharma, saying: "Within the mind is the self-mind; within the Dharma is the ultimate Dharma.

Now I may entrust it to you; the mind-Dharma is no mind-Dharma. Desiring that the multitude might transcend the world, the Master withdrew his traces and left the mountains, leaving behind this verse:
For half a year we relied on one another, chanting the ancestral pivot; several times we discussed the Way, receiving his majestic presence.

Upon leaving the mountain, he spoke of the path back home—once again adding eyebrows upon eyes. He concealed his brilliance in crags and valleys for over thirty years, as expressed in his lifelong favorite lines:
"I have always loved to nestle among crags and valleys; for over thirty years I have been too weary to see others off or welcome them."

When the Master resided at Nanji Temple, he would single out the word "Mu" (無) to test those who came to study under him; for this reason, he was known throughout the various quarters as "Nanwuzi" (南無字).
During the Hongwu era, by imperial decree, he ordained a thousand monks. Upon arriving at Mount Bafeng in Fanchang, the assembly requested that he open the hall at Donglou Mountain.
He gave a general discourse to the assembly, saying: "The very character 'Chan' (Zen) is but a provisional name. What, then, is meant by 'investigating' (參)? It lies in faith."

It is simply this. To deliberate is to deviate; to open one's mouth is to err. If one’s resolve is not sincere and one’s aspiration is not fierce and sharp, one will spend the winter on this side and the summer on that side;

advancing today and retreating tomorrow, one will search for a long time without finding anything, and then say, "The Buddha-dharma has no efficacy. Instead, one turns outward to memorize and transcribe entire volumes, like a stinking bag of filth.
This vat of dregs! You are just like this kind of wild fox spirit. Even if you were to wait until Maitreya’s descent, what would it have to do with you?
A true follower of the Way, if they wish to escape birth and death, must pass through the patriarchs’ barrier. Once the patriarchal barrier is passed, birth and death are escaped.
This is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then stopping; one must take the various ancestors of the past as a model. Elder Zhaozhou—
For over forty years, this man did not allow his mind to be distracted. For what purpose? Master Changqing Ling sat through seven worn-out bundles of rush mats. For what purpose?
The venerable Master Xiangyan spent forty years before finally attaining a state of single-minded unity. For what purpose?
Even down to those of successive generations who truly practiced and strove with arduous diligence—for what purpose? This mountain monk [asks].
Today, with mouths flapping and babbling, you cite antiquity to verify the present. For what purpose?

O Zen practitioners, since there have been those from of old who did not spare their own bodies or lives, accumulating merit and virtue until they attained wondrous awakening and personal realization—why do you not summon great courage and exert great diligence?
Before the Triple Gem, make deep and solemn vows: "If I do not clarify birth and death, I shall [not rest] before the Patriarchs..."
If you cannot pass through the barrier, vow not to descend the mountain. After making such a vow, cut off the paths of manifold distinctions and do not consort with the myriad dharmas.
Upon the long couch, before the seven-foot mat, hang your alms-bag high and stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms tall.
Set a firm limit for your time and apply yourself with urgency; spend this entire life practicing until it is thoroughly mastered. If you are so resolved—
This mind will certainly not deceive you. I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. [Ascending the hall:
Today, Eight Peaks, I have donned fur and horns, bit iron and borne a saddle. I carry the five Mount Sumerus and roam the four great oceans, with nowhere to hide or flee.
My very life rests entirely in the hands of all of you. Fortunately, you are pitiable beings—if...
This is one who divides the wind and moon equally, guarding the boundaries of his domain. He does not wander about on his own; he must be pressed right here until he is crushed to pieces.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "The fish leaps in the deep abyss, but it cannot leap upon the steps. The *tāma* insect can go anywhere."
"Conditions cannot take as their object that which is above the flames. For those of the patch-robed monks' lineage, they transcend Buddhas and patriarchs;
they wrap the heavens and earth in their satchels, yet with one nostril missing, it cannot be made whole. After a long silence, he said, "And what can be blamed for this?"
Ascending the hall: The dragon rises from the bottom of the sea; waves surge upon the mountain peak. Not a moment too fast, not a moment too slow.

Like sparks struck by stone or flashes of lightning, one cannot reach them with the hand; like a sudden gale or torrential rain, one cannot avoid them. There are some who, in this state, try to drag it across or pull it down;
they cannot help but wound their hands and dull their blades. Little do they realize that outside the azure heavens, a clap of thunder resounds, and the rain clears.
The clouds have gathered, leaving but a single moon.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "At the hearth in the south, there is a 'no guest, no host' koan. To this day, for thirty years, no one has brought it up.
Zhaozhou speaking thus has already become the stench of excrement. You all—should you not simply lift your robes and go? A sword!"
"Treading upon the edge of a blade? Corpses strewn across the ground. Can you avoid this directly?
Today, Bafaeng shall reveal it for you; you must also save yourselves by half."
In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era, he again received imperial summons to Tianjie Monastery. One day, manifesting illness, he wrote a verse:
"Uttering 'wu wu' and 'tu tu,' surging and soaring; all are now shattered throughout every land and every speck of dust. Having cast down his brush and closed his eyes, he passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Bafeng.

Chan Master Wujie Mingwu of Daolin Monastery in Puzhou, a dharma heir of Chan Master Tianjie Jun, the sixth generation successor of Jing Mountain; his alternative name was Cangu; he was from An’e in Shu.
He was the son of the Mo family of Tongxian Town. At the age of twenty, he left the household life and requested instruction from an elder monk on the essentials of seated meditation (*zazen*).
Later, he went to Lushan to visit Master Qing. Qing instructed him with the "Mu" (No) kōan of Zhaozhou.

The Master then bound bamboo together to construct a hermitage and applied himself to his practice with unremitting diligence. He did not even notice when his fingers grew four inches long from writing; he simply practiced with blind persistence like a dull laborer.
Now, when the head seat Wushou of West River was pointing toward Tianjie for study, the guest Wunian passed through Songyin; both praised his resolve.
Later, upon meeting Baiyun, Baiyun posed the question, "The myriad dharmas return to one," to the Master. The Master replied, whereupon Baiyun let out a shout and sent him away.
One night, while walking in the corridor, Yun entered the hall and seized him, saying, "Everyone, quickly bring fire! This old monk has caught a thief.
The Master replied, "He is a member of the household. Yun covered the Master's mouth with his hand and said, "What is this 'matter of the household'?
Speak quickly, speak quickly! At these words, the Master attained realization.
Yi Lin composed this verse: The great forge and red furnace smelt the Buddhas and Patriarchs; In a mere moment, their forms were entirely melted away.
Returning to the ancient path, autumn colors spread across it; With staff in hand, he brushes away the speckled traces of flying sun and moon.
Shimen Yun’s Verse says: The wind comes; the vermilion waters hold emerald pearls. The moon arrives; the Lantian fields emit the luster of jade.
I spur my horse through the twelve gorges of Mount Wu; A single cry of the ape breaks my bowels in nine turns.
One day Baiyun said to the Master, "Bafeng is your teacher; you should not remain here. The Master returned to Bafeng.
Bafeng said, "Give me back my illumination and function (*zhāoyòng*). The Master said, "If there were illumination and function, they would immediately become obstacles.

Bafeng said, "This fellow clings to emptiness; even a Buddha could not save him. The Master said, "Both existence and non-existence are quiescent; both emptiness and Buddha are entirely non-existent."
Feng said to his attendant, "This monk has the marks of merit and virtue. He picked up his staff, leaned it against his chair, and sat down, ordering the Master to recount his travels.
The Master related them directly and honestly. Feng said, "Go for now; I do not yet know the measure of your practice."
One day, the Master again went up to the Abbot’s quarters. Feng let out a thunderous shout, brandished his staff, and made a gesture as if to strike him.
The Master presented himself to receive the blow. Feng said, "My staff has eyes; I would not strike a dead man like you.
He then pulled his staff and went out. The Master stood with palms joined, remaining motionless. Feng returned to his seat and suddenly asked, "The great earth sinks away—what about you?"
"Where is it? the Master said, "The Dharma King’s body is fully revealed. Feng said, "'All phenomena return to the One'; where does the One return? Speak quickly, speak quickly!
The Master said, "I do not speak. Feng said, "Why do you not speak? The Master said, "From antiquity to the present.
Feng said, "Setting aside 'from antiquity to the present,' what thing was it that came like this when you were in Sichuan? The Master—
After a long silence, Feng said, "A mute man has a dream—whom can he tell it to?
One day, Feng bestowed upon the Master the additional title of Wujie (Boundless). The Master said, "If that is so, then even 'the boundless' does not yet suffice.
All the old monks of the world attain the Way here; all the ancestral masters of successive generations attain Buddhahood here."
At that moment, someone said, "The Buddha has spoken, and the Patriarchs have come forth; let them all be sent out the door. It is better to snore and sleep soundly here with this fellow.
Feng laughed and said, "From now on, this man will no longer allow himself to be deceived. He then bestowed upon him a verse, saying:
"A single path of mindless radiance, Illuminating the three times and the ten directions. How is it within this clarity That there is further clarity?"
There was a lack of clarity.
The Master declined. Feng said, "When you encounter a person who has attained the Way on the road, if you do not respond with either speech or silence, with what will you respond? The Master said:
A blow across the face and over the cheek; to hesitate is to lose him. Feng said, "You have deeply mastered the application of the Great Function.

When the Master appeared in the world at Daolin, Guting came to visit him. The Master said, "Recite once more that passage from where you previously practiced your cultivation. Guting then recited it.
When he reached the place where the Truth is seen, he joined his palms and remained silent. The Master said, "At the place where you see the Truth, why is it different from mine?
Baizhang spread both hands wide and displayed them, saying, "This is not something else. The Master asked, "Does this still involve words and phrases?
Baizhang replied, "In truth, there is not a single word. The Master said, "In this very state of having not a single word, I bear witness for you."
The explanation is complete. Chushan came forward. The Master asked, "Where have you been staying for these past few years? Chushan said, "My dwelling is vast and empty;
it has no fixed location. The Master asked, "What have you attained? Chushan said, "Fundamentally there was nothing lost; what is there to attain? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Is there nothing that does not come from learning? Shan said, "If not a single dharma exists, from where could learning come?
The Master said, "You have fallen into emptiness. Shan said, "I am not 'I. Who falls and who is empty? The Master said, "In the end, what is it?"
Mount Shishuang said, "The water is shallow and the stones are exposed; the rain has cleared and the clouds have dispersed. The Master said, "Do not speak so recklessly.

Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, I would not take them into account. Even if you were to swallow the Tripitaka scriptures whole and manifest hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers, here you still would not be permitted.
Mount Shishuang said, "Although you, Master, see fit to block off the vital pass, how can you avoid the difficulty of exhausting your own spirit? The Master struck his knee.
The Master said, "Do you understand? Yunshan then gave a shout. The Master smiled and said, "One who can uphold the family must be one who can break it;
