doing so will make the management of the household less arduous. Yunshan covered his ears and departed.
When evening arrived, the Master again summoned Xiangshan and questioned him, saying, "Bring forth everything you have previously clarified and explained, in its proper sequence.
Xiangshan answered truthfully and in full detail. The Master said, "Give me back the meaning of the word 'No'. Xiangshan replied, "That monk’s question was already far too complicated.
What did the Old Man from Zhao ever do with conceptual thought? A single word spoken offhand revealed everything; yet it has turned out to be a mere fabrication."
The people were doubtful. The Master said, "What is that place where you have no doubt? Shanshan said, "Green mountains and blue waters; swallows singing and orioles calling;
everything is vividly clear—what more is there to doubt? The Master said, "Not yet. Speak further. Shanshan said, "My head touches the void;
my feet tread upon solid ground. The Master said, "Still not yet. Speak further. Shanshan then bowed. The Master said, "So it is."
Thus it was.
Xinglong remarked: "The walls of Daolin’s gate tower a thousand feet high; those who have reached its inner sanctum are perhaps few.
The beauty of its ancestral temple and the abundance of its officials are so profound, firm, remote, and deep that no one can reach them. Only by chance did I open my breast to him."
From within the svastika, clouds of radiance from a hundred jewels surged forth and met with Chushan.
Chushan said, "The head reaches toward the void while the feet tread upon solid ground; I thought there might be something quite extraordinary about this."
A monk asked, "What is it like when one penetrates through water and through sand? The Master said, "The hard does not break the soft.
Yufeng Qian’s verse says: "Penetrating, penetrating—how could there ever be penetration to that other side? Ten thousand acres of autumn light, a vast expanse of blue reaching to heaven."
"A single sound of the fisherman’s flute at dawn in a thousand gates; having finished fishing, he returns as the moon fills his boat.

In the ninth year of the Zhengtong era, he preached the Dharma in response to an imperial decree. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the purple robe, conferring upon him the title Chan Master Miaoxin Pujie (Wondrous Mind, Universal Salvation).
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wind of Yao clears the universe; the sun of Shun illuminates heaven and earth. From the Purple Tower, the vermilion edict is proclaimed;

at the Spirit Mountain, this assembly is renewed. He then raised another instance: When Emperor Xianzong welcomed the Buddha’s *śarīra* into the inner palace, five-colored lights appeared and all the officials offered their congratulations.
Only Han Yu stood upright. The Emperor asked, "All the officials offer their congratulations; why do you alone not congratulate? Han Yu replied: "Your servant..."
"I have read the Buddhist scriptures before," [Li Ao] said. "The Buddha’s light does not possess the characteristics of blue, yellow, red, or white;

this is the light of the nāgas, devas, and asuras. The Emperor asked, "What then is the Buddha’s light? Li Ao had no reply. The Master (Huihong) spoke on his behalf, saying: "Your Majesty is sagely and wise; it is difficult for anything to escape the illumination of your wisdom."
Shimen Yun ascended the hall for the Imperial Birthday. Having finished citing the public case (gong’an), he said: “The Dharma-gate of the Great Benevolence has its dragons and elephants;
the House of Xianzong has its Son of Heaven. Nevertheless, though guest and host harmonize and Way and sovereign accord, this meeting of a thousand-year era must still be scrutinized.
Shimen encounters this great age of peace on the auspicious day of His Majesty’s birthday.”
Someone asked, "What is Buddha-light? [The Master] replied, "I dare say: 'The sun and moon illuminate the celestial virtue; the mountains and rivers magnify the imperial abode.

He ascended the hall, crouched upon the tiger's head, and grasped the tiger's tail, yet this was not the ultimate standard for a monk. He took up his staff, let out a shout, and said: "Grasping the tiger's head and holding the tiger's tail is not yet the ultimate limit of a patch-robed monk. He brandished his staff and gave a shout.
Descend from your seats.
Entering the hall: Throughout this winter at Long’en, everything has been provided in full; we simply lack one who can calculate it.
Thus, when a person of the Ox year encounters a pillar, they collide with it.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Deshan carrying his almsbowl—how pressing is that hunger! Puhua shaking his bell—is it not much like a feverish eye? Yunmen’s cakes and Zhaozhou’s tea:
having examined them from beginning to end, what is different about this than pushing through a door only to fall into a mortar?

To take a mistake and turn it into a success—if there be seven bends and eight turns, three curves and four twists, let the silver mountains and iron walls stand as they are; they shall vainly bring forth the claws and fangs of the patch-robed monk."
Not so. Even if he were to come forth from within the Buddha’s belly, he would still be nothing more than a functional wooden stake.
Entering the hall, [the Master said: "At the head of the wild-grass ferry, the true eye opens; it is like parting clouds and mist to see the blue sky.
Striking the jackpot on level ground, the lion cub suddenly increases its valor. Taking him by the hand, he is pulled to the top of a hundred-foot pole. One thrust, one..."
Memorandum. When the urge for excrement and urine is urgent, let it all pass by. Thirty years hence, you will wear out your straw sandals and cover yourself with a tortoise shell.
*Zhu*. Long’en speaks for you a phrase for turning around.
Chan Master Xing Tianru Jiao of Hupao in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhou family of Siming.

He underwent tonsure under Zhongzheng An and attended upon Master Guzhuo, receiving his rigorous training. One night, as he drew back the curtain and saw the moon, he attained realization and said, "So this is how it is!
The following morning, he went to see Guzhuo and let out a thunderous shout. Guzhuo said, "Is it like a poor man finding a treasure?"
The Master said, "Treasure is not to be attained; that which is attained is not treasure. Zuo asked, "On what basis do you say this?
The Master stepped forward to pay his respects, stood with his hands folded, and Zuo said, "Bring me back that phrase from above! The Master then covered his ears and departed.
He again presented a verse, saying: At midnight, I push back the curtain—there is a crescent moon; Gently, I have stepped through the gate above. There is no need to seek it elsewhere from others;
Just so, with a joyful countenance, I display a smile. Zhuwei offered his congratulations. Later, while residing at Hupao in Wulin, he addressed the assembly at the time of his death, saying:
"Scripture and Dharma are but empty forms; Names, marks, body, and mind are like mist upon willow trees."
"Only death and rebirth are truly momentous matters. Diligently prepare for them; do not delay. The assembly asked, "How does one prepare?

After a long silence, he said, "I have no leisure now to explain it for you. Listen instead to the sound of the pines and the wind at the bottom of the mountain stream. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
His remains stayed in the shrine for seven days, his countenance appearing as if alive.
The Dharma heir of Layman He Mi’an, the Great Being Tian Su’ān of Yangzhou, addressed the assembly: "Lately, those who are earnestly devoted to the study of Chan are few.

As soon as they bring up a *huatou*, they are immediately ensnared by the two demons of dullness and agitation. What they fail to realize is that dullness and agitation are precisely [the opposites of] the state of doubt."
As for the antidote: if the weight of faith is heavy, the gravity of doubt must likewise be heavy; when the gravity of doubt is heavy, both dullness and distraction will naturally cease.
*Jingshi Dinaru Ji*, Volume One. *Jingshi Dinaru Ji*, Volume Two.
May this be perpetually circulated. I prostrate and pray that we may together clarify Prajñā. May the Way flourish.
*Guo heng xin*.
*Jing shi di ru ji*, Volume Two.
Compiled by the monk Qing Sizu of Jiangzhou, Zhenzai.
The Dharma heirs who succeeded him were Qian’an Jiyun and others,
continuing the lineage of the seventh generation under Master Donglin Wu of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Cheng of Yuexi at Taigang in Jinling left the household life under Wuzhuo of Yuanzhao Temple. He studied the *Tiantai Zhiguan* with great diligence.
A certain monk said to him, "In the future, you shall be the nectar for the Dharma-gate; do not linger here for long.
The Master then requested instruction on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma. The monk told him to investigate it for himself. One day, while casually reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he saw—
Dizang cited the *Zhaolun*, saying: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me.

Only then did he realize that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, plants, trees, and insects are all the essentials of the wholesome Dharma. From then on, he traveled everywhere with his single staff to seek instruction.
Finally, he arrived at Daolin in Dongpu and presented his insights. Daolin did not approve. Because Daolin had forcefully suppressed him, the Master spoke some discourteous words.
Lin knew that he was a vessel for the Dharma, so he carried his bag and escorted him to the mountain gate.
Suddenly pointing to a yellow dog, he said, "This beast—why does it have karmic consciousness but no Buddha-nature? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
Master Taixun Sun said: "Dao Lin dangled his hook across the four seas; Yue Xi trailed his skirt at Longmen.
Although they were whole-bodied and all-pervasive, they could not avoid having a dragon's head and a snake's tail.
Is there anyone who can come forward to thrust aside the spear and seize the drum for Yue Xi? Step forth and meet this staff."

One day, Daolin held up the character for "nothing" (wu) and showed it to his disciples. The Master was standing nearby and deeply grasped its profound meaning. Daolin gave him this verse of entrustment:
"I have no Dharma to transmit; You have no mind to receive. With neither transmission nor receiving, who would not achieve success?"
Shimen Yun said: "The ox eats the grain, and the horse’s belly swells. He further composed a verse: "Produced and held forth, it brings grief even to ghosts before one's eyes;

Lifting up to heaven to demand a price—who would dare offer recompense? A single cry of the cuckoo at dawn across a thousand forests— Spring fills the imperial capital and its four hundred provinces."
Dufeng Shanshan visited Master [Zhaozhou]. The Master asked, “What is the word ‘wu’? He replied, “Originally it was just fine;
I have always followed people by saying it is this word ‘wu. Looking at it today, however, it is the Diamond King’s Precious Sword. The Master said, “Bring me that sword back.
He replied, “Frosty rime blazes forth, illuminating the ancient and soaring through the present. The Master said, “Give me the sword back! He replied, “...”
"Any attempt to move immediately strikes against his sharp edge. The Master asked, "What about when you hold [your sword] crosswise across the gateway?

He replied, "Even if a Buddha comes, I kill him; even if an Ancestor comes, I kill him. The Master said, "What about when I, this old monk, come? He replied, "I will not spare you either. The Master said, "After being defeated, what then?
He replied, "Fortunately, all under heaven is at peace."
The Master was staying at Taokang. He ascended the hall and said: "To raise an eyebrow and blink an eye is not permitted; not to raise an eyebrow and blink an eye is also not permitted;
to both raise an eyebrow and blink an eye and not to raise an eyebrow and blink an eye—neither is permitted. Taokang gives you two options, and these two are both [equally] two."
"One by one. "Can you get back? A monk stepped forward; the Master struck him. The monk shouted; the Master struck him again. The monk shouted twice in succession.
The Master said, "Did you say that was a good shout? The monk hesitated; the Master then shouted.

At the beginning of the Jingtai era, he resided at Guang’en Temple in response to an imperial decree. The Emperor came in person daily to listen to the Dharma and was greatly pleased, bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Cipu.
After three years, he was ordered by imperial edict to return home. One day, in his quarters, he took out the patriarchal robe and showed it to his disciples, saying:
"This robe was presented by the Princess of the Tang Court; it has been more than eight hundred years since then. It has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch down to Dongpu Xian."
The Master said: "My late teacher entrusted this to me. Only those who possess the seed of a true heir are fit to inherit and uphold it.

How could one who merely borrows the tiger’s prestige dare to harbor such aspirations? Furthermore, he said: 'Just as Baizhang attended Mazu, Mazu attended Nanyue, and Nanyue attended the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi—each of them served for a long time, polishing their brilliance and blunting their sharpness until they were able to burst through the heavy gates and cast off their shackles.'"

He has swept away all traces, revealing even the subtlest vestiges of his training; he has profoundly attained the great function of the great capacity and is fit to serve as the eyes for gods and humans.

Entering the hall, he said: "Highly upholding the ancestral seal, he makes the sun of wisdom shine brightly in the midst of heaven; once again shaking the collapsing net, he fans the pure breeze in this final age.
Turning the pivot to trap the tiger, he transforms the command to slay the dragon. If you simply proceed in this manner, those of the Two Vehicles will lose heart, and those of the Ten Stages..."
The spirit dissolves; let loose a single thread. Wondrously accord with the Heart-Essence; sit firmly upon the triple-forked path.

Meeting on a narrow road, they are dragged down to ten-thousand-foot heights, where there is no longer front or back. Secretly shifting a single step, the earth broadens and the sky opens. Thus, the wind strikes the wondrous wings.

A thunderbolt escorts the roaming dragon; neither attached nor detached. Continuing the life-force of wisdom of the Fourth, Seventh, Second, and Third Patriarchs—neither detached nor attached—they propagate the illustrious legacy of the Stone Bridge and Shuangjing Patriarchs.
Penetrating the profound mysteries directly beneath, they expose their very hearts and livers from within. With descendants covering the earth, who among them is not a true man?
Following his footsteps, he tramples the flowing stream; gazing freely, he brings forth his realization in writing.
The tracks of birds: upon the point of a needle, no monk is permitted to crouch. Why is it that beneath the feet of all people there is such pitch blackness? Question:
When a wooden horse sucks dry the waters of the vast ocean, by what means do the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs sustain their lives? Question:
Throughout the boundless realms of all lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Why has the Dragon King lost his Treasure Pearl of Samādhi?
Question: When the *kūn* transforms into a *péng*, its eyes remain; where does the earthworm go when it transforms into a lily?
Question: Why does the iron ox sleep at Shaoshi? Question: The upward path cannot be caught in a net and cannot be summoned back;
why does a person of great power sit atop a hundred-foot pole?
One day the Master said to the assembly, "The old monk will travel to Tiantai tomorrow; the monastery should prepare everything with haste. The Superintendent asked, "When will the Master return?
The Master bent his index finger and said, "Two fives. At the fifth watch of the night, he sat upright and passed away.
At that time, a great wind arose with a roar, and a white light illuminated the ground. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the mountain monastery.
Chan Master Cheng of Huaisong was asked by a monk, "What is that which is not contained within the six? The Master said, "The stone *gandhang*.
Chan Master Xuan of Miaofeng in Jinling was asked by a monk, "What is the 'different species'? The Master said, "Horns at the corners, whiskers reaching the beak;
beneath the brows, two bright red eyes."
Chan Master Wuyi of Tianchi on Mount Lu was asked by a monk, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
The Master said, "The ox pulls the plow; the horse drags the plow; the horse drags the millstone."
Chan Master Fu Niu Wugaijian was visited by a monk for an audience. The Master shouted, “Look at the sword! The monk said, “Fortunately, it is I;
had it been anyone else, it would have been a disaster. The Master asked, “Who is ‘anyone else’? Try pointing them out to me.
The monk overturned the meditation seat. The Master said, “Fortunately, it was I, the old monk; had it been anyone else, I would have broken your donkey’s back.”
Chan Master Shanjian of Guting on Mount Dayong in Jintai was a native of Kunming in Yunnan. He took up the koan, "Where does it all return?
One day, while in meditative concentration, he heard a monk say, "To see nothing is true seeing. At these words, the Master was suddenly liberated.
In the *Zhengtong* era, year Yichu (1025), he received the Dharma from Chan Master Wuji and settled at Mount Dayong. Disciples from all quarters gathered there without ceasing.
Fearing that he might emerge into the world too early, Wuji appointed him as the head seat (shouzuo) and asked, "Where else do you dwell apart from here?

The Master replied, "Where the Buddhas and patriarchs cannot reach. Wuji asked, "Do you still reckon with people coming or not? The Master replied, "Tranquil and unimpeded. Wuji said, "From the time of the ancestors..."
"Of the ancients, who possessed wisdom that transcended their own patriarchs? The Master replied, "Huangbo. Baizhang Ji said, "Have you seen Huangbo?
The Master replied, "Even if it were Huangbo himself, he would still have been expelled. Ji said, "How dare you speak such grand words here in my presence?"

The Master said, "The True Eye is impartial. Guoji said, "Observing your view, I am not your teacher. The Master said, "If there were no transgression beyond measure, how could one avoid being diminished?
Guoji said, "So it is, so it is. Later, the Master returned to the Ancient Courtyard (Guting) in Kunming and passed away.
Guting stands in parallel with Panshan; to this day, the physical remains of these two Great Beings are preserved there.
Chan Master Shaoqi Jingbi, known as Huansou Chushan of Toudi in Shuzhou, was the son of the Lei family of Tang’an in Shu.
At the age of nine, he received his training under Xuanji Tong. He first visited Daolin, where one day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, he attained realization.
He further visited the various masters Haizhou and Yuexi, all of whom praised him highly. In the sixth year of the Zhengtong era, he again attended Daolin and attained the Dharma.
Later, he emerged into the world at Tianzhu. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master said, "The stream is broad, clouds return at dusk;
the mountain is high, the sun rises late. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Below the forehead, the eyebrows..."
[The Master] covered his eyes. [His] jaw was at his ear and his ear reached his shoulder. He asked, "What is the house style of Tianzhu?
The Master said, "A cloud-steamer cooks pine powder; an ice-cauldron boils the full moon. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The Sea God casts forth a night-bright pearl. He said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his crystal cup."
In the fifth year of the Jingtai era, [Zhaozhou] moved to Touzi. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Having left Mount Xuefeng far behind, you have come to occupy Touzi.

With the assembly of the four seas gathered before you, we pray that the Master will offer a benediction for the Emperor. The Master said: "The eternal seal within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. The monk said:

"I have already received the Master’s direct instruction regarding the benediction for the Emperor. As for the 'house style' of Touzi, what is it like? The Master said: "Carrying a water jar through the marketplace."
[The guest] said, "That is not the point. It is like when the Patriarch said: 'I do not permit traveling at night; one must arrive by dawn. Is this truly so?
The Master said, "Though there is sinew in his eyes, what can he do about the lack of bone in his tongue?
[The guest] asked, "Zhaozhou said, 'I am already white as a monkey; you are already black as a monkey. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "It is not because of the bow..."
His arrows were exhausted, yet he was unwilling to hoist the flag of surrender. He asked, "When the Master ascends the seat today to preach the Dharma, what auspicious signs are there?
The Master said, "The Qilin strides beyond the vermilion heavens; the Utpala flower blooms amidst the raging flames.
He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The snow melts and the mountain peaks are revealed; the wind passes and the treetops sway. He asked again.
"How is it when the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard? The Master said, "The spirits wail and the ghosts weep. "How is it after it has emerged from the scabbard?
The Master said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs swallow their voices. "How is it when it has emerged and when it has not yet emerged?
The Master said, "A hairless chain rattles at both ends. The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master then shouted. The monk hesitated; the Master struck him. Then he said:
To rub one's itch upon the head of a venomous serpent, or to cast oneself across the mouth of a fierce tiger—only such a person as this can do it.
That monk who arrived just now was much like a seasoned warrior, daring to come here to clash his war drums and challenge the banners. It is a pity that he failed to maintain his resolve to the end;
he died beneath the staff. Had he been able to turn back and find a path of life, he surely would not have been struck by its sharp edge. As for the rest...
By means of the Way. To handle a snake, one must be a master at handling snakes; if one does not know how to handle them, the snake will bite and kill. Again, he cited:

Fadelan addressed the assembly, saying, "This mountain monk originally intended to hide deep within rock caves and live in seclusion until my time passed away. It was only because of the Elder Qingliang."
There is an unresolved koan; I cannot help but come forth to resolve it for him. At that time, a monk asked, "I do not know, Master Qingliang, what unresolved koan you have?
Dēng took up his staff and struck him, saying, "The patriarch has not yet resolved it."
"The calamity reaches the children and grandchildren. [The Master] asked, "Where does the fault lie? Dēng said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity reaches you.
The Master said, "Generally, when a patriarch appears in the world, he must first bring forth his own insight, and only then may he pass judgment on the ancients and the present.
Look at Fǎdēng’s strategy: it is beautiful indeed, yet it is not yet complete. Today, Huàn’ǒu also..."
"For the old man Silk-Bone, there is an unfinished kōan. Come forth and settle it for him! If someone asks, "What unfinished kōan does the old man Silk-Bone have?
one should immediately shout, and with eyes fixed and moving, strike them out with a staff.
"O Assembly! When I, this mountain monk, uphold the Dharma in such a manner, tell me: is there any difference in quality between this and the way of Faldeng?"
Nor is there any. If either a monk or a layperson can emerge [from this], I grant that they are a fellow student of the same rank.
He ascended the hall; when the assembly had gathered, the Master adjusted his robes and took his seat. After a long silence, he said, "Keep this clearly in mind," and then descended from the seat.

To demonstrate the practice of the Pure Land, he ascended the hall and said: "Who has no Buddha in their mind? Who has no mind in their Buddha? Mind and Buddha are different names; in essence, they are not two distinct things.
Therefore, to recollect the Buddha is to recollect the mind; to recollect the mind is to recollect the Buddha. Without recollection there is no mind; without mind there is no Buddha."
When both mind and Buddha are forgotten, thought cannot be apprehended. In this very state of non-apprehension, the whole body is manifest and clearly distinct, with not a speck of dust intervening.

Thus, the true mechanism is encountered at every glance; it is difficult to conceal throughout the entire realm. The colors of the mountains and the sounds of the streams are revealed in every single instance.

The nature and its characteristics are equal; principle and phenomena are interpenetrating. Within this state, even a hair’s breadth of distinction between self and other, or purity and impurity, cannot be found at all.

How, then, could there be ordinary people and sages, or delusion and awakening? If you can here suddenly open the eye of wisdom and realize its truth, knowing directly where you belong, you will experience a joy beyond measure. Do you recognize the Buddha of your own mind? You must examine it until you see it clearly.
"Empty space-bone. Behold the *udumbara* flower blooming within the fire.
He ascended the hall and looked over the assembly, saying: "This very slight point of confusion has existed throughout antiquity and the present.

How many monks have reached this place and been unable to open their mouths, unable to conceive of it through thought, and unable to bring it forth? [He] suddenly took up his staff and said: 'Now...'"
What was once considered most profound has now fallen into the hands of this mountain monk. Holding his staff horizontally, he said, "Whether it is held horizontally is up to me.
Raising the staff upright, he said, "Whether it is held upright is also up to me. Lowering the staff, he said, "Even putting it down is up to me.
Thus, whether rolling it up or spreading it out, killing or giving life—all is entirely up to me. Then, pointing with the staff toward the air, he struck once and said, "This is precisely..."
At such a time, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the elder monks of the world, upon reaching this point, they have no choice but to beg for their lives.
Is there anyone among you who can speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said:
"I gouge out the adamantine eye and topple the precious palace of the Empty King. You people, go seek it!"

"What kind of bowl? [The Master] addressed the assembly: "The field for selecting Buddhas has opened; the ancestral mechanisms have been fixed. To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, the tongs and hammers are applied.

The waves of the Yu Gate are warm and the wind-thunder roars; this is precisely the time when fish and dragons undergo their transformations. Is there anyone among you who can surge through the waves and stir up the billows?"

After a long pause, he struck [the ground] with his whisk and said, "A single move before the pivot; the total presentation face-to-face. He struck the meditation seat once and said, "A single word beyond the phrase;
revealed along with the sound. He did not permit secondary thought or looking back; there was no room for deliberation or discrimination.
By the time you blink an eye, the sword has been raised for a long time. Even if it were the Buddhas and Patriarchs, upon reaching this point, they could do nothing but knit their brows.
[This is] a division. Why? It is because it is not a path that can be traversed, nor is it something that can be fathomed by the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).

If one were a truly outstanding monk, one should nod the head and smile before [the words] have even been raised; this would still leave some room for excellence. In recent times, people's hearts are not as they were in antiquity;
those who study do not strive for authentic inquiry. They merely pass on echoes and inherit empty space, relying on their learning and knowledge.
To take general understanding as enlightenment, to engage in intellectual dissection of karmic conditions as investigation,

to treat the destruction of monastic discipline as liberation, and to rely on worldly connections for status— this has caused the ancestral wind to wither and decay, and demonic teachings to flourish.

It blocks the level path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and blinds the true eye of Heaven, causing the Way of our Ancestors— the separate transmission outside the scriptures— to be cast to the ground here.
Great World-Honored One, regarding the mental illnesses of sentient beings in the two [eras], You have already established many [remedies] and bestowed rules.
Therefore, it is said that for sentient beings in the final age who seek the Way, do not allow them to pursue awakening;
rather, let them only increase their learning, so as to grow in the view of self. Furthermore, [You have taught] so as to cause all to open [the Dharma].
[Square Seal]. By observing the retreat for the summer rains (*varṣā*), one must strive to realize [the truth] within this period. Only then will unobstructed wisdom arise;
therefore, it is precisely at the time of entering the retreat that one should exert oneself. Venerable ones, during these ninety days, you must attain realization.
As for those who have already attained realization, let them be set aside for now. However, if you have not yet attained it, then this entire period will again be spent in vain.
[The text is] complete. If one is truly [engaged in] practice, one takes the entire Dharma-realm of the ten directions as the site for the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Whether it be a hundred days or a thousand days, regardless of the duration, one simply raises the critical phrase (*huatou*).
One may take a year to begin, or spend a year in inquiry; whether it be ten years, twenty years, or thirty years, it is all level ground.

Though born into this world, you have not awakened; you must remain resolute and never waver from this intent. You must simply see that place which is thorough from beginning to end, the true and ultimate state.
Only then, on the day you let go of your formal inquiry, will it truly be as the saying goes: "One moment lasts ten thousand years. How could this be empty talk? [The Master] raises his whisk.
"Virtuous ones, do you know where it lands? Today, this old phantom has exhausted his tongue; he can say no more."
O people, let me offer this commentary: A golden bullet forged in a fierce fire—when the moment strikes, it is crushed to pieces and becomes utterly indistinct.
Carelessly cast aside both gain and loss; the sound of the tide is carried forth by the wind from the depths.
In the first year of the Tiānshùn era, he returned from Mount Kuānglú to Shǔ. Mān Dūhòu constructed Yúnfēng Monastery on Mount Fāng and invited the Master to serve as its abbot.
On the full moon day of the third month in the ninth year of the Chénghuà era, the Master manifested a slight illness.

When the assembly requested his final words, the Master extended both hands and asked, "Do you understand? He then added, "On this very day this year, pushing a cart, I have crashed into a wall; I have smashed through empty space."
A thunderclap from the blue sky. Aha ha! An earthen ox swallows the old dragon’s pearl; the tranquil ocean of nature is stilled, like the subsiding of foam-flowers.
He passed away peacefully at the age of seventy, with sixty-one years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Taixuchong of Dading in Puzhou asked Wuji, "Deshan employed the staff and Linji practiced the shout;
do these suffice? Wuji said, "Let us set aside Linji and Deshan for a moment; give me back the core of the matter.
The Master said, "If we speak of the point of intimacy, even you, Reverend, must step aside. Wuji picked up his staff; the Master then let out a shout.
Chongqing Xixi Chan Master Xuefeng Rui. Tianqi came to attend him. The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'Mu'? For some time, Tianqi was suddenly awakened.
He replied, "Hard ice at the bottom of the ravine swallows the universe; the bright moon in the lake of nature fills the coldness of heaven.
The Master gave a great shout and said, "Do you still have a mind that detests the mundane and loves the sacred? Sweep away all deluded seeking!"
"Seeing the ultimate reality," Ji said, "Yes. The Master said, "If you loathe the ordinary and cherish the holy, you sever the roots of goodness of Prajñā.
If you sweep away delusion to seek the truth, you cut off the life-vein of all Buddhas. Shaking his voice, he shouted again, "Who is the 'true'?
Who is the 'deluded'? Who is the 'ordinary'? And who is the 'holy'? Ji was suddenly enlightened and prostrated himself.
Chan Master Wunian Yuanxin of Funiu was the son of the Gao family from Jintai. He was born in the Jiyou year of the Xuande era.
He left home at the age of nine, and after receiving full ordination, he first met Wuji at Long’en, where he attained realization.
In the Jimao year of the Tianshun era, he returned to Mount Niu to build a thatched hut. In the Xinsi year, he went to Fanchang to visit Yuehuan, who asked him, "Where have you come from?"
The Master said, "Niu Shan. Huan said, "A person is right here; what about the ox? The Master said, "Face-to-face yet not recognized; the whole body is revealed, vast and majestic.
Huan said, "Even so, its horns and head are not fully present. The Master said, "Today I am weary from walking in the mountains.
Huan again picked up his bamboo whisk and said, "To call it a bamboo whisk is to encounter resistance; not to call it a..."
[Zhaozhou] turned his back on the bamboo whisk. "How about you, Senior Monk? the Master asked. Wuhuan said, "You have exerted your mental faculties; say something more.
The Master stepped forward, seized the bamboo whisk, and threw it to the ground. Wuhuan laughed heartily. The Master said, "I have committed an offense," and prostrated himself.
Wuhuan then patted him and certified him. The Master lived in retreat in a hermitage for thirty years before opening a Dharma center at Fojian.
The Ox. A monk asked, "Master Pang said, 'There is a single stringless lute; only you, Master, can play it wondrously. Today I beg the Master to play it for me.
The Master coughed once. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The bell makes the sound of a bell;
the drum makes the sound of a drum. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Mazu passed away long ago. [The monk] asked again.
"What is 'this very mind is Buddha'? The Master said, "A wealthy child is easily spoiled. [The monk] asked, "What about 'neither mind nor Buddha'?
The Master said, "A deep pit is difficult to fill. [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you say 'this very mind is Buddha,'..."
This is very much like gouging a sore from healthy flesh. If one says it is neither mind nor Buddha, how is this different from applying moxa to a spot that does not ache?
Even if you say, "It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing," you are still begging for alms on level ground. But tell me, what is it ultimately like?
Sitting, he wipes the table and adds incense; after the gruel, he calls the boy to wash the bowls.
Chan Master Huangjing Jie Kongyuantong of Shimen Mountain in Huangzhou ascended the hall and said:

"Before the whisk has even been raised, needles and awls are scattered all over the ground. Yet, as soon as it sweeps across the faces of you all, there is birth and death, there is the provisional and the real.
To lose one's virtue through ornate carving—who is to blame for this? If you have a staff, I shall give you a staff."
Canyou, you have no staff. I shall take away your staff. This stone gate is not the place where moxa is applied for pain;
it is intended to shake one’s sinews and bones like the ancients. As the saying goes: "The pearl curtain half-drawn, she is justly bashful;
her colorful sleeves, like lingering sunset clouds, brush against the mossy rocks."
Chan Master Guangshan Baoyuetan of Mount Bafeng in Taiping Prefecture was visited by Dahui.

The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dahui replied, "There are clouds atop the eastern ridge. The Master asked, "Are they clouds that will rain or clouds that will not rain?
Dahui said, "It is pouring with rain. The Master asked, "And after it has rained? Dahui said, "White waves surge to the heavens. The Master [nodded].
[The Master] said: "The entire great earth is a single fiery pit. What samādhi must one attain so as not to be burned? Huì replied:
"A carp from the Eastern Sea swallows the sun."
During the Chenghua era, one day he struck the drum and ascended the hall. Having completed his solicitation for offerings, the great earth, mountains, and rivers were cut off from all news;
in the golden palace there was no one with whom to share understanding. To spare the multitude from further vain disorder, he then passed away.

Chan Master He’an Zhong of Tiantong Monastery in Yangzhou was a dharma successor of Great Being Su’an Tian. A monk came for an audience. The Master asked, “Where have you come from? The monk replied, “From Mount Song.”
The Master asked, "Have you ever been to Wuyufeng? The monk replied, "I spent the summer retreat there. The Master said, "Listen to the rocks by the side of the Moon Rock:
why are the large ones large and the small ones small? The monk had no reply. The Master struck him, saying, "When did you ever actually go there?"
Dayun entered and asked, "Must one reach Wuyufeng Peak? He held up his whisk and said, "All people throughout the great earth shall meet one another here.
Chan Master Zhongkan of Faming arrived for an audience. The Master held up his whisk and asked, "What do you call this?"
The monk said, "I would rather sink into eternal samsara than seek liberation from the various sages.
The Master threw down his whisk, then raised his fist and asked, "What do you call this? The monk replied, "I will never make my livelihood within a ghost cave.
The Master laughed and said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. The monk bowed.
Master Zhenshi of Yigan, at the Buddha’s Footprint, addressed the assembly: "The green mountains rise in layers; the green waters flow on and on.
If you can realize this, you will walk alone in sublime transcendence. Even so, it is merely ordinary tea and rice. An ancient worthy said:
'If you wish to exhaust the view for a thousand li, you must ascend one more story. There is a saying from the past: 'If the function does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison.'"
If one’s words do not startle the listener, one falls into the common stream of worldly convention.

Yet, if one can distinguish the black from the white amidst the sparks struck from flint, and discern life from death within a flash of lightning, then one may sit and cut off all manifold differences, standing as steep as a ten-thousand-fathom cliff.
Do you know if there is such a time? Wrong! You have been exposed. Those who discuss Chan nowadays stand with their heels firmly planted on the ground and their nostrils reaching toward heaven.
Those who possess the True Eye are rare and few; thus, the biased and the correct are not unified, and each establishes its own heterodox path.
They stubbornly cling to their own interpretations and fail to penetrate the ultimate reality. As it is said: "When the Right Dharma is difficult to uphold, false dharmas flourish in competition.

An ancient proverb states: "If there is ten parts of faith, there will be ten parts of doubt; if there is ten parts of doubt, there will be ten parts of awakening. One should take this to heart... [within one's eyes].

Whatever is seen by the eyes and heard by the ears—whether it be evil thoughts and views, strange words and marvelous phrases, matters of Chan, the Way, or the Buddha-dharma, or even a mind of arrogance and conceit—pour them all out from the very depths;
do not retain even a hair’s breadth. Focus solely on those koans that remain unclarified and unresolved.
Plant your feet firmly, straighten your backbone, and without distinction between day and night, practice where there is no place to practice, and seek where there is no doubt.
Stuck in doubt, one is unable to distinguish east from west or south from north; remaining dazed and motionless, one is like a living corpse.

The mind is transformed by external conditions, yet it still knows when touched. If one were to smash open the skull and realize that [enlightenment] cannot be obtained from another, would this not bring lifelong joy?
Chan Master Ning of Yifeng at Taigang in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Cheng of Taigang, the eighth generation patriarch of Jing Mountain.
He was the son of the Qian family of Hangzhou. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent and his deportment was refined. His movements and gestures...
He was extraordinary. At the age of twelve, he had extensively mastered the classics and histories, yet he harbored no intention of serving the world.

He received the tonsure under the Venerable Shan of Xuefeng and personally attended Lingyin, where he questioned Xuegu. He served Miaofeng for many years; wherever the Master went, there was no one who could dismantle his spiritual mechanism.
Later, while serving Yuexi, a monk requested instruction, to which Yuexi replied: "The Buddha-dharma is not fresh fish; it fears rotting."
"Stop! he said, and immediately struck him. The Master attained great enlightenment while standing by his side.
Shimen Yun composed a verse praising this: "The imperial memorial reaches the Sovereign’s heart beyond the misty peaks; The jade insignia stand in solemn array, yet still lingering with affection."
Suddenly hearing the golden bells at dawn as he drew back the curtain, each person returned to their own quarters before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion.
Yuexi bestowed upon the Master a dharma verse, saying: "The mind can know the mind; the dharma can know the dharma.
The dharma-mind now entrusted to you is neither mind nor dharma. The Master succeeded Cheng in occupying the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind-king is sovereign; the nature of phenomena is without partiality.
All Buddha-activities are like the moon in water or flowers in the sky—originally quiescent. Old Śākyamuni is, in his entirety, within the crevice of your eyebrows.
Do you all understand? If you do not, Taigang shall descend for you into the Nirvana Hall."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In general, when upholding and proclaiming the fundamental principles of our school, one must possess three essentials.

The first essential is to clarify the essence and understand the intent, thereby discerning the heterodox from the orthodox. The second essential is to recognize the true body of the Great Way, which belongs neither to existence nor non-existence.
The third essential is to be able to let out the great lion’s roar, its majesty subduing all things. Possessing these three essentials is like a chariot having wheels or a bird having wings."
If its wings are broken, it cannot soar high; if its wheels are broken, it cannot move forward. The ancestral masters serve as eyes for those who come after;
if they do not possess these three essentials, how could they possibly exert their influence over all things? Nevertheless, the crux lies in receiving this under the first phrase.
Ascending the hall: If you do not understand this single phrase as a single phrase, the heavens have no four walls and ten-thousand-mile clouds vanish.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs knit their brows; gods and men lose heart. This brings grief to Kāśyapa, whose hair has turned white and teeth black.

If you understand this single phrase as a single phrase, you will mislead the thousands of sages and myriad worthies, emerging and submerging in birth and death, wearing horns and shrouding yourself in fur. [Within] the eye...
[Sand. Water in the ear. [He suddenly strikes the meditation bench with his staff and says:
"For now, let this pass. He ascends the hall and says: "The Great Master Linji said: 'If you realize it through the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher of Buddhas and patriarchs.
If you realize it through the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher of devas and humans. If you realize it through the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. Ciming—
The Way. To realize it through the first phrase is like mixing mud with water. To realize it through the second phrase is like binding oneself without a rope.
To realize it through the third phrase is like having all four corners touching the ground. The Master said: "Ciming only knows how to pour oil to save a burning fire;
he does not know how to apply medicine to remove the illness. Taogang, however, is not like this. To realize it through the first phrase, I shall bargain with you at the mountain gate."

As for the measure: if you can realize it in the second phrase, I will discuss it with you before the Sangha hall; if you can realize it in the third phrase, I will discuss it with you in the quarters.
Although Taigang makes the presentation in this way, everyone must understand it prior to the single thought-moment of its being raised;
there is a slight difference therein.
In the twenty-first year of the Chenghua era, he was commissioned by imperial decree to rebuild the mountain gate, receiving exceptionally generous honors.
On the third day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Hongzhi era, he manifested illness; at that time, a flock of cranes circled the hall as he passed away.
By imperial edict, he was posthumously granted the title Great Master Yuanming Pujue, and his stupa was named Jizhao.
Chan Master Guxin Baoshan of Niu-tou in Nanjing was the son of the Guo family of Chu and Xiang. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

While reading the *Zhongyong*, upon reaching the passage on "the non-emergence of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure," he attained a sudden and clear realization of the ultimate truth. He then paid his respects to Jubaizhang of Mount Nanyue and took him as his teacher.
Zao Daimai received full ordination. Hearing that Yuexi had returned to Taigang by imperial decree, he humbled himself to seek instruction from him.
One day, Yuexi presented the "Mu" (No-thing) koan, whereupon Zao attained thorough enlightenment. In the seventh year of the Jingtai era, he passed away.
Chan Master Dong Yongfu Zixiu of Huangmei was once asked by a monk: "Regarding 'true emptiness is not empty,' what is emptiness?

The Master said: "Beyond the kalpas there is nothing extraordinary; even a hair’s breadth is devoid of characteristics. The monk asked: "Regarding 'wondrous existence is not existent,' what is existence?"
The Master said, "Established according to conditions; how could it be confused with the ordinary? The monk asked, "When both emptiness and existence are severed, how can they not be severed?
The Master said, "Seven long, eight short."

Chan Master Xingtian Zonggao of Lingyin studied under Yuexi, investigating the "Mu" (No-Word) kōan. One day, by accident, he dropped and shattered a pure water jar, at which point he attained awakening.
He passed away in the second year of the Jingtai era (1451). His verse of farewell reads: "My illusory body has reached fifty-seven;
The affairs of daily life are profound and secret. Having shattered the barrier of the Patriarchs, A thunderclap resounds through the clear sky."
Chan Master Tianyuan Daozhan-yiyuan went to consult Yuexi for instruction. Yuexi said, "The Buddha-dharma is not fresh fish;
it is afraid you will let it rot. He then gave him a severe beating. One day, seeing flowing water, he attained realization.
When a monk asked Chan Master Guxin An of Deshan, "The entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa;
why then are there towers, pavilions, and halls? The Master said, "The moon over the楚天 (Heavenly River) is entirely hidden, yet the stars of the 漢地 (Han land) still remain."
Chan Master Zhongyong of Nanyang ascended the hall and said: "The Elder Yuexi has the Northern Dipper stored within his breast and his eyes cover heaven and earth.

I, the Monk Yong, have been unfortunate throughout my life in being exposed to his poisonous breath; today, before this assembly, I reveal it, yet I still end up making a fool of myself through my cleverness.
He struck the meditation staff and said: "Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!"
Chan Master Tianzhen Dufeng Shan of Hangzhou was the son of the Wu family of Fengyang. His father was serving in the government while traveling in Guangdong, and he was born in Leyang.
At the age of seventeen, he left the household life. Initially, he encountered Master Yuanming, who assigned him the "Mu" (No) koan.
The Master was able to attain realization immediately; when he presented this to Yuanming, Yuanming said, "For twenty years I have been looking at this 'Mu,' like a mosquito..."
Zishang climbed onto the Iron Ox. As soon as he began practicing the method, he already possessed many intellectual views. [Dongshan] spoke again, saying:
"Observing your capacity, you are unlike others; do not let yourself be deceived by people along the way, lest an elder lead you astray and ruin your great matter."
Having received the Master’s instruction, he immediately made a vow to apply himself single-mindedly to his practice, swearing that in this life he would take awakening as his goal.
Admiring the spiritual style of Master Wuji, he traveled to Sichuan to seek instruction. Later, when Master Wuji was summoned to the capital, he subsequently shut himself in a meditation cell.

He did not set up a bed, but placed only a small stool. When he grew weary from sitting, he would leave the stool. One day, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained realization and spoke this verse:
He said: "Profoundly still and utterly silent, all activity and effort are cut off. Upon contact, there is no beginning; it roars like thunder.
With one sound that shakes the earth, all news and traces vanish; the skull shatters and the dream first returns. He went again to visit [Zhao] Ji, but just as he arrived, Ji had passed away.
He then sought certification from Yuexi, who said: "The Buddha-dharma is not fresh fish; one fears it will rot. Day by day, strike east and strike west."
[Zhaozhou] struck him. [The Master] secretly set up an examination. One day, while attending Master Xixi, they were sitting in the garden.
Xixi asked, "Ultimately, what is the meaning of the word 'wu'? The Master said, "The thief is clearly exposed. Xixi said, "Setting aside the thief for a moment, bring me back the stolen goods.
The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. Xixi said, "Not yet—speak further. The Master said, "The night is short and my sleep is insufficient. Daylight.
Changji said, "There is a surplus. Xixi said, "When an ox passes through a window lattice, its head, body, and four legs all pass through;
why is it that the tail cannot pass? The Master said, "There is not a single dharma that stands before the mind; in an instant, one's entire being is revealed in the open field. Xixi said:
"Where are you now? Where do you dwell and establish your life? The Master replied, "Where would I not be honored as supreme?

Later, he took his leave of Xixi and traveled through Zhejiang, where he shut himself in seclusion at the Wanfeng Hermitage on Mount Tianmu. Yueshi also received an imperial decree conferring honors upon him and returned to Taogang in Jinling.

He sent a letter by messenger to entrust the Master with instructions. It happened that the Master had gone elsewhere on business when Xixi approached the time of his passing and issued his final charge.
He sent him off with a robe and a whisk. The Master resided on the mountain for over forty years.
During the Tianfùn era, he constructed the three pagodas at West Lake, as well as the Zhāomíng at Tíemù, the Bǎolián at Wúshān, and the Gānlù at Nánshān.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà era, he closed his retreat at Shíwū; later, he resided at Tiānzhēn. A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style? The Master said:

In front, the river tides are swift and fish travel with difficulty; behind, the mountain peaks are high and winds are fierce, making it hard for birds to settle. He passed away in the *Ren-yin* year and was interred at his home mountain.
Chan Master Gūyuè Jìngchéng of Wutai Mountain in Dàizhōu returned to Qīngliáng in the first year of the Tiānshùn era, at the invitation of the Prince of Dàizhōu.
He went to the inner palace to inquire after the Way, moved by the radiant brilliance illuminating the courtyard. The King was greatly pleased and treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.

He subsequently allocated his stipend to build a temple in Huayan Valley, naming it Pujie (Universal Salvation). His mountain-dwelling verse says: "Within the world, only Wutai is permitted to be high;
The person of no rank keeps company with the silent void. Let the winds from all quarters blow as fiercely as they will; My two eyes remain ever empty."
Looking toward the clouds and the sky.

Chan Master Daohui of Guanzhe was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huaisong of Huakong. A monk asked, "The vast and boundless source of spiritual wisdom—how is it realized? The Master then folded his hands.
Facing the monk as he entered for an audience, the Master said, "If you can utter a phrase that turns the body, I shall give you thirty blows of my staff;
if you cannot, then the rice in the basket and the soup in the bucket are yours to enjoy as you please. The monk had no reply.
While engaged in manual labor, Chan Master Dezhang Jingman of Jianning Dufeng saw that the monk Lang had a look of joy on his face.
Calling him forward, the Master asked, "How do you handle this koan? Lang replied, "I do not understand. The Master laughed heartily and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Chan Master Fuyuan Guang of Fengxue in Ruzhou, successor to Chan Master Miaofeng Xuan, ascended the hall and said: "A single hair manifests divine transformations; all Buddhas speak of it together.
He struck his staff, let out a shout, and descended from the seat.

Chan Master Shending Baozang Jingyu, a successor of Chan Master Tianchi Yi, ascended the hall and said: "An ancient worthy said, 'A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.
The Master laughed. He then said: 'The green vines wind their way up to the crest of the cold pine; the white clouds linger in quiet stillness.'"
Appearing and disappearing within the great void, he struck the ground once with his staff and descended from the seat.

Chan Master Wuyin Zhengdao of Yangshan, a successor of Chan Master Fu-niu Jian, ascended the hall and said: "This fellow existed even before the state of primordial chaos; he is manifest and perfectly realized."

He requested that the Master ascend the seat. The Master stepped forward and asked: "The thunderous voice shakes the earth; the field for selecting Buddhas is opened.
This single assembly at Vulture Peak remains solemnly as if it has not yet dispersed. I wonder, how may the Imperial Grace and the Buddha’s Grace be repaid? Chushan replied: "Vast and boundless."
The wind of Yao’s virtue purifies the six realms; the brilliant sun of the Buddha shines upon the three thousand worlds.
The Master said, "The jade plum pierces the snow; the crimson leaves wither in the frost. Where is the Dharma King’s golden countenance right now?

Shan竖 (Shan-zu) held up his whisk and said, "It is upon this mountain monk’s whisk, having attained equal and perfect enlightenment and emitting great radiance. The Master said, "In this way, the entire realm is free from concealment."
Mount said, "There are eyes that cannot see. The Master said, "In the place where it is not seen, there is not the slightest separation. Mount said, "This is the subtle.
The Master said, "What is the subtle? Mount said, "When both extremes have been wiped away, only then does one see the person prior to the kalpas."
The Master said, "Having been pointed out by you, my teacher, the adamantine eye, I have no further doubt regarding death and rebirth. Xiangshan said, "How brilliant is this monk!
Your words express the essence of our school; you shall not be made a successor to Xichan. The Master said, "May humans and devas bear witness; I thank you for your seal of approval."
He left the world. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "A hundred does not equal one.
The monk asked, "What is the matter that has been transmitted? The Master said, "In this place, there is no room for talk; it is transmitted as a smile before the pivot of the mind."
Chan Master Wuxiang Zhen was serving as the head gardener at Mount Dongshan.
When Chushan entered the garden and saw the master binding a gourd vine to a frame, he pointed to the gourd and asked, "This one has no mouth; why does it grow so large?
The master replied, "I have never been idle for a single moment. Chushan said, "Does your 'true host' (the self) exert any effort on your behalf? The master said, "I rely entirely upon him."
Mount [Shishuang] said, "Come out and meet this old monk. The Master bowed. The Mountain said, "You are still just a servant boy.

The Master picked up a bamboo splint and bound it into a frame. The Mountain looked at his attendant monk and said, "There are insects in the vegetable garden. Later, the Master received the Dharma from Xuefeng.
Chan Master Taichuxingyuan composed a verse on the question, "What is the most bitter? It says: Before the wind, a single melody stirs the sorrow of parting;
It provokes the sufferings of the three realms of existence, which never cease. Turning one's head, the cold pond reflects a void of azure; The evening sun sinks in the west as the waters flow east.
Chan Master Zhengfa Xueguang of Qianzhong was a successor of Chan Master Jiekong Tong. His clan name was Zhao. Having traveled through various regions, he spent the summer retreat at Lingfeng.
Upon hearing the kōan concerning Venerable Yan’yang’s question to Master Zhaozhou, he attained realization. He related this to Jizhao, who said, “It is effortless.”

This is precisely the point where you must apply your efforts; do not mistake some mere glimmering light for the truth, lest it mislead your entire life. He again entered the winter retreat at Jingde Monastery.
One day, while in meditative absorption, he was triggered by the sound of a mountain waterfall. He silently brought to mind the kōans and pivotal encounters of the Buddhas and patriarchs of the past.

Having thoroughly penetrated each point, he went to visit Jie Kong and recounted his realizations from the beginning. Jie Kong said, "Have you not heard it said: 'Do not say that mindlessness is the Way;
even mindlessness still leaves one separated by a further barrier'? Having spoken thus, he entered his quarters.
From then on, the Master was at a loss, his mind devoid of direction as he harbored doubts and could not reach a resolution. One day, he saw a poem by Hanshan: "My mind is like the autumn moon..."
At these words, his doubts and obstructions were instantly resolved. Later, he lived as a hermit at Gusan. When the time of his death approached, he wrote a verse and passed away.
Chan Master Wuben of Bohu Deran studied under Chusan; his practice was pure and singular.
One day, he asked Baishan, "Who is it that does not encounter cold or heat? Shanshan replied, "What did I just say to you? As the Master was about to respond, Shanshan—
He shouted, saying, "The moment you conceive a thought, you have already deviated. The Master said, "So that is how it is? Shanshan asked, "What principle have you seen?
The Master replied, "Face and features are distinct; they are not revealed when the occasion arises. Later, he studied under Jie Kong and attained the Dharma.
At Shimen Mountain in Qizhou, Chan Master Huangjing Yin of Kanhai studied under Jiekong. Jiekong presented the "Mu" (No) kōan and instructed the master to provide a response;
after forty turns, he remained in discord with the teaching. The master asked, "Is there no expedient means? Jiekong then presented a verse by Shuzhong.
The Master attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words.
Chan Master Wuyong Wenquan of Huguo Temple on Mount Cha in Fengyang Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Bafeng Tan. He was a native of the Liu family in Shanghe County, Jinan.
At the age of nineteen, he went to Lingyan to shave his head. Initially, he met Yuetian, who bestowed upon him the essential points of the Dharma.
Subsequently, he studied under Bietuan and attained realization. Bietuan asked, "The void has shattered and the great earth has sunk flat;
where do you dwell and establish your life? The Master replied, "Last night the clay ox swallowed the bright moon; this morning the wooden horse breathes forth the pure wind. Bietuan said, "One..."
"Where has he gone? [The Master] said, "Since the white ox returned to the snowy peaks, its traces have not been seen until this very day.
Chang-chen nodded in approval. He then went to Mount Jin to visit Wujie, who instructed him to see Bao-yue. Bao-yue asked, "Do you have the money for straw sandals?
The Master replied, "The green mountains do not show their peaks. Bao-yue asked, "How is it that you manifest form in response to things? The Master replied, "Solitary..."
The light of the moon shines universally across the heavens; the myriad phenomena of the universe are fully manifested. One day, Dayue entered the room and, while seated, cried out, "Cold!
Cold! The Master then moved the brazier forward toward him. Dayue asked, "What is the matter by the brazier?"
The Master struck the brazier three times. Yue smiled and went out. Upon entering the room again, Yue held up his staff and said, "This is the staff;
tell me, where is the host? The Master snatched the staff away, threw it to the ground, and stood with his hands folded.
Yue said, "Look! This fellow has run right into the staff! The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Later...
Having received the seal of approval, he went forth into the world at Mount Cha. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it manifests only by relying on conditions.

The Way is fundamentally wordless, yet it is revealed through words. Now, with dragons and elephants gathered together and the various mountain monasteries dwelling in harmony, this is no small occasion.
It is due to the profound grace of His Majesty the Emperor, the protection of worthy scholars and officials, the joyful generosity of donors, and the pure cultivation of the monastic community."

He established a period for meditation to assist in this sacred transformation, charging the mountain monk to propagate the eye of the school so that those in the final age might plant seeds in the field of merit.
Even so, this is still not yet the matter beneath the patched robe. Tell me, what is the matter beneath the patched robe?
A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles; as for the matter of direct pointing, how is it? The Master said, "The Double Peak."

A crane perches upon a tree atop the peak; beneath the Nine Dragon Mountains, birds sing and flowers bloom. [The student] asked: "The meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West has been pointed out by you, Master;
how is the matter transmitted here in the Eastern Land? The Master said: "On the ridge, the wind is eternally elegant;
by the stream, the flowing water is ten thousand years pure. He asked: "What is the realm of Baishui? The Master said: "A single expanse of wasteland stretches across the four fields; three..."
A thatched hut stands amidst the grandeur of the myriad mountains. [The monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm?

The Master said, "The Imperial Temple at the head of the White Tiger; the royal foundation at the bottom of the Black Dragon Pool. [The monk] asked, "When both person and realm are forgotten, what then?
The Master said, "Su Wu did not understand the intent of the green ram; Qi Lang always lamented the white crow’s return. The monk bowed. The Master struck the desk once.
[The Master] descends from his seat. A monk enters for an audience. The Master asks: "What is the essential teaching of Gaofeng? The monk replies:
"A stone horse neighs in the wind beyond the mundane world; a golden rooster cries out before the imperial palace. The Master says: "What extraordinary thing is there? The monk replies:

"If one does not meet a true connoisseur, it is all in vain to speak of the severity of winter. The Master says: "The patriarchs have transmitted this to one another; what exactly have they transmitted? The monk replies: "The bottom of the sea."
The clay ox overturns the great waves; amidst the forest, the stone woman fans a pure breeze. The Master said, "The entire earth is fully revealed.
Who is it that enjoys this? He replied, "Li Erge of the eastern village. The Master said, "How can that mountain be so high?

He replied, "It is simply because it forces its head out. The Master said, "How can this mountain be so low? He replied, "Because it speaks of things that are not clever. The Master looked to his left.
The one on the right said, "There is a snake in the grass. He replied, "Watch out for the dog's leg! The Master said, "A-ye, A-ye! (Alas! Alas!)
Chan Master Dahui Juehua of Chongfu Temple in Nanjing ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he said:
"Beyond the limit of Vipaśyin Buddha, it was originally just this very thing; even now, before our eyes, it is also just this very thing. He swept the whisk up and down and said:
"If you call it a whisk, you blind the eyes of humans and devas; if you do not call it a whisk, you also blind them."
He puts to rest the eyes and faces of gods and men. Great assembly, tell me: what do you call this?
If you can understand it here, you will know the reason for Kāśyapa’s smile and why the Second Patriarch could not find his mind when he sought it.

You will know how the lamp of the Tathāgata was transmitted and the true pulse of the ancestral temple was continued—linking the brilliance of twenty-eight generations and inheriting the marrow and bones of thirty-four.
The assembly remained silent. The Master struck them with his whisk and said, "Not recognized by the thousand sages.
Chan Master Mota Xuan of Tianning Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture first visited Chushan, where he suddenly realized the subtle essence of the teachings. Later, he went to study under Bafeng.
When Bafeng raised the case of Yunmen’s bestowing of three blows of the staff upon Dongshan, the Master spoke of it in terms of the path of conceptualization. Bafeng rebuked him.
The Master forgot both sleep and food. One day, he happened to hear a monk from a neighboring cell mention that five hundred arhats had subdued a venomous dragon.
The Master sprang up from his seat in great excitement. The monk said, "Is this fellow mad? and gave him a slap. When [the monk] saw Feng, [he realized his mistake].
Feng said, "To open your mouth is already an error. Show me some sign of your realization. The Master made three prostrations with the words, "I take my leave.
Feng gave him his deep approval. One day, he bestowed upon the Master a verse, saying: "The meaning of the flower held up in the land of India, The principle of the arm severed at Mount Song.
This transmission from humans and devas is now entrusted to you; It has neither beginning nor end."

If anyone composed such works privately, he would investigate the truth of it and expel them. When his disciples requested a final verse at the time of his death, the Master said, "This old monk has never had a single word or half-sentence in my ordinary life;
why make this superfluous addition? He then sat upright and passed away.

Chan Master Jichan Qian of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Zhong of Tianning, offered this verse on the end of summer and the beginning of autumn: "The jeweled halls and jade towers lock away the void;
The steps and courtyards are clear and green, their shadows blurred. The eye of Maheśvara is blinded at the crown of the head; Empty hangs the [medicine bag] behind the elbow."
The Life-Seizing Talisman. A monk asked, "What is the person of original nature? The Master said, "In front of the donkey, behind the horse.
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You wretched fellow! You cannot even recognize good from evil."
Chan Master Yonggang Zongruan of Mingzhou studied under Guzhou, receiving the kōan of the "Three Not Is.
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn era, he visited He’ān. One day, as He’ān was ascending the hall, he said: "The mind-seal of the Patriarchs is like the mechanism of an iron ox:
if you go toward it, it stays fixed; if you stay still, it breaks through. Neither going nor staying—how will you deal with this? The Master, standing by his side, attained great rest.
Xie. After settling into his residence, he addressed the assembly: "In general, when practicing the Way, one must simply give rise to a great state of doubt and maintain right mindfulness.
A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. As soon as there is an interruption, you have already fallen into views.
You practitioners have not yet spent half a month or a month to achieve 'one piece. How could you avoid wandering astray? If it were truly a genuine doubt..."
When it manifests before you, shake it and it will not move; naturally, you will have no fear of being deluded or distracted. Furthermore, you must not give rise to even a single thought of joy.
Should there be even the slightest aberrant thought, strike it down immediately as two separate pieces.
Simply maintain a state of fierce, relentless intensity, remaining all day long like a dead man. When you reach such a state, what need is there to fear a turtle escaping from its jar?
Chan Master Tianran Zonghao of Huangmei Guangfu was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhichen Foji. Once, a monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Carrying tea and passing the cup.
The monk asked, "What is one who is on the Way? The Master said, "The servile countenance and the crouching knees of a slave."
After Chan Master Baofang Zang of Bieping retired from his post at Foji Temple, he lived for over twenty years wearing a lotus-leaf robe and eating pine nuts.
He eventually built a pointed hut by a cliff, as expressed in the verse: "A broken-legged bed leans against the crumbling rocks.
When a monk came to visit, the Master brandished his staff and danced, saying, "You are a thief; I am also a thief! The monk let out a long sigh and departed.
Chan Master Wuliang Cang of Baimu in Chuzhou addressed the assembly: "During the twelve periods of the day and night, follow the *huatou* while walking;
follow the *huatou* while standing; follow the *huatou* while sitting; follow the *huatou* while lying down.
Let the mind be like a chestnut burr, so that it cannot be swallowed or devoured by any personhood, ego-clinging, ignorance, the five desires, or the three poisons. Thus he acted.
In movement and stillness, one's entire body is a single mass of doubt. Doubting on and on—doubting the profound mystery—one remains dazed and motionless all day long.
Upon hearing a sound or seeing a form, you may take it for granted that there will be a sudden "clunk" of realization.
