"I entrust this to you. Take it and offer it throughout all lands as numerous as motes of dust.
Jinming Xu said, "Wuhuan is much like a single rolling pearl on a tray; the more it is polished, the more it shines.
That he sought verification from the Patriarch and obtained a clear title—this too is merely robbing the thief of his own home."
While the Master was tending the fire, a monk asked, "What is the self-nature, the original, true Buddha? Huanchu replied, "Bring me some firewood.
After the monk had brought the firewood, he repeated his previous question. The Master said, "This little slave does not even know good from bad," and struck him.
Jingshan submitted this verse: Great wealth must return to the house of the patriarch; naturally, there is a livelihood wherever one is.
Pitifully, failing to recognize the treasure within the world, one mistakes genuine gold for red sand.
Master Mu praises him, saying: "The fish swimming beneath his feet he knows not at all; out of pity for the [咸*鳥] and [感*鳥] birds, how can he be so deluded?"
How many are there who betray righteousness and forget kindness, possessing nothing more than a pair of arched eyebrows?
An iron-faced man’s dark verse says: "Young men of Chang’an pity the fading flowers; Who recognizes the purple peony of Ci’en?"
Separately, there is a jade platter bearing dew that is cold; no one rises to go and gaze upon it within the moon.
Qianfu’s lofty eulogy says: "Seeking the spring colors at the mouth of the Peach Blossom Spring, the rustic old man calls out repeatedly, 'It is here within!'"
Wandering through the gardens, he still asks the way; unaware that he stands amidst ten thousand blossoms.

While two guests were playing chess, a monk requested instruction. The Master said, "If one discusses this matter, it is like two families playing chess; there are few who do not achieve victory if they apply their minds. Why is this?
If you do not first understand the layout of the board, every move you make will surely be completely wrong. He was not skilled [in explaining].
As for expedient means: wherever one encounters adversity, it is simply because the "horse of the mind" has been lost and the "wild elephant" is without a hook.

One does not recognize the chariot of the army; the mechanism of the mind is coarse, and one constantly travels through perilous terrain. Not only will one repeatedly suffer defeat, but one will soon see the skin torn and blood flowing.
If the commander-in-chief is majestic and stern, the path for the soldiers will be level. In such a state, the cannons do not fire in vain; once they are fired—

Breaking through the heavy encirclement, the troops advance without disorder. Who would dare to retreat as they press straight forward? Like celestial horses chasing the wind from all eight directions, the divine chariot proceeds with no barriers at all.
Not only does this lead to victory and the accomplishment of merit, but ultimately it is like the wind blowing over the grass, which bends in submission.
After a long silence, he said, "Great Peace was originally settled by the General; we do not permit the General to see Great Peace.
A monk asked, "What is the Tīpā school? The Master said, "A single character does not admit of a stroke. [The monk] said, "I am not asking about that."
The Master said: "A perfect circle does not adhere to its circumference.

Yunwei of the Second Patriarch asked: "If you wish to understand that a single character does not adhere to its strokes, then when it comes to a perfect circle not adhering to its circumference—you must retreat three thousand li!"
The Master resided at Chexi for over twenty years, daily discussing the Great Matter with his disciples; there was none who did not submit with joy.

In the thirty-eighth year of the Wanli era, he returned to reside at Mount Jing. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Way has no front or back; the Ultimate Principle is beyond words and explanations.
It transcends the Three Vehicles and towers above the Ten Stages. Where the ten thousand dharmas do not reach, there is a singular brilliance. Life..."
Before the Buddha had yet divided [the teachings], the spiritual source shone alone, falling neither into seeing nor hearing, nor following sound nor form.

Directly beneath it, there was not so much as a single hair’s breadth; it was fully manifest throughout the entire world. Even if one were to attain realization through the staff or take responsibility under a shout, this would still be a mere accommodation to the times.
Should one forget all appearances and accord with the mind in its state of equality, even this is not the ultimate point. Therefore it is said:
The upward path has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections.

Upon reaching this point, there is no practice and no understanding, no illumination and no function, no principle and no phenomenon. It is like a long sword leaning against the heavens, its divine majesty awe-inspiring.
Like the mechanism of an iron ox, it cannot be confined within a cage. Today, before those with clear eyes, I dare not hide it away or cover it over;
I open it wide, revealing the eight characters. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you all understand? Shining through antiquity and soaring through the present, this is precisely it:
the great trichiliocosm is but a single idle body."
While he was ill, a monk asked, "Where will you go after the Master passes away? The Master said, "Bent and curved among a thousand pine trees;
leaping and bounding wildly at the tips of the hundred grasses."
The Buddha said: "When Che-xi answers in this manner, one knows that for future generations throughout the world, ten thousand lamps and myriad flames shall issue from beneath his feet.

If a monk were to ask about the hands and feet used by Che-xi when he threatened to kill the *jia* and nearly killed the Head Seat, and waited until Che-xi had just begun to respond, [the monk] would cover his ears and leave—merely to test the old fellow."
On the fourth day of the late winter month of the Xinhai year of the Wanli era, he rose from his seat and departed. To the Head Seat Chuan Guang, he spoke this verse regarding his *kāṣāya*:
"Before the stupa, there was little to entrust; among the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, who would seek it? I do not know who has leaked this secret, which remains to this day."
"Calamities will reach their descendants.
Diru said, "I have examined the *Chuan deng lu*. Only Nanyue served Caoxi for eight years, saying only:
'To describe it as being like any thing is already off the mark. Yet he attracted a horse that can keep pace with the wind. Nanming served Chuxi for eight years..."
In the end, he obtained nothing but a tattered kashaya robe. Tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different?
*Chan*. He sat upright and passed away. His body was cremated and a stupa erected at Mount Jing; he was seventy-two years old and had thirty years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Hanshan Deqing of Caoxi in Shaoyou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yungu Hui. His courtesy name was Chengyin. He was the son of Cai of Quanpiao.

At the age of seven, he witnessed his paternal aunt give birth to a child and subsequently saw her die; this immediately gave rise to doubts regarding birth and death, coming and going. He was twelve years old when—
He took Master Xilin Ning as his teacher at Nanjing Ba’en Temple. At that time, Yungu Hui of Jiaxing was residing at Qixia Ba’en;

the Master served him with great diligence, and Yungu opened his mind and awakened him to the true nature of the mind. The Master then requested Xilin to grant him the tonsure, whereupon he burned all the texts of his previous secular studies.
He visited Wuji to receive full ordination and listened to lectures on the *Huayan Xuantan* (Profound Discourses on the Avatamsaka Sutra).
Record. In the year Yi-chou, I entered the Zen retreat at Tianjie Temple under Master Gu. He raised me into the hall and showed me the ultimate core of the teaching.
In the year Xin-wei, I took my leave of Gu to travel north. Gu said, "My great Dharma rests upon your shoulders; be careful not to treat it lightly."

While reading the *Wuqianlun* (Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things) in his residence, he reached the section on the Brahmin’s renunciation of the world and suddenly attained full realization of the lines concerning "the whirlwind that topples mountains.
His doubts regarding birth-and-death and coming-and-going were thereby resolved, and he composed a verse: "Birth-and-death are day and night; The water flows and the flowers wither.
Today I finally know: The nostrils point downward. In the year Yihai, he paid homage to Mañjuśrī at Longmen on Mount Wutai and settled in a thatched hut on Mount Kuang.
Chekong (Chechong) and Yunqi Lianchi followed in succession to enter the mountains, where their discourse with the Master was in perfect accord.

In the second month of winter in the year of Xinsi, the Empress Dowager Cisheng established a ritual site for praying for an heir at the Great Pagoda Temple on Mount Wutai for one hundred and twenty-two days;
the Master and Miaofeng were the presiding masters of this affair. In the eighth month of the year of Renwu, King Gwangjong was born. In the year of Guiwei...
In the spring, he retired to Mount Laoshan in the eastern sea and restored the Nārāyaṇa Cave. Although Empress Cisheng summoned him twice, he did not comply.

In the year Jiashen (1574), she finally obtained the Master and immediately granted him funds from the imperial treasury. Following the ancient precedent of issuing a forged edict to relieve famine, the Master used these funds to provide relief for the people of Shandong.

In the year Bingxu (1576), Empress Cisheng bestowed the Tripitaka scriptures and provided gold for the construction of a temple, granting it the name Haiyin. In the year Dinghai (1577), the construction was completed.
He immediately opened his forge. In the year Jǐchǒu (1439), he invited the Tripitaka to Nánjīng Bào'ēn Temple. He was moved by the radiance emitted from the Precious Pagoda.

In the year Yǐwèi (1455), he was arrested due to slanderous rumors spread by a court sorcerer; though summoned to the Imperial Prison for interrogation, no evidence was found, and he was instead charged with privately establishing a monastery.

He was sent to serve as a military guard at Leizhou Commandery. On his way there through Jiangxi, he was welcomed by Zou Yuanbiao to Tiefo Monastery, where they reached a profound accord in a single conversation;

their former animosity was instantly overturned. In the year of Bingshen, he paid homage to the Sixth Patriarch and arrived at the You Gong Pavilion west of the city to reside during his term of exile.

Due to famine and pestilence in Leizhou, the Master gathered and buried tens of thousands of corpses, established an Ullambana assembly, and preached the Precepts for the Netherworld. Heaven... [greatly responded].

It rained, and the pestilence ceased accordingly. On the wu-xu day, he compiled the *Tongzhi* (Comprehensive Gazetteer) of Caoxi. He commanded his attendant Lingtong to return the wine and sell it to purchase fields;
the slaughterhouses and taverns were all converted into sacred sites (*ratnasthāna*). Thus, the Way of Dajian flourished once again.
The Master cites the causal conditions for Yunmen’s statement, “Light not penetrating through has two kinds of causes,” and offers this verse: Flowers and moonlight shimmer along the imperial street;
Intoxicated by the eastern breeze, one leans alone upon the balustrade. After the morning audience, when the nine palaces are hushed, The six courts still adjust their robes and caps.
A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still any transgression? Yunmen said, "Mount Sumeru. The verse says:
The sky is cold, the frost falls, and the moon sinks in the west; The clear night stretches on as the crane’s dream wanders lost. The sun’s orb beneath the sea is red as fire;
Yet the traveler still hears the cock crow at the fifth watch.
A verse on the occasion of Deshan’s alms-bowl: "Leisurely watching the lion deceive its cub, Yawning and stretching, exerting all his strength;
Touched, he turns over and flings it with a toss, Then lowers his head and returns, bringing the teaching to full completion. Summer of the Jia-yin year.
When the imperial decree arrived announcing that the Empress Dowager had passed away, the Master returned to his monastic robes.

In the year Ding-si, he established Fayun Temple at the foot of Wuru Peak on Mount Lu, where he emulated Master Huiyuan by practicing the Pure Land path during the six periods of the day. In the Ren-xu year of the Tianqi era, he returned to reside at Caoxi.
On the eleventh day of the tenth month of the Gui-hai year, he manifested a slight illness; having bathed and burned incense, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell and said: "Now..."
One day, he severed all entanglements and passed away while sitting upright. His secular age was seventy-eight, and his monastic seniority was sixty.

He had authored more than twenty works, including commentaries on the *Dream-Travel Collection* (*Mengyou ji*) and various sutras and treatises. In the year of Yichu (1625), his reliquary shrine was returned to Wuru Mountain, where it was enshrined in a stupa.
In the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era (1643), people from Guangdong again escorted the shrine back to Caoxi. Twenty years having passed, he sat upright as before.
Hesheng then had his body lacquered in gold and ascended the throne; he was enshrined facing the *mummified body* (meishen) of the Sixth Patriarch.
He was provided with offerings at the site of the old stupa monastery on Tianshi Ridge, named Hanshan Monastery, located about half a li from Nanhua Temple.
Li Yuanyang, a lay practitioner of Juelin on Zhongxi, was exceptionally intelligent from birth; he could recite any text after reading it once.

Initially, he received instructions in the arts of *dhyāna* and *prāṇāyāma* from a Daoist adept, believing that the state of a transcendent immortal (*siddha*) could certainly be attained through them. Later, upon reading the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, he was greatly astonished and exclaimed, "Is there such a scripture as this in the world?
Thereupon, he devoted himself to the Buddhist canon and delighted in associating with monks, adopting the name Juelin ("Awakening Forest").
When the Layman was serving at the imperial court, he frequently attended Dharma assemblies and met Yungu, from whom he subsequently received certification of his realization.

Together with the two masters Moan and Dingtang, he formed a bond beyond the secular world. His writings include the *Record of the Source of Chan* (*Chanyuan ji*) and the *Collected Drafts of Zhongxi* (*Zhongxi leigao*).
It circulated throughout the world.
Zen Master Longchi Wen was the dharma heir of Zen Master Tianmu Lanfeng Zhending.
A native of the Chen family of Yuyao, he possessed spiritual capacity from his youth and had long admired the Chan school.
At the age of twenty, Zong took the master Xuan of Tianmu as his teacher. Not long after, he traveled to Mount Wutai. Thirteen years later, he arrived at Tiexi Temple in Xuzhou.
One night, while the wind blew open the temple doors, he attained a profound realization. He subsequently went to consult with Longchi.
Having attained the Seal of the Mind (Cittamudrā), he traveled through various regions for more than thirty years. Between the Yangtze and the Huai rivers, his reputation became widely renowned.

The Master once composed a verse on "Responding to Sentiments According to Conditions," which includes the lines: "Seated in Bodhi throughout the realms as numerous as atoms, turning the Wheel of Dharma without moving a single hair.
The Master authored the *Binghu Zongjian* (The Mirror of the School of the Ice Pitcher) and a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, totaling twenty-seven [volumes].

[This work] circulated in the world. On the eighth day of the first month of the Renwu year of the Wanli era, he manifested a slight illness; by the fifteenth day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Chan Master [Name] of Ehu in Guangxin Prefecture was the son of the Zhu family of Shangrao in the prefecture. He once encountered a relative...

When he joined the assembly on Mount Dao, they were discussing the meaning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). At these words, the Master thoroughly realized the great significance of the equality of self and others.
He went to Datong in Luoyang to shave his head, then returned south to Jiaoshan to observe the winter retreat.

While pushing a boat upon the river, he attained a profound realization. His verse says: "The night is still, the river vast and empty; The sound of the boat being pushed, *li-li*. I know not where it goes—this burden."
One side was light. He heard this from Yeh Huashan, who presented the saying: "A lifetime's livelihood, neither six nor seven.
For seven days, he applied himself with fierce intensity until his body and mind were liberated. He then returned to his native village and resided at Lingshan.

He drew a great circle on the wall and said: "Write 'do not let it be blackened' inside; write 'do not let it be marred by white' outside. If anyone can apply themselves within or outside the circle...
If you can grasp the sub-commentary, I grant that you have no doubt in your study of the Way; otherwise, it will all be nothing but failure. Later, he resided at Gēhú.
For ten years, no seat-holder (abbot) had been established. Boshan went to visit him and attained accord through the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou.

He was invited to occupy the position, and [the master] presented him with a verse, saying: "For ten years at Gehu, the seat remained vacant; In an instant, how could the seat be established for one so young?
Two eyebrows and eight strands— One must know that Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot stand before it. He once set up the 'Gateless Lock'... [The text ends here.]
A blank wall. To verify this for all quarters, he spoke a verse: "The locks have been passed down since ancient times; Rely on your own wisdom-key to open them.

If you lack the method for opening the lock, Though we meet, there is no need to come. On the final day of the second month in the Dingmao year of the Wanli era, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma.
He concluded the funeral feast and offered this verse: "Within eighty-odd years of illusory dreams, the iron ox has plowed through the great void.
At the moment of departure, I entrust you with this one phrase: at midnight, the golden sun bears its crimson light. He then sat upright and passed away.

Chan Master Yun’an Zhenji of Foyan on Mount Wudang in Junzhou was a successor of Chan Master Fuli of Fu Niu. During the reign of Emperor Shenzhong, he recited the Tripitaka for Empress Dowager Cisheng and was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Lingying Temple;
his imperial favor was exceedingly great, and he was granted the honorary title of "Great Master Wubai" (Non-Dual).

Ascending the hall to instruct the assembly, [the Master] said: "Bimao’s staff; carrying snow to fill the well. Heshan’s drum; scattering sand in the eyes. Starving and hollow, they constrain themselves;
entering the Dharma Hall with their alms bowl. Suddenly picking up his whisk, he said: 'This lot of people guarding ancient tombs—how many times have they failed to grasp the essential?
Today they have fallen into the hands of Foyan; if I do not pierce their nostrils, I shall surely gouge them out.'"
Your eyes—why do they not enter the surging waves? Only then can you see the one who plays amidst the tide.
The Dharma heir of Chan Master Chong of Mount Jing, the thirteenth generation successor of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Nanyue Huiguang of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Han family of Yanguan. He received the tonsure under Qinquan at Xingshan Monastery.

Aspiring to the study of Chan, he lamented that the tradition’s influence had not yet flourished; thus, he traveled extensively through lecture halls before returning once more to close himself in retreat behind a barred door.
Regarding wordless discourse, he remained in profound stillness until he realized that the principle of things was fundamentally one.

Having heard that Gu-zhan possessed a sincere resolve, he went to the mountain pass to seek him out and inquire; immediately, there was a karmic affinity between teacher and disciple. He then opened the pass and proceeded to visit Gu-zhan at Che-xi.

Not long after, he entered Baiyun Mountain, the former hermitage of Gu-zhan, where he observed the *jinzu* (ascetic retreat) for three years. The elder Jifeng of Mount Jing invited Gu-zhan to expound the Dharma.
Whenever the Master heard his instructions, he would invariably shed tears and investigate them with intense diligence. One day, while casually picking up a scrap of paper, he came across the lines:
"Only by observing the direction does one know where it goes; that which goes does not arrive at the direction. Upon this, he attained realization. He presented this to Gu-zhan, who...

He gave his seal of approval and immediately appointed the Master as the head of the assembly. He then bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "The attainment of the source is no attainment; the transmission likewise has nothing to be transmitted.
Now I transmit this dharma that cannot be transmitted; east and west share one single sky."
The Eulogy by Tian Duo Yuan says: For eight years with bowl and cloth cap, he has exhausted himself to the bone; The great trichiliocosm is gathered within the tip of a single hair.
How pitiful, at a place where the house is ruined and the people are lost, He still treats the envelope as a letter to be read.
Hu Ji’s eulogy says: Suddenly severing doubt, he probes the profound from afar; In the void of the kalpa-vessel, the wondrous is difficult to describe.
Now, gathered upon the tip of a single hair, A single roll of thunderous sound pervades the great trichiliocosm.
Kim Myeong-uk’s verse says: The Tribute of Yu inherited the virtue of Yao and Shun; Its flourishing brilliance still reveals the spirit of Han and Tang.
At this time, there is no need to inquire about the "End-gong" (reigning with hands folded); The imperial enterprise of maintaining fullness has already reached the present day.
Yushan Yue’s Verse: The River produced the diagrams; the Luo produced the books. Lantian yields fine jade; the dark waters nurture the black pearl.
This immortal form is not of human breed; Hiding its body within the shell, it serves as delicacy for the imperial kitchen.
Shimen’s Verse on the Clouds says: Leaping up from the cauldron of boiling water, one ascends the mountain of knives; The breath gathers between the brows, as vast as the sea.
Turning the head, one strikes the drum of lethal poison; Blood flows over the earth, its light chilling the heart.

Staying at Mount Jing, he addressed the assembly: "The five peaks stand out with bold clarity; the two paths of Mount Jing reach to the very heavens. At the Shihyan Cliff, [the Master] leaps and bounds."
"Clear moon, bright pool, leaning toward heaven. These four phrases: in one phrase there is the "sword that kills" but no "sword that gives life";
in another phrase there is the "sword that gives life" but no "sword that kills"; in another phrase both the "sword that kills" and the "sword that gives life" are present;
and in another phrase neither the "sword that kills" nor the "sword that gives life" is present. A sharp-witted monk must be able to discern these distinctions.
"The matters of a lifetime of study are finished.
Kongzhuxing said, "Beyond the four propositions, there is still one sentence that possesses all hundred flavors; it is not merely a matter of killing or enlivening.
Although Nanming has indeed reached this, he has ultimately been unable to bring it forth. Now tell me, what is that one sentence? Liang [replied].
Jiuyun said, "To look at it is to go blind.
Jibei Hong said, "Chu’s yellow paper has become expensive; one document settles the matter.
He addressed the assembly, pointing his whisk at this mark and saying, "At the very beginning, Jingshan had only this one move."
Thereupon, he stood firm on his heels. One thrust after another, the more he investigated, the further away he went. Suddenly, one day, without investigating, there was investigation;
without exhausting [the inquiry], there was exhaustion. Neither investigating nor exhausting, he unconsciously realized that all his clever stratagems were suddenly empty.
Startled, he looked back and drew this symbol (☯), saying: "It turns out it was always just this. Only then did he know this. He then drew another symbol (○).
He said, "It is precisely this very thing. Brothers, tell me: how can you understand this?
Only when you possess a single eye here will you be permitted to arrive home."
Addressing the assembly: Leaping out of the diamond circle, he pulverizes the bones of empty space; cleaving open the secret treasury, he releases sands of Buddhas.

Taking grand strides across the vast expanse, he wondrously maneuvers within the world; he finely shears the white clouds into seven or eight fragments, and densely arranges the yellow chrysanthemums in clusters of one or two.
The heart of the ancient Buddhas and the intent of the patriarchs are all revealed at once—majestic and imposing are these dragon-elephants.
There are many eyes and ears; why then do you not see and hear? [The Master] suddenly held up his whisk, struck the meditation seat, and said:
"In this very place, upon a single movement you see, and with a single strike you hear. Upon this mass of flesh, there is nothing that is not present, and nothing that is not empty.
Within it, the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—are manifested. Within it, the ten stages of the sages and the three levels of the worthies find their rest."

To take formlessness as one's body and to take the empty dharma as a phenomenon: in its intensity, it responds to the myriad existences without end; in its stillness, not a single dharma can be found.
This is the point of numinous clarity, like a pearl resting in a bowl. By means of this, the mind is illuminated—what mind would not be clear?
By means of this, principle is manifested—what principle would not be revealed? Thus it is said: "If you seek through the marks of intention, you will be biased."
Seeing. Without a mind to observe or grasp, the essence is fully manifest. Everyone must investigate this at the very base of their heels before you can attain it.
To the assembly on New Year’s Eve: In the year before last, the nostrils were missing half; In last year, the two eyes could not be whole.
This year’s age is thirty; my refined bones are offered to the blue heavens. I have already finished speaking on my meditation; what do you all make of it? *Chan*.
Addressing the assembly on New Year’s Day: There is the Buddha-dharma in the New Year; Zhao Er drinks village wine until Li Ma-hu falls drunk. Wang... *Wang*.
A third laugh breaks his mouth open: "In the New Year, there is no Buddha-dharma. Pressing a gourd upon the water, a cloud of dust rises from the bottom of the sea.
Majestic and imposing, yet halfway along the path—this which the ancients could not grasp or lift up, Jingshan thus proclaims.
Is there any Buddha-dharma here to be deliberated? Joining his palms in greeting, he says: "The first day of the new year begins its reign; all things are renewed."
At the Lantern Festival, he addressed the assembly, citing Dahui’s ascent to the hall: "On the fourteenth and fifteenth of the first month, at Shuangjing, gongs are struck and drums are beaten.
If you wish to recognize the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, look at the village songs and communal dances.
The Master said: "Dahui has shaken his three hundred and sixty joints and gathered his eighty-four thousand pores; this may truly be called magnificent."
Throughout antiquity and the present, upon the seat of the Dharma King before the assembly of devas and humans, for what reason has there been no illumination?
Today at Jingshan, I intend to split the rock and divide the gold. You all must recognize the intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West;
if you fixate on village songs and communal dances, it is much like walking in the shadow of a lamp—before the sun has even been seen.
Addressing the assembly: "At Black Rock Ridge, I have already met you. At the Gazing Pavilion, I have already met you.
Before the Sangha Hall, I have already met you. Great assembly, how do you explain the principle of this meeting?
Furthermore, tell me, what is it that you see when you meet? After a long silence, he said: "A turtle bites the flagpole; a dog carries a lamp."
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the case of Yuehuan returning to Bafaeng. Bafaeng said, "Give me back my illumination and function.

Yuehuan said, "If there were illumination and function, they would immediately become obstructions. Bafaeng said, "Whether you cling to existence or cling to emptiness, even a Buddha could not save you.

Yuehuan said, "Both existence and non-existence are quiescent; both emptiness and Buddha are entirely non-existent. The Master said: "Yuehuan’s spirit and discernment surpassed the crowd; he was like the Great Sword emerging from its scabbard."

The box is opened; the great gate of Mount Bafeng stands wide open. Like the ocean receiving the flow of the brilliant, it may be said that host and guest are in mutual accord, and illumination and function are applied together.
Nevertheless, do you know that Bafeng only knows how to seize the tiger’s head, but does not know how to grasp its tail?
Addressing the assembly: In the past, Zen Master Guizong of Zhushan was exceptionally unconventional. One day, while wandering at Foyan, he heard the sound of wind chimes on the corner of the hall;
leaning on his staff, he passed away. His body was cremated, and countless śarīras were recovered.

Yet, as for us monastics, having attained a single pivot or a partial understanding, we retreat to forests and springs. If we maintain our practice long enough, we will sweep away all subtle attachments, until finally there is—
Such is the general state of affairs. Nowadays, as soon as teachers and monks have acquired a mere fragment of understanding, they immediately seek to act as models for others.
They possess no stillness in their practice and have not yet penetrated the subtle details; thus, at the final stage, they cannot avoid being like a crab thrown into a boiling pot. Why is this?
Once cast upon the ground, it makes the sound of gold; the Yellow River of nine bends is cleared to its very bottom.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the kōan concerning Nanyuan’s "simultaneous pecking and hatching. The Master offered this verse: "Simultaneous pecking and hatching, yet not simultaneous;
The arrowhead flies red as it strikes a single blow. Countless entanglements, the head shattered— Standing amidst the chaos of war, one is most supreme."

The platform was leveled. Descending from his seat, he addressed the assembly. He cited the encounter between the two Hall Heads. The Master offered this verse: "The current rolls and surges as it flows between the two banks;
A single pool of living azure flows on endlessly. If my disciples can turn their bodies back and leap, The mud beneath the sea bottom and the ox-horns will point toward heaven."
Staying at Yongqing Temple, he addressed the assembly: "This kind of extraordinary marvel is difficult to describe; in a straight line, Gaoteng leaps up into the heavens.
Indra’s bridge of the nose is struck and broken; the Persians fall in pain before the Sea Gate."
Addressing the assembly: "When Master Zhang first became friends with Master Li, he intended to offer a cup of wine to Master Li, but instead was offered a cup by Master Li.
A master of hand presents his skill before another master of hand. Does anyone here wish to see this master of hand? The Head Seat stepped forward and withdrew immediately.
The Master struck them all apart with his staff and retired to his quarters.
Addressing the assembly: What thing comes in such a manner? The stone man dances his sleeves with a smile filling his cheeks; the clay ox enters the sea without a trace.
The wooden horse neighs in the wind and cannot be caught. If it were suddenly caught, the iron walls and silver mountains would all be flung open.
[The Master] suddenly grasps the staff, draws a line, and says: "Here there is yet another layer."
Addressing the assembly: To seek the Buddha with the mind is to fall into a sea of poison. To transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness, there is no gate through which to approach.
My brothers, if you can truly rest and let go, you may take Mount Sumeru to be the four great oceans with white waves surging to the heavens;
you may take the four great oceans to be Mount Sumeru with red dust filling the earth. You may boil the marrow of empty space and taste its flavor.
Newly, he picks up the lamp from the kalpa-vase, its radiance blazing intensely. Here, hook and chisel have no place; there, whip and rope are applied in vain.
Therefore, the single path that leads upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages. Students exhaust their bodies, like monkeys grasping at reflections.
Opening the pavilion of Maitreya, every dharma is fully revealed; entering the practice-gate of Samantabhadra, every point is manifest.
Renounce it. Arriving here, one can only hear the wooden boy singing the "White Snow" and the stone woman chanting the "Clear Spring. When the fingers are pressed, the Sea-Seal radiates light;
when the strings are plucked, the sound fills the ears. Since there is already a Bo Ya to strike the rhythm, who among those seated before you is the Ziqi?
Addressing the assembly: When the ancients received three blows of the staff, they were like dragons finding water or tigers relying on a mountain;

they could not be caged, nor could they be summoned back. They overturned mountains and emptied valleys, submerging the entire earth. Yet when brought back, they were all nothing but horse winnowing baskets—winnowing this, winnowing that.
If one’s spiritual mechanism is free and unimpeded, one will manifest a distinct family reputation; every move will be comprehensive, and every step will be subtly directed.

Upon reaching this point, you must know that when the rooster crows by day and the dog barks in the red dust, whether it be Buddha or Mara, thirty blows are due—regardless of whether one comes by boat or by land.
Whether hungry or full, it is but a single meal—what need is there to discuss the bright side or the dark?
Where the body is hidden, there is no trace; yet as the cloth bag is dragged across, where there is no trace, do not hide the body; for the staff is planted upside down.
The Great Way is right before one’s eyes; yet, for all its importance, it is difficult to behold within those very eyes.
It is not a phenomenon of the present moment, nor is it something that can be reached by the ears or the eyes. Does the great assembly still understand this news? After a long silence, he said:
“If only the spring breeze could exert its full strength, blowing everything at once into my gate.”
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] cited Chan Master Yuexi Cheng, who went to visit Master Donglin Wu. Cheng presented his understanding, but Donglin did not approve.
Because Donglin had forcefully suppressed him, Yuexi spoke disparagingly. One day, when Yuexi took his leave of Donglin, Donglin carried his bag and escorted him as far as the mountain gate.
Suddenly pointing to a yellow dog, he said, "This beast has karmic consciousness but lacks Buddha-nature.
At these words, Xixi attained great enlightenment. The Master said, "The place where Donglin extended his hand was very much like a gill-skin the size of a cun;
Daogang’s realization was likewise like gouging a sore on healthy flesh. Nevertheless, there is another principle here; you all must not be careless."
Accepting the responsibility, he addressed the assembly. Raising the precedent for the mid-period formal lecture, he said: "It has been forty days of cloudy weather since we entered the retreat.
Today the sky is clear and bright—a fine day for drying out the mold! Although one’s own arm does not bend outward, you must still examine yourselves within your own sphere."
Ming. The Master said: "At the Hu Lake retreat, it has been forty days of constant rain;
at the Gaoteng retreat, it has been forty days of parching dryness. Within each of you, there must also be clear inspection.
Setting aside for a moment whether it is dry or wet, he struck the ground with his staff once and said: 'Try here! "
Let us speak of the principle. Addressing the assembly:
The setting sun is like a suspended drum; observe it closely before the peak. The rosy clouds mingle with the great earth; the mountains and rivers are a single expanse of brocade.

If you interpret this as a description of external scenery, you betray your lifelong practice. If you do not interpret it as a description of external scenery, you likewise betray your lifelong practice.
"I have failed my entire life. In the end, what is to be done?
Huiding Dong said, "When I first read Jiaoshan’s verse, 'A monkey carries its young back to the green peaks;
a bird carries fallen flowers before the azure cliffs,' I felt the words of awakening were chillingly clear. Then, at Mount Jing, I saw the sunset glow merge with the great earth."
A single expanse of brocade mountains and rivers—only then does one come to know this principle. A needle cannot pierce it; water cannot leak through.
Unless one shatters the bottom of the lacquer bucket, even to understand it correctly is truly difficult.
Addressing the assembly, [Zhaozhou] cited Chan Master Fangan Bao. A monk asked, "What is the essence of prajñā? The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone.
The monk asked, "What is the function of prajñā? The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone rolling in empty space. The Master then said:
Suīyán only knew how to follow the heterodox and pursue evil; he did not know how to turn the rudder and head for the shore.
Had he been asked, "What is the essence of Prajñā? he would have suddenly given a slap. Had he been asked, "What is the function of Prajñā? he would have given two more slaps.
This not only pointed out the essence and function of Prajñā, but also showed that within our school of patch-robed monks, there is something else—namely, claws and fangs.

Addressing the assembly, [the Master] cited the story of Master Fangshan. Before he had left the household life, he happened to read the *Platform Sutra* and felt as though it were something he had practiced in a former life.
He then raised the karmic conditions regarding the robe and bowl of Huangmei and asked: "Since he did not understand the Buddha-dharma, why did he succeed to the position of the Patriarch?"
Gong said, "Not only the Patriarch, but there are many who do not understand the Buddha-dharma yet still succeed to the Patriarchal seat.
Shanshan asked, "Does the Master also succeed to the Patriarchal seat? Gong said, "If one succeeds to the Patriarchal seat, then one understands the Buddha-dharma.

The Master remarked, "Ruigan was like a worm gnawing through wood, accidentally forming characters; when Jingci was pressed by him, he immediately leveled his heights and conformed to the low ground."
Within the gate of chanting the Way, there is a slight comparison to be made. As for the robe and bowl of Huangmei, you have not even dreamed of them yet.
Does the assembly wish to know where the robe and bowl of Huangmei fell? (He strikes the ground once with his staff and gives a shout, then descends from the seat.)
He addressed the assembly. A monk asked, "Why do the Buddhas of the three periods of time not know that [it] exists? The Master said, "The clever are often misled by their own cleverness.
The monk pressed further, "Why then do the black oxen and white cows know that it exists? The Master said, "A blow strikes the head of a stone man."
"Bravo! Bravo! To discuss the reality of things. The assembly prostrated. The Master raised up the discourse from Duanqiao Hall, saying:

"The clouds and moonlight of Mount Yan and Mount Taiqiao—sometimes rolling up, sometimes unfolding; sometimes full, sometimes incomplete. In pairs and threes, they wander in the morning and return in the evening.

Upon the corners of their *kāṣāyas* and at the tips of their staffs, they carry what is carried; within and without, they are beyond hindrance, delighting and gladdening themselves. But if you reach Ruiyan, you will certainly—"
"This staff for striking and teaching has been broken. Why? For what kind of occasion is this now? The Master said, "The ancients were sincere to the core;

they only wished to have their merit and reputation cover the ages. Had there been anyone at that time who acted with righteous courage, as soon as he heard him speak in such a manner, he would have stepped out from the side and let out a thunderous shout. See what kind of maneuvers he would have made! Let him shout two more times!"
Drink it down! Shuigan immediately possessed a plan for settling the chaos; he would certainly have no choice but to withdraw. To the assembly:
He cites Zen Master Jin of Tianmu asking Master Ning of Yifeng, "What is the secret meaning of the West?
Ning stepped down from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "There is no meaning in what came from the West. Tell me, what is this here?"
Yi said, "Since that day, I have forgotten both sleep and food. One day, while ascending to the latrine, I heard the sound of a monk striking the counting sticks (*zhōu*).
Suddenly, I had a profound awakening. The Master said, "Dagang possessed a gift that drove away the plow and seized the food; he lacked the sudden flash of lightning or the crashing of thunder.

Consequently, Tianmu became mired in heavy words and stagnant phrases, falling into the realm of mechanical triggers. When he heard the sound of the counting sticks, he was met with his own strange laughter."
This is Mount Jing; he has thrown open the vast gates of heaven, allowing the crimson steed to chase the wind and refined gold to leap from the crucible.
Why is this so? "Countless green mountains, yet few passing travelers; red rain falls with the mist upon silken robes."
The Master was serving as the head seat in the quarters at Longju. A monk asked, "Now that you have arrived at Chexi and no longer teach others, what is it like?
The Master said, "The spring breeze on the tower is about to cease; who can take up a mirror and look upon sorrowful brows? As the monk prepared to offer further words, [the Master struck him].
The Master shouted him out.
Tie-rong-huan composed a verse, saying: "True pearl curtains and bamboo blinds conceal the fragrant chamber; The bright moon sinks low as the guest’s watch-tower clock draws long.
Jade pendants have just caused the spring grasses to turn green; A delicate countenance surely shall no longer grace the dressing mirror."
Yun’an Liang’s verse says: The jade flute has been blown clear to the Phoenix Terrace; The ancient hall is deep and silent, unopened at dawn.
Falling flowers fill the ground as spring has departed; Green shadows vainly lock the old moss.

A monk asked, "If a single thought-moment of dependent origination is non-arising, transcending the provisional views of those who study the Three Vehicles, then who is it that has dependent origination with arising?
The Master let out a thunderous shout. The monk bowed.
Master Huimù’s verse says: Clouds gather and rain ceases; the heavens and sea are vast. Waves surge as they are stirred by the wind, giving rise to the source of calamity.
If one recognizes that the waves of the long river are but water, The sand gulls will settle for the night amidst the reeds and rushes.
Wen Gu asked: "If it is true that karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty, why was the Venerable Siṃha beheaded by the King of Kaśmīra?
The Master said: "Fundamentally empty. [The monk] asked: "What about his head? The Master said: "Fundamentally empty. [The monk] asked:
"Why did one of the King of Kaśmīra’s hands fall to the ground? The Master said: "Fundamentally empty."
A Verse on Fine Dust: Willow groves slant against the hermit’s window; Scattered, withered branches accompany the morning river.
Precisely where the frosty wind severs them, Cold gulls take flight, two by two.
Because a donor was providing a meal for the Sangha, the guest prefect was distributing the alms. The rector (karmadāna) announced:

"Three parts for the head of the hall, two parts for the administrative officers, and one part for the assembly. The Master asked his attendant, "What portion do you receive? The monk remained silent.

The Master called to the guest prefect, "Why did you not give him any? The monk remained silent as well. The Master looked toward the assembly, and the rector came forward to pay his respects and withdrew.
In the Hall, while it was snowing, an attendant pushed open the window and said, "The entire mountain is covered in snow. The Master said, "A fellow who follows after sounds and pursues forms.
The monk said, "I ask the Master to provide a phrase apart from sound and form. The Master said, "The entire mountain is covered in snow."
Puming said, "That monk encountered a blade of white steel and managed to survive; he is indeed a skilled hand.
But Jingshan has exhausted all his salt and sauce and still has not achieved his heart's desire. Is there anyone here who can utter a single phrase apart from sound and form?
After a long silence, he said, "Above all, do not say that the whole mountain is covered in snow."
Donglin said: "That monk asked in such a manner, and Nanquan answered in such a manner;
though they were indeed of one level of equanimity, Puming’s critique in this way cannot avoid planting thorns in the path. Donglin would have boldly said:
'The whole mountain is covered in snow. He knew only that the dragon emerged from the Ge slope, but failed to realize the thunder and lightning were upon his own tongue."
He struck with his whisk and descended from the seat.

Following the communal labor (pǔqǐng), the Master took up his work tools and led the assembly to the mountain gate. At that moment, the garden head was washing vegetables, and the matting head was sunning cloths.
The Master pointed to the two men and said to the assembly, "In the garden there is a head gardener; in the mill there is a head miller.
He then pointed to himself and asked, "As for you, what will you do, you fellows? The assembly was speechless. The Master threw down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Yun’an Liang’s verse says: In spring there are a hundred flowers, in autumn there is the moon; In summer there are cool breezes, in winter there is snow.
If there are no worldly affairs hanging upon the heart, This is indeed a fine season in the human world.
The Master presided over the Dharma for more than ten years, maintaining purity and integrity while strictly regulating the assembly.

He lived in solitary refinement, such that those who frequented his side doors or relied upon his household feared him as they would boiling water or fire. Only Yuanhu alone was intimately nurtured by the milk of his Dharma. The Master’s aspiration lay in the ancient Way;
every fragment of paper and single character is truly the rich essence of Prajñā.

On the twenty-seventh day of the second month of winter in the year of Gengshen, the first year of the Taichang era, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), having finished his final instructions, he passed away while sitting upright.

His body was cremated and a stupa enshrined within the Universal Stupa at Mount Jing, all in accordance with the Master’s own wishes. His worldly age was forty-five, and his years of monastic ordination were twenty-three.
Chan Master Langmu Benzhi of Huayan Temple on Mount Fudu was a successor of Chan Master Tianmu Ding. He was the son of the Li family of Qujing.

He received the tonsure under Baizhai and subsequently visited masters such as Foyan Buer and Xingtian. Later, he ascended Mount Tianmu, where he studied under Lanfeng and attained realization of the essential meaning.
Renowned throughout the world as the "white-browed elder" of the monastic community, he was treated with the etiquette of a disciple by princes, dukes, and high officials of his time.
When Empress Dowager Cizheng’s Dharma-treasure resided at Jingu Valley, she designated this Master as the presiding abbot of the monastery.
On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the Wanyili year (1585), he washed his hands with water and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

When the news reached Empress Dowager Cisheng, she was deeply grieved and expressed her compassionate condolences. She subsequently granted funds for the return of his remains to Mount Fushan, at the southern foot of Miaogao Peak, so that they might follow the Master’s own wishes.
Several volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) have been circulated in the world.
The National Preceptor Funi-ji was the dharma successor of Chan Master Miaofeng Fudeng of Mount Wutai in Taiyuan Prefecture. He was the son of the Xu family from Pingyang in Shanxi.

He left the household life under Master Lang at Wanngu Monastery in Manchuria. Possessing both aspiration and practice, he undertook the conduct of Samantabhadra; beginning at Zantan Temple, he established a meditation retreat for three years.
While traveling, he encountered an extraordinary monk who pointed out to him: "The practice of Samantabhadra is a hidden cultivation and subtle application for harmonizing all states of mind;
it does not mean exhausting one's sinews or toiling one's bones. The Master then traveled south to Jinling to visit Yungu.

Yungu presented him with the koan "Who is reciting the Buddha's name? and instructed him to investigate it. Later, together with Hanshan Qing, he traveled north to visit Bianrong, Yuanxiaoyan, Bao Daqian, and others.

Zhunzhugong. At the beginning of the Wanli era, he again attended upon Dàqiān at Shaolin. He lived in seclusion on Mount Tai, where he received the blessing of Mañjuśrī’s hand-touching and a formal prophecy.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming, the Emperor issued an imperial decree for Fǒng'èr to travel to the capital to offer prayers for the longevity of Empress Dowager Císhèng.
By imperial decree, he was invited to the palace, where he stayed with the Emperor for several days. Their spiritual affinity was profound;

one day, struck by Master Fubai’s sudden challenge, he attained a great awakening. Thus his reputation for the Way became most eminent, reaching the point where a fierce tiger cleared his path and a bodhisattva delivered him lamps.
Emperor Shenzong dreamed of the Master’s likeness and summoned him to the capital, bestowing upon him purple robes and a title of honor. He subsequently passed away.
His stupa was enshrined at Mount Tai. By imperial decree, he was posthumously honored as a "True Son of the Buddha.
Master Iryan of Xingshan Temple on White Tiger Mountain in Huangzhou was the son of the Zhu family of that prefecture. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
By nature he was compassionate and kind, and he frequently engaged in acts such as releasing captive animals. Because he failed to pass the provincial examination, the Master said: "I have left..."
His lifelong ambition was thus fulfilled. He traveled specifically to Cao Dian Temple in Xiangzhou to undergo the tonsure and dye his robes.
He entered Huotang Hall on Mount Funiu to observe the retreat regulations and visited Master Fubai, from whom he attained profound awakening. Fubai subsequently conferred upon him the Dharma.
During the Wanli era, Empress Dowager Cisheng established the Shoulengyan Daochang; Emperor Shenzong summoned him to the inner palace, where he was granted the purple robe and the title Hongji.
He styled himself [as such] to signify his retreat to Mount Lu at Huanglong. Together with several others, including Cherkong and Hanshan, he re-established the White Lotus Society.

In the year Wumu (1618), the Grand Music Master of Huangzhou, who had long admired the Master’s spiritual influence, led the scholar He Qixiang and others to invite him to reside at Master Zhi’s White Tiger Monastery.
Within a few years, he restored the monastery to its former regulations.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The life-blood of Śākyamuni, the eyes of Bodhidharma—who does not possess a share of these? It is simply that one must not allow them to be lost to discursive thought.
What is called 'attaining it in the mind' means that even *eranda* (Iraṇa) becomes a sandalwood tree; what is called 'losing the essential meaning' means that even nectar becomes a garden of thorns.
Long ago, National Teacher An asked a monk: 'A single phrase contains both the meanings of gain and loss. How do you understand this?'"
The Master said, "A monk raised his fist and said, 'This cannot be called a fist. An-guo did not approve.

The Master also raised his fist and said differently, 'It is precisely because you call this thing a fist. If the assembly could produce a single appropriate word here, you would finally know that a difference of a hair’s breadth leaves heaven and earth between them."
Having remained in seclusion for twenty-two years, he passed away peacefully while seated without illness on the fifteenth day of the second month of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era.
He was cremated and interred on the dry side (the north) of Linsan River. His secular age was eighty-four, and his monastic seniority was forty-one.
He had four disciples who inherited the Dharma.

Leaving the gorges, he visited various spiritual friends (*jñānaka*) at length. He built a thatched hut by the Double Creek (*Shuangxi*). One day while cooking his midday meal, he heard a sound from within the steamer;

suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse containing the lines: "The white clouds and blue peaks nod their heads. He once traveled through Zhejiang and established a hermitage at Qingping in Hangzhou.
The monk Zhenji Yin had relied upon him in his youth. One day, [Yin] raised the case of Qingfeng’s "Ceding" lad.

Yinzhi replied, "At first, he attempted to settle his mind through conscious cognition, and for that reason he did not awaken.

The Master replied, "Fire burns at both ends, yet smoke issues from only one. The Master often held a small hand-drum (*tiao-gu*) in his hands; on one side was written the character *chu* (standing), and on the other, the character *ben* (running).

On New Year’s Eve, the weather is cold. At nine years of age, one must observe the retreat. Raising a cup and picking up fruit, everyone knows there is something great.
But tell me, what is it? If you can realize it here, you may take the tail as the head.
Beneath the three wooden beams and before the seven-foot mat, scrubbing your trousers and grinding your skirts, forgetting food and neglecting sleep—yet this very matter does not reside in movement.
In its application, it is also not upon the eyebrows or eyelashes. This is why Zhaozhou, whenever he saw a monk arrive for an interview, would ask:
"Have you been here before? If the monk said, "I have been here," Zhaozhou would say, "Go drink tea. Or if he said, "I have not been here," he likewise said, "Go drink tea.
The head monk asked, "Master, why do you tell both those who have been here and those who have not to go drink tea? Zhaozhou called out:
The head monk responded, "Yes. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea. Zhaozhou was presiding over this matter and deliberating with the monk on equal terms.
The head monk did not recognize good from bad and ended up receiving a ladle of foul water. At Puming’s place, they do not care whether one drinks tea or not;
they only want the person to enter directly with a single blade. A monk stepped forward, and the Master shouted.
A single shout. He dragged his staff and descended from the seat.
On the occasion of the New Year’s Day discourse: The ancient Way naturally returns to the phoenix calendar; The songs of Yao and the hymns of Shun bring boundless joy.
Clouds enshroud the vermilion cassia, its golden stalks exquisite; Rain nourishes the jade forest, its emerald leaves flourishing.
On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he took up his brush and wrote a verse:
"Life is a mistake; death is a mistake. The iron lion seizes and snaps the golden rope. Having cast down his brush, he cried out, "Tut! and passed away.
His secular age was fifty-six, and his monastic seniority was thirty-nine. His remains were cremated, and his sacred relics were enshrined in the Tooth Stupa at Xingshan on this very mountain.
During the Shunzhi era, his bone-relic stupa was moved to Xingshan, where it stands facing the tooth-relic stupa.
Chan Master Cheryong Zhouli Miaofeng, a successor of Chan Master Zhishan, was a native of Yunnan. His family had long been devoted to agriculture; he entered the monastic order in his youth.
His faculties were dull and his speech stammering; however, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, he attained a sudden and great awakening.

At the age of eighteen, upon reading the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he came to know the proper application of his mind. Furthermore, by practicing meditative concentration through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), he gained significant mastery.
Furthermore, upon reading the various writings of Dahuai and Zhongfeng, I came to know the state where there is nothing to employ and nothing to attain;

yet, I did not yet dare to consider my work finished. By chance, I encountered Master Mizang, who verified my understanding at its four corners, and only then did I realize I had finally reached the ground.
In the year Ding-si, I visited Tiantong Wu; as soon as he saw me, he asked, "Having come from ten thousand miles away, how much money for sandals have you spent?"
The Master said, "I have come by boat. The boy asked, "What do you intend to do here? The Master said, "May I ask you something?
The boy asked, "Where are you from? The Master said, "Does the Monk see me? The boy took up his staff.
The Master then shouted; the boy struck him. The Master caught the blow and gave it a push. The boy asked, "What are you doing?
The Master said, "The Abbot wanted the staff, so I am returning it. The boy was greatly pleased. The Master’s spontaneous utterances were often of this sort, and his spirit overwhelmed all quarters.
The gentry of Jinling, including Mr. Ye Zengcheng and Mr. Yang Xiuling, became his spiritual friends outside the monastic community.
Ascending the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Great assembly, do you understand? The Old Man Śākyamuni has arrived.

If you do not understand, I, this mountain monk, shall speak at length for all of you. It is just as it is said in the teachings: 'The Dharma-nature pervades all places—within all sentient beings and all lands;
throughout the Buddhas of the three periods of time, there is nothing left over, nor does it have any form or appearance.'"
"Yet it can be attained. Furthermore, he said: "In the heavens above and the earth below, there is none like the Buddha. Since he says the Way has no form or appearance, yet it can be attained;
and again, he says: "There is nothing at all that is like the Buddha. You people of the assembly, how do you deliberate upon this?
After a long silence, he said: "Welcome, World-Honored One! Remain here in peace. He then took up his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Taking one step forward is not as good as taking one step back. To take one step forward is death;
to take one step back is annihilation. As for neither advancing nor retreating, you cannot avoid being drowned in stagnant water.
How will you all find the path to emerge?"
He entered nirvana in the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era. His *Guxiang ji* (Collection of Valley Echoes) circulates in the world.
Chan Master Wengu Guangyin of Tiantai on Mount Xiling in Huangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Baima Tuan; his alternative style name was Zhangshi, and he was of the Zhou clan of Jiaśan.
His father was Shan and his mother was Lady Zhao. She dreamed that Chan Shuai led armored soldiers to guard the gate; upon waking, she gave birth to the Master.

During his childhood, the shadow of a stupa was constantly visible at the corner of his left eye. His father ordered him to study Confucianism, but he did not wish to do so. He was then sent to Kaiyuan Temple in Hangzhou to receive the tonsure.
One day, pointing to a diagram of the ten dharma realms, he asked his teacher: "The ten dharma realms arise from the mind; from where does the mind arise?"
The Master was unable to respond. At that time, Yifeng had built a hut on Mount Qingping. The Master went there to visit him and raised his previous question.
Yifeng said, "If you wish to understand, you must first attain wondrous awakening. He then instructed him to contemplate the word "Dew" (Lu) from Yunmen.

After a long time, while reading the story of the Seven Sages’ Daughters wandering in the Śītavana cemetery, he suddenly attained realization. Upon seeing Yifeng, Yifeng brought up the case of the "Cengding Boy coming to seek [instruction]."
Huohua questioned him, saying, "Qingfeng and Fayen both spoke in this same way; why then is there awakening and non-awakening?
The Master replied, "At first, one attempts to settle the mind through conceptual consciousness, and for that reason does not awaken. Later, by directly taking it up, one attains great awakening.
Qingfeng raised his fist, struck the desk, and said in a stern voice, "If that is so, then have you attained great awakening? He then scolded him harshly and drove him away.
He departed. Master Zhide’s sweat flowed down his sides and back. From then on, he applied himself even more diligently to investigation.
At the age of twenty-four, when Huifeng returned to Shu, the Master went to visit Wuhuan. He lived alone at Mount Fahua, observing the retreat under Baiyun Peak.

While studying with Preceptor Liang, he had not yet resolved the karmic conditions regarding Mazu. One day, while gazing at yellow fragrant flowers, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed [this verse]:
The verse says: "It is actually empty space that can preach the sutras; Common bricks and rubble are precisely fit to listen.

In the past, one twisted one’s mother-born nose, Mistaking a gourd for an imperial vase. Thereupon, he led the assembly at Jingshan, resided at Lianju, and stayed at various places including Yongqing.
In the *Renzi* year of the Wanli era, he restored Zhenji Monastery. In the *Wuwu* year, he withdrew into seclusion at Huang’an in Hubei.
At Tiantai, he subsequently founded Baoshan Monastery in Jianning. Later, he returned to Zhenji Monastery.
On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era, he manifested his passing. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Qingshan Peak.
He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-eight years since his ordination.
*Jingshi Dilu Ji*, Scroll Four;
*Jingshi Dilu Ji*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir of the Patriarchs, the Śramaṇa Zhenzai of Jiangzhou.
The Dharma heirs who succeeded him were Qian’an Ji and Yunxu;
they continued the lineage of Chan Master Puming Yong, the fifteenth-generation successor of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Wujun of Mount Ziyun in Jianning Prefecture was the son of the Pan family of Qiantang. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and his spiritual nature was extraordinary.
During his youth, he resolved to transcend the mundane world. At twenty, he received full ordination and immediately traveled extensively throughout various regions.

Although he attained moments of realization, he never claimed final mastery for himself. He subsequently visited Furi, under whom he finally gained a profound understanding of the subtle principles of the Dongshan school.
Furi was close friends with Yuanhu. In his later years, Yuanhu suffered frequently from illness and worried that he would not have a successor.

Furi, following the precedent set by Daowu and Jia Shan, directed Master Shenxiu to attend upon Yuanhu at Puming. There, Shenxiu attained a profound and thorough realization of the perfect and eternal.
One day, Yuanhu asked: "When a conjured person asks a phantom man, and the echo answers the sound of the spring—how do you wish to recognize me?"
The Master said, "The fundamental principle is: 'A clay ox walks upon the water. What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "It is like seeing flowers in the sky with eyes that are dreaming.
Yuan asked, "Linji has a single phrase; what do you make of it? The Master gave a shout. Yuan struck him. The Master shouted again. Yuan struck him once more. The Master shouted yet again.

Yuan struck him again. The Master prostrated himself. Yuan said, "So, you are just a blind donkey. The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Yuan appointed him to oversee the affairs of the monastery.

In the *Xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era, when Yuanhu retired from his residence, the fourfold assembly requested the Master to open the Dharma hall. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "In days of yore..."
The Elder Wuzu said, "This morning, Master Hengshi, what is it that has its source far away and its flow long-lasting? It is no different from the past or present.
The Master said, "Opening the pond reveals the bright moon; waving the fly-whisk stirs the pure breeze. Wuzu said, "A single drop of water from Yunfeng; the entire earth receives its grace.
The Master said, "Understand this for the sake of the future. He then said, "Clouds arise from the jeweled trees; the wind knocks against the verdant peaks."
Bamboo. Having thoroughly penetrated the crowing of the cock, and having smeared poison all over the ground—this is the place where Old Man Wuzu settled.
Is there anyone present now who knows this place of settlement? If so, come forth and convey a message. After a long silence, he struck his whisk and descended from the seat.

The Master resided at Yunfeng. At one time, the monastic and lay communities gathered in full. During the Yiyou year of the Shunzhi era, Emperor Longwu, admiring the Master’s spiritual influence, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the inner palace.

There, he questioned the Master in detail regarding the essentials of the Dharma; the Master responded with his authentic realization. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him purple robes, a title, and a posthumous honorific.
He was posthumously titled the Great Master Guangjue of Yuanhu, and his stupa was named "Wondrous Adornment. This occurred in the fourth month of the Cixu year.

He entered nirvana on the fourth day of the first month. His worldly age was thirty-four, and his years as a monk were fifteen. Fifteen volumes of his recorded works, including the *Yanyi* (Explication of the Meaning) and *Dahxiang* (Responses to Echoes), have been circulated in the world.
He emptied all inherent natures. It is said that since the time of Patriarch Wuzu Fayan of the Linji school, the transmission of the lineage had become increasingly rigorous;
by the time of Yuanhu, three branches flourished in competition, and the Master stood as their leader. Amidst the chaos of war and strife, he maintained the tradition.

Witnessing their plight, my compassionate heart grew ever more urgent. At that time, civil and military ministers offered prayers for his elevation and protection, never neglecting a single day in their earnest reception of him.
Had the Master’s Way been granted a longer life by Heaven, he would surely have rivaled Kim-myeong.
The mutual poetic exchanges between Yongzheng, Min, and Zhe greatly illuminated the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
yet, encountering a time of chaotic beginnings, the Dharma-vessel was first shattered. Alas, how lamentable!
Chan Master Jiān Wùjìn of Jì'ān at Jīnmíng Temple in Jiāxìng Prefecture was styled Juéxiān. His surname was Zhāng, and he was a native of the same prefecture.

His mother, née Hè, dreamed that the sun’s orb entered her bosom when he was born. From childhood, he did not indulge in children’s games; he delighted in visiting temples, and upon seeing Buddhist images, he would linger with such affection that he could not bear to leave.
Upon reaching adulthood, he studied for the civil service examinations, yet he frequently perused the Buddhist scriptures, his aspirations being set upon them.

In the Chan school, [Zhaozhou] received the tonsure from Chan Master Weiming of Longchi. While lying ill, he heard the sound of a craftsman’s axe cutting through a large tree and attained realization.
He immediately presented this to Weiming, who nodded in approval.
The Master went to visit Yuanhu. As soon as he stepped through the gate, Yuanhu asked, "What is this? The Master was about to respond when Yuanhu let out a thunderous shout.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment and, covering his ears, walked out.
The inscription on the triangle reads: "A great bell upon its stand will surely ring when it meets an object; one must draw the sword to the edge of the blade before being called a true master.

At that time, although the Elder Puming opened a single thread of light atop the crown of Vairocana, had he not encountered those with the eyes of a hawk and the gaze of a dragon, he too would likely not have seen the day of today. Therefore it is said: "Piling up grain and heaping gold."
Easy. Seeking the worthy, one encounters the "Guest's Difficulty. Today, this unworthy descendant judges such things to be wrong;
I recklessly handle my grandfather’s legacy, valuing only the raising of the sand basin. I dare ask: among the assembly present here, is there anyone who can provide mutual testimony?
Striking the floor once with his staff, he said: "Release the waters of the Bridge-Breaking Car River!"
Let it flow freely and fill the Five Lakes.
A verse by Yun of Shimen says: "Breaking through the vast void of chaos, Turning over the azure map of the heavens. The plum blossoms on Shaolin Mountain produce jade;
Spring fills the imperial capital."
Longxing’s verse says: Striking out the five-colored marrow of the golden phoenix, Smashing to pieces the bright moon pearl of the black dragon.
Heaven and earth alike are rendered speechless; A single stream of wind flows forth from Mirror Lake.
The ancient grove is as described in the verse: "A gentle spring breeze carries the fragrance of the Imperial Garden; travelers cannot help but grow intoxicated by their cups and goblets.
In a casual glance, they pierce the face of the Lord of Spring; they rein in their horses and return as the moon turns across the vast expanse."
Hymn on the Steep Celestial Pillar: Ten thousand layers of silver waves surge at the Yu Gate; Whales and sea-monsters raise their fins and lash their tails.
A single clap of thunder startles heaven and earth, Causing wind and thunder to darken the universe.
Dream Hall Ni’s verse says: Meeting on a narrow path, a sudden squeeze; the root source is utterly bottomless.
A bolt of lightning cuts off the twilight rain; the four seas are vast as a black wind rages.
Longmen’s Verse on Nature says: As soon as he received the imperial decree to dwell in the Eastern Palace, He was not of the same nature as ordinary beings.
Within the flash of a stone-fire, the burden was clearly manifested; North and south of the Yangtze River, the wind of sorrow stirred.
Xi Jueyi’s eulogy says: Reclining drunkenly upon the flowered balustrade, the sun has not yet slanted; Yet one mistakes this inn for home.
A single melody of "Spring's Warmth" is enough to turn back the head; Amidst the misty village, the evening crows cry out.
Yuanhu was unwell. While the Master was attending to him, Yuanhu ordered tea and asked, "Your name is Jue-xian (Awakened-First).
What do you call 'first'? The Master replied, "I am glad that today I have attained mastery. Yuanhu said, "What is it like after awakening? The Master replied, "Please, Preceptor, show me respect.
Yuanhu said, "Can you still distinguish between first and last? After the Master had remained silent for a long while, Yuanhu gave a shout. The Master [remained silent].
Yuan said, "Just keep drinking tea. Yuan asked, "What is the matter of drinking tea? The Master said, "Persimmons, dates, and dried tofu are all here.
Yuan asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Swallow it all at once. Yuan asked, "What is its flavor?
The Master said, "Sweet is sweet; salty is salty. Yuan said, "Not yet—speak further! The Master bowed.
He said, "I decline the tea. Yuan Shen agreed.
Jin Mingxu said, "A great man, when facing the furnace, does not avoid the fire; when stepping onto the stage, how could he shun the 'cutting off the tongue' pivot?
Mingxu was the fourth-generation descendant of Puming. [Jin Ming] dared to say that it was not yet so. Jin Ming waited for him to speak.

"I have swallowed it all in a single gulp. He then suddenly held up his bamboo staff and said, "As for this one, Puming—if you can get out of it, you must also spit out what this old fellow with one hand has swallowed."
Puming ascended the hall while the assembly was gathered. He then raised his whisk and said, "The World-Honored One held up a single flower;
this old monk raises a single whisk. Tell me, are they the same or different? The Master stepped forward, prostrated three times, and returned to his place.

Puming bestowed upon him the verse for the transmission of the Dharma: "This matter along the current Has ultimately no beginning and no end. I entrust it to the lion cub, Who roars throughout the ten directions."
Heaven and Earth.
Tie Rong’s *Mystic Eulogy* says: The lute dances as it plays a new melody; It is all the sentiment of parting from the frontier mountains.
The chaotic sorrows of the borderlands can never be fully heard; High above, the bright moon shines upon the Great Wall.
The Master’s Verse on the Peak says: Meeting on a narrow path, it is difficult to avoid; A single blow behind the head reveals the cheek.
Had he not repeatedly stroked the tiger’s whiskers, How could he have possessed the talent to transform into a dragon until this day?
Kim Myeong-uk’s verse says: "Once I took a withered paulownia lute and traveled to the capital; As the strings were plucked in a different tune, my thoughts drifted far away.
Suddenly, as I was pressed head-on, a mournful wind arose; Generation after generation of descendants have harbored the anxieties of the *qǐ* tree."
A monk went to visit the Master, who asked, "Are you a monk from Gaofeng? The monk replied, "I am. The Master said, "Since you are from Gaofeng, why are you here at my feet?
The monk was speechless. The Master struck him out.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The golden wind blows over the embroidered waters; paulownia leaves fall upon the moss.
Hu Ji said, "If one is a truly outstanding monk, they will know for themselves that there is a covering upon the crown of their head. With a single gust of the golden breeze—
Night falls; the leaves of the *wutong* trees upon the steps and thresholds. My intention is like an autumn cloud; my mind is like the bright moon.

In the winter of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era, while residing at Mount Jing, he ascended the hall for the opening of the retreat. A monk asked: "Under the sky of Yao and the sun of Shun, the rustic elders sing songs of joy.

As all the patrons are present at this assembly, we rejoice to hear the essential teachings of the Dharma. The Master said: "Heaven is long and earth is enduring. [The monk] said: "A single phrase..."
"Within it, the sun and moon are contained. With these few words, he thereupon revitalized the tradition of his school. The Master said, "I am caught by what you have just said.

He then continued, "Today, as the retreat begins everywhere, it is unavoidable that some will gather flowers and cluster brocade, employing clever and novel turns, spreading nets across the heavens with phrases aimed at 'beating the phoenix' and 'snaring the dragon.
Such words deceive and mislead people. At Jing Mountain, we follow a different path; for your sake, I shall speak another way."

All people clamped their mouths and tied their tongues; they departed in cold silence. They departed like withered trees on a frigid cliff; they departed as a single thought spanning ten thousand years.
Let them have a faculty like that of an iron ox—take it for granted that such a phrase will flash like lightning and land one ten thousand *li* away in Yuezhou.
While residing at Guangfu Monastery in Yuhang, the Master ascended the hall. He cited the verse presented by Chan Master Guangfu Weishang to Jueyin.

Jueyin held up his fist and asked, "At this very moment, what is it? Weishang overturned the meditation seat. Jueyin then shouted. Weishang said, "It is like drawing one's bow after the thief has already fled," and he departed.
The Master remarked, "Jueyin was like a king wielding a sword; when it came time to strike, he failed to do so. Weishang...
Still, he could not restrain his display of prowess as he charged against the gate of the military camp. If one were to act according to the command, each would receive twenty blows of the staff.
But tell me: what kind of eye does the new Guangfu possess?

Residing at Tianchi in Wukang, he ascended the hall and raised the following case: Xue’an addressed the assembly, saying, "Having just settled in this city temple, there is nothing to the east and the west is missing.
As soon as you lift your eyes, I lower my head. My beard and hair are white as snow; my body and mind are rotten like mud.
Originally there is no Buddha-dharma; where is there anything to be fully presented? The Master said, "If one speaks of the full presentation of the Buddha..."
As for the Dharma, from where could it possibly come? As for Tianchi, it was not so; city and mountain forest are entirely one and the same.
Hearing sounds and seeing forms, he was never deaf. Recognizing that the great beast is originally a tiger—Xuansha was just like Old Man Xie San.
Staying at Taiping in Zhongxi, he ascended the hall on the Dragon Boat Festival: "Today is once again the fifth day of the fifth month.
The great ghosts clap their hands and the little ghosts dance. Suddenly they run into the Tao Fu deity; With both hands they beat their breasts, crying out in grievous suffering. Da Hui speaks thus:
it is just like a person whose official debt is not yet settled being caught by a hook; in a single squeeze, their divine heads and ghostly faces all appear together.
He stepped out. "I give you, Taiping, a small secret prescription. He struck his staff down and said, "Today happens to be the fifth day of the fifth month;
