there is no need for realgar or mugwort tigers. Principle can subdue the leopard, and the marsh hides the mountain; the clouds disperse from the blue sky as the sun stands at its zenith. He struck once more.
In the Wuzi year of the Shunzhi era, he resided at Jinming. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the Sahā world, vocal sounds constitute the Buddha-work;
in the Gandhavatī world, fragrant food constitutes the Buddha-work. Here at Jinming, a dilapidated monastery constitutes the Buddha-work. Do you see it?

A dilapidated meditation hall with heads covered in dust and faces smeared with grime; a dilapidated Buddha Hall; a dilapidated mountain gate with the forehead of a horse and the jaw of a donkey. He raised...

Holding a pestle in his fist, he shattered the Buddha-hall; with eyes like the moon, he waited for the clouds to break through the bell tower. Those who truly understand are few; let one group shatter it.
When a patch-robed monk dwells here, he uses shattering to shatter what is not shattered. Shattering, shattering, yet not shattered;

where there is no shattering and nothing is shattered, its application is inexhaustible, making one thoroughly proficient in every direction. If you are one who transcends the school and differs from the common eye, then at this point, simply apply yourself lightly.
Pressed and prodded, they respond in kind; call them oxen, and they can naturally pull the plow and drag the harrow.
Call them horses, and they immediately take up the bit and carry the pack-saddle. This mountain monk has no choice but to look upon them with another eye.
Among the assembly, is there anyone who can split open what is already broken? If so, Jinming will act as their axe to break it further. Come forth! Break it open! Break it open!
After a long silence, he struck them with his staff in a whirlwind and dispersed them. He returned to the Abbot’s quarters and ascended the hall for a formal discourse.
A monk asked, "The long sword that leans against the heavens is brandished, and the lion’s majesty crouches upon the ground.

As a student, I have come before you; I pray the Master will grant me an encounter. The Master then shouted. The monk said, "That was a phrase from the gateway of expedient means. What is the full manifestation of the true command?"
[The monk] spoke. The Master shouted again. As the monk prepared to offer a word, the Master struck him. He then cited Baiyun Cuan, saying:
"If you can truly achieve one instance of breaking into a sweat, you will manifest a palace of jade and precious stones upon a single blade of grass.

If you have not yet achieved one instance of breaking into a sweat, even if there were palaces of jade and precious stones, they would be covered over by a single blade of grass. The Master said, "Baiyun..."
Yun-bu is not a well-intentioned person here at Jin-ming; he does not place shackles upon you all.
If you truly manage to break into a sweat once, every point will be a jade palace and every place a crystal tower. If you truly do not break into a sweat once, [it remains as it is].
Everywhere is a jade palace; in every place is a crystal tower. Do you know where they fall? A sweet melon is sweet to the very stem;
a bitter gourd is bitter to the very root.
Addressing the assembly: "The east is bustling, the west is bustling; in the frantic turmoil of karmic consciousness, one knows not of old age.

Others suffer as the fierce flames blaze ever more intensely, yet I alone, Tao Zhu, remain serene and still. If the insects of summer could understand the ice of winter, the iron ox would never be bitten by mosquitoes.
Should it suddenly be bitten, the three-legged donkey of Yangqi would startle awake and trample down billions of Mount Sumerus."
The Master once posed three questions to test his students. The first was: "Since this is a hall consecrated by Heaven, it should logically transcend both 'this' and 'that';
why then is there welcoming and seeing off? Why is there a dog within the Lion’s Den?
Why did Fan Li, the Grand Minister of Yue, reside in the land of Wu?"
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the Gui-chou year, he bathed, changed his robes, wrote a verse of farewell, and passed away.
His worldly age was sixty-two; his years as a monk were thirty-seven. Upon cremation, his bones were white like jade, and his teeth remained unbroken.
His bone stupa is at Daici-ān on Yinchuan; his tooth stupa is at Huangjing on Mount Shimeng in Chuhuang.

Chan Master Yichu Wuyuan of Yongzheng Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture was surnamed Cao and was a native of Danglu County. From birth he was precocious, upright, and quick-witted; he delighted in sitting in meditation.
At the age of ten, he requested his father to teach him the Buddhist scriptures, and he was able to comprehend their profound meanings. At ten...
At age five, he began investigating the Chan school (zongcheng). At twenty, he attained great enlightenment.
He took Xingshan Hongyuan as his teacher and attended upon Puming for a long time. One day, Puming asked him, "My heart is uneasy;
have you attained peace yet? The Master replied, "Heaven! Heaven! On another day, while entering the inner quarters, Puming held up a fist and said, "Speak a word."

"Look," the Master said, and he struck him with his palm. Ming laughed loudly, whereupon they reached a mutual accord through this kōan. He then returned to Xingshan and remained in seclusion behind closed doors for over ten years.

In the Xinchao year of the Shunzhi era, while residing at Yongzheng, he ascended the hall and said: "The flowers smile in the spring breeze; the extraordinary true rule is suddenly manifest in the fisherman’s song by the flowing water.
Within this, the essential message is fully revealed. To take up and point toward the Ultimate, there is no hindrance for those who penetrate the Way.

Singing and responding as appropriate, what obstacle could there be to such expedient means? Those who have attained the truth deliberate thus: when it is cold, they add robes; when it is hot, they open their chests. Do not say, 'I seek...'"
Fire and smoke. When hunger comes, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Do not say: "Carrying water from the spring, returning with the moon.
Clenching a single fist, the great chiliocosm of fragrant waters is encompassed without remainder; extending a single palm, the ten billion Mount Sumerus are grasped with a firm basis.
Therefore it is said: "The great man attains the great capacity; the great wisdom achieves the great function. Even if the dust of the passions...
"Not yet liberated; the cataract over the eyes still remains.
He addressed the assembly, striking once with his staff and saying, "If you can speak, your nostrils have been pierced by him.
If you cannot speak, your nostrils have been pierced by him. At that time, a monk asked, "If one cannot speak, one's nostrils are pierced; what then?"
"Stop! Tell me why. [The Master] pierced their nostrils. The Master threw down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a phrase that was already entrusted to everyone before the drum was even struck.
If you can understand it, only then may we deliberate together; if not, how can you even be spoken to? Picking up his staff, he struck them all at once.
He dispersed and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
He then cited the Sixth Patriarch, saying: "I have a thing that has no head and no tail; it has no name and no character; it has no back and no face."
"Do you all still recognize it? At that time, Heze Shenhui stepped forward. The assembly said, "This is the original source of all dharmas;

it is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui. He then spoke in verse: "Horizontally holding the jade flute, he blows against the wind; Without violating the notes of gong or shang, its melody is naturally extraordinary."
"I most regret that this song capable of inviting the immortal was called by others the 'Partridge’s Lament'.
A monk came for an audience. Before the Master had finished citing the story of Xuefeng washing rice, he struck the monk on the head and said, "Leftover gruel and stale rice—no need to bring it out.
The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "A mere follower of words," and drove him straight out.
A monk came for an audience. As soon as he spread out his sitting cloth, the Master struck him. The monk said, "I thank the Master for your compassion.
The Master said, "Today I have suffered a loss."
The nun asked, "What is the original face of a student? The Master said, "A complete display of shame. The nun bowed;
the Master said, "It is difficult to deceive the eyes of the multitude."
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the Wuma year of the Kangxi era, after all the donors from East Tong had assembled, the Master joined his palms in farewell and passed away.
He was sixty-four years of age and forty-two years since his ordination. He was interred in his own quarters.
Chan Master Zuhong Zhendi of Bashi Temple on Mount Bai in Wukang was the dharma heir of Chan Master Jinming Jin,
the sixteenth-generation successor of the Jing Mountain lineage. He was the son of the Chen family of Haicheng, Zhangzhou.

When he first visited various senior masters at Yulin, he was unable to attain liberation. Subsequently, he paid his respects to Ji’ān at Tianchi and attained realization of the fundamental principle.

In the gengzi year of the Shunzhi era, while presiding over Baishan, he ascended the hall for a formal discourse: "The north wind blows fiercely, its cold majesty pervading everywhere; the sun of wisdom shines across the six directions."
Brilliant and radiant, it shines universally throughout the great trichiliocosm. The pivotal mechanisms of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are revealed all at once;
the adamantine eye of true insight is opened wide in unison. If a hot-tempered fellow were to seize upon this and act, he would be no man at all—what further words could there be for him?

The Buddhas appear in the world with their myriad words and ten thousand phrases, merely to untangle the entanglements and loosen the bonds for people. When the Ancestor came from the West, he spoke crosswise and spoke vertically;
his sole purpose was to have them realize the mind and reach the source. But tell me: how does one reach the mind? How does one clarify the bonds?
How does one remove the entanglements? How does one untie the knots? This majestic and dignified state—this is realizing the mind and reaching the source.
"Ya! Sa sa! Luo lo! Is this 'untying the sticky' and 'removing the bonds'? If you understand it in such a way, you will merely become like a hunting dog chasing after clods of earth.

This is not the place for a monk’s practice. If you, great assembly, wish to understand the place of a monk’s practice—" [He] suddenly took up his staff, struck it once on the ground, and descended from the seat.
A monk came to pay his respects; the Master asked: "The Buddhas of the three periods and the successive generations..."
[Blank]. Why is it that one cannot exit from here? When the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
Shimen Yun composed a verse on this, saying: "Flying thunder and flashing lightning as dragons overturn the sea; The collapsing mountains and swirling gales are all but black winds."
Reeds on both banks were blown into snow; half followed the flowing water, half drifted into the void.
The Master joined the assembly in their labors and once preached the precepts to a tiger, after which the tiger ceased its malevolent deeds.
Consequently, monastics and laypeople from near and far revered his virtue and conduct, lamenting that they had not lived to see the Master in person.
On the sixteenth day of the [blank] month in the *guimao* year of the Kangxi era, having returned from soliciting firewood at the home of Mr. Zhu, he said to the assembly, "My task is finished.
He then returned to his quarters and entered *sitting-meditation nirvana*. His worldly age was fifty-five, and his monastic seniority (*lǎ*) was twenty-eight.
Chan Master Zhen Ni of Wanyan Mengtang in Yongjia ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the pure Dharma-body?
The Master said, "A broken dung-sieve. He then ascended the hall and said: "Before one's eyes there is no dharma; the true and constant alone is revealed. The meaning lies right before one's eyes."
Who could possibly grasp it? It is not wrong; the Dharma is turning right before one's eyes. One cannot change even a single word of it;
it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes, and neither sound nor form can deceive it. When you, great assembly, arrive at this point, you must also penetrate through to it before you may succeed.
Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation staff once and said, "Does the assembly understand? If you can understand it here, you may return home and sit in peace.
Do you understand yet? He struck the staff again.
Chan Master Benze Shigao of Anhua, Beijing, presided at Yongquan during the Xinchou year of the Shunzhi era. He ascended the hall and said:

"Meeting a fine craftsman, encountering a master hand—before such a person, one may as well roar in vain. Mounting the Kunlun upside down upon Sumeru, he turns his body to hide behind the Northern Dipper.
Letting loose the 'tortoise-nosed snake' of the Southern Mountain, the eight-armed Nalakūvara meets its fang once."
"Ha! Who among you does not know this very thing? Brothers, Lingyun did not know this thing when he saw peach blossoms and awakened to the Way;
Xiangyan did not know this thing when he heard the bamboo strike and clarified his mind; Yangqi did not know this thing when one lamp illuminated a thousand ages;
Baoshou did not know this thing when a few slices of ginger were spicy for ten thousand years. Suddenly the cat cried out—Master!"
He said, "Upāḍhyāya Maomiaozi, you have already explained it for [the sake of] □□. What more juice can one seek within a sesame cake?
He struck his *śakti* (jeweled staff) and said: "Repeatedly calling for 'Xiaoyu' was originally for no reason; it was simply that the husband wished to recognize the voice."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "This monk’s staff has suddenly sprouted branches last night; this morning it has just burst forth with buds.
A single flower opens into five petals, its fragrance permeating the very marrow of heaven and earth. It does not depend on the spring breeze beyond kalpas;

how could it be constrained by the pitch-pipes of the present age? He struck the ground once and said: "A few cries of wild cranes startle them as they arrive from heaven; infinite fish and dragons [emerge]."
The surfer arrives; the elegant style of Yueke flourishes from this point on. Everyone claps their hands and dances the *Santai* (Three Terraces).
Chan Master Dongyan Can of Jinming Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture was surnamed Bao and was a native of Huizhou. He once composed the "Song of Delighting in the Way," which says:
"Do you not see the one who delights in the Way in the mountains? Always content with three short strips of bamboo cord bound around his waist for years."
Many years have passed; a hundred anxieties have been shattered by the side of my cracked earthen cauldron. Not one thing above brings me honor nor shame;
three pecks or half a bushel is my sustenance. Daily I lean on my staff and wander along the mountain stream, where I see again the cowherd driving his wild oxen.

I sigh that the fair blossoms of youth are like a spinning candle; worldly affairs rush on—what end can there be? I have stolen this moment of pure leisure for a joyful dwelling; let it be neither Buddha nor Immortal.
Have you not seen how, since antiquity, Yi and Qi were ashamed of the Zhou grain? The Four Sages of Mount Shang maintained their lofty conduct;
in bamboo groves and thatched huts they set their minds at ease, planting fruit and growing lotuses to distance themselves from the mundane world. At this—
This joy is true blessing; it surpasses the accumulation of gold and jade by lords and dukes. Following conditions and acting as one pleases, one roams in leisure.
With a clod of earth for a pillow, one sleeps and sings a song. "A-he-he!"—opening wide both eyes—who else in heaven and earth is so carefree?
Let them laugh or revile me; they may call me a mad monk. A monk asked, "What is the news of arriving home? The Master said, "Wait until you..."
Firmly planting your heels, you should say for yourself:
Chan Master Suying Jian of Miaofeng Yian in Jianning Prefecture was a son of the Chen family of Putian; he resided at Puming.
A Teaching for the Assembly on Mid-Autumn. Mid-autumn is the fifteenth day of the eighth month; the moon’s orb is perfectly round and brilliantly radiant.
Where is its pure light not present? At Stone Tower it is especially worth admiring. Have you not seen Ma Boji of Jiangxi? He hooked thieves and ruined his own house—truly lamentable!

Yet he provided offerings and cultivated practice, transcending the mundane world; even now his legacy remains scattered, beyond all bounds. Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.
The Great Elephant of Jia Prefecture and the Iron Ox of Shan Prefecture have been quarreling over this old public case; it was necessary for Miaofeng to adjudicate it for them.
I, this mountain monk, said to them: "Whether there is profit or loss, one does not depart from the marketplace"—I struck each of them twenty blows.
Chased away, both were left without a foothold and grew increasingly alarmed, going straight to Japan to submit their ancestral accounts. There, they struck the ground with a resounding thud.
[He] struck the drum and called out, "A Bodhisattva! How very joyful! You people, under this clear blue sky and bright sun, what kind of bowl are you seeking here?
With his staff, he struck them all at once and dispersed them.
In the late summer of the Guihai year of the Kangxi era, he passed away peacefully without illness. During the cremation, the smoke and flames formed auspicious patterns;
his cranial bone, teeth, and tongue remained entirely intact. He was interred in a stupa at Xunyan.
Master Wenchan of the Ancient Wall at Zijiao Temple on Longmen Mountain in Qizhou was a native of Xiangyang. His surname was Cheng.
The Master planted his staff at Hanlian Monastery on Mount Lu. In the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era, he began teaching the Dharma at Wanshou Monastery in Xichuan.
Jihai: Relocating to Sanjiao. Ascending the hall, [the Master said:
"Shutting the door to build a carriage; opening the door, the tracks coincide. At the summit of the solitary peak, both are unestablished.
This morning, snow scatters across the vast sky; the ten thousand mountains share a single color. Suddenly, the ashes fly from the hearth, burning the one standing before the courtyard."
The Ancient Cypress: Hurry down from the clouds; rescue the stars and moon of the heavens. Carefully examine the forged blade—it is originally Bin-iron.
A single streak of pure light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox. In the four wilds and cold forests, the wind whistles. Suddenly grasping the staff, he stirs the soup with purpose;
one must seize the moment while the incense smoke is still hot. In the summer of the Gui-mao year, he was commanded to bathe and offered his farewell to the Golden [Buddha].
The portrait of Master Minglao depicts him sitting upright in his quarters as he spoke a verse before passing away;
his stupa was erected at his home mountain. Chan Master Yuanfa of Mount Zhong at Santasi Jingdesi in Jiaxing Prefecture was a native of Huizhou.

He was a descendant of the Duke of Mu of Yingtian. While serving as a *langjiang* (colonel), the flower of the Dharma suddenly blossomed within his mind, whereupon he shaved his head and became a monk.
The monk went to visit Jinming. Ming held up his whisk. The Master (Zhaozhou) then gave a shout. Ming said, "All the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have flowed forth from this very place;
do you see it? The Master said, "All the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have come from this very place."
Yilin Neng said: "From here one emerges onto the celestial highway; from here one comes riding a swift steed.
The supervising charioteer has already crushed the official streets—do not be surprised that we do not dismount when meeting. Once, he danced the Three Terraces with a full flourish."
Zongru Sheng said: "Jinming lifts up the head; the three pagodas lift up the tail. Father and son exchange places—this is truly worth beholding.
As for the matters that have come down from of old, there are many who merely speculate upon the words and phrases, while those who understand them without error are few."
The Cloud Verse by Shimen says: A traveler from the sea boards a raft, wishing to trace the source; He wanders through the realm of immortals, yet knows not its majesty.
One morning, beneath the blossoms, he personally turns his head back; Only then does he believe that from the profound stillness, the transformation into a Peng-bird arises.

In the autumn of the Jiyou year, he wrote a letter bidding farewell to Cao Siliu (the Minister of Agriculture) and, having finished his parting with the assembly of Dharma protectors, the layman Shi Bo asked, "When you go hence, Master, will you be heading for heaven or descending into hell? The Master opened both hands to show him.
The layman prostrated himself. The Master said, "Take care," and passed away. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at his home temple.
Regarding this *Qian* hexagram, the Chan Master Jin Minghuai Ruanyan Zhenjing of Jiaxing once offered this verse: "All that can be returned is naturally not you;
That which cannot be returned— if it is not you, who else could it be? He said: "The ethereal form of the immortal maiden is inherently elegant; she has no need for the application of rouge."
Descending from the Jade Tower, the cloud-belted pendants and frosty rings have all fallen away, leaving her nowhere to hide her shame.
Chan Master Xing of Tianfeng Peak at Sanjiao Longmen in Qizhou was a native of the Wang family of Huangmei, a descendant of Lord Zhongxuan.

From birth he was detached from worldly things; in his youth he studied the "Green Box" classics, yet he delighted in the life beyond the world. Whenever he read the Buddhist scriptures, he would penetrate their depths.

Day after day he forgot his weariness. When the world changed, he drifted off in all directions until he reached the Xiao River in Zhejiang, where he paid homage to Master Zhilang at Jinshe and received the tonsure.
He served him diligently for several years. One day, reflecting that the matter of birth and death is of great importance, he went to seek out Shiqi at Xuedou.
He was instructed to investigate the "original face" koan. After several days of intensive inquiry, he attained realization and presented a verse expressing his extraordinary insight.
Qiqi nodded in approval. Later, he visited Jinming. As soon as he entered the gate, the Master gave a shout; Jinming also shouted, and the Master shouted again. Jinming then raised his staff.
The Master said, "This old fellow has met his match today. Jinming struck him. The Master said, "Now I am truly at a loss. Jinming then ceased. Next...
On the day he ascended the seat, the Master came forward and asked: "For many years I have sought a true companion; now that we have met today, what shall be done?
Ming said, "I grant you thirty blows. The Master let out a thunderous shout. Ming looked at the assembly and said, "Behold this warrior!
The Master shook his sleeves and returned to the ranks. In the autumn of the Yiwu year of the Shunzhi era, Ming said to the Master: "This matter must indeed be..."

Only such a person as this can truly shoulder the burden. Observing that your realization is exceptionally transcendent, do not linger here for long. This winter, he appeared in the world at Qingliang Hermitage in Songjiang;
in the year Dingyou, he moved to Zhongfu Monastery in Xiaozhen. In Wuyou, he returned to his hometown. The assembly requested him to restore Duoyun Mountain.
In the summer of the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era, the ancient Master Sanjiao passed away, and the assembly requested him to preside over the seat.
In the year Jiayin, the gentry of Huangmei requested that the Master restore Dongyongfu, Puti, and other locations.
Wherever the Master went, he established a monastery.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "Having just left Xiushui, you have already crossed into Yunjian; I wonder, how do you manifest the primary principle?"
The Master said, "It breaks forth suddenly, difficult to discern. [The student] asked, "Entering the marketplace with hands hanging down is the old family style;
what is the brand-new phrase? The Master said, "Cutting off the current and penetrating the sea. Then he said, "The standard for a man of the Way is originally not fixed.

When directed toward movement, it is like wind passing through grass or water reaching the channel. Encountering things, it immediately becomes the source; the perfect sound flows forth beautifully. This is one phrase."
"Kāla! A thousand differences are cut off at once. You who have come here must know the single step of turning back.
[The Master] took up his staff, struck it once, and descended from the seat."
Chan Master Pei Gongqi of Cui Peak;
and Chan Master Biezhuan Zhenhua of Jinming Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture, son of the Tu family of that same prefecture. At the age of nineteen...

He relied upon Master Jie to shave his head, receive the full precepts, and undergo tonsure. Upon hearing the "Three Are Not" dialogue, he attained realization. Master Jie appointed him to oversee the record office (*jishi*).

One day, Jie entrusted him with his robe and whisk, and he subsequently took up residence at Qinxi. By nature, the Master was tranquil and simple; whenever he ascended the hall to instruct the assembly, [he spoke thus].
He provided spontaneous guidance and did not allow anyone to record his words.
Chan Master Tianyan Zhenqi of Haiyue in Guangling was the son of the Mao family from Rugao; he left the household life through the Dharma.
In a small assembly: Confucius could not read; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan. Yet people do not believe it. A bird as large as a mountain;
a fish as large as the sea. Yet people do not believe it. A father younger than his son; a younger brother older than his elder brother. Yet people do not believe it.
The morning star appears at noon; the red wheel shines by night. People do not believe it, yet Haiyue speaks thus. You people do not believe it, yet you speak thus.
Haiyue does not believe it. You people do not believe it; Haiyue does not believe it. Now tell me, are they the same or different?
Looking left and right, he said: "In the end, what is it? Again, looking left and right, he said: "Investigate! (Chán).
Chan Master Chen Yongxiu of Taicang Wenmei Yuan was a native of the Li family of Wulin. He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the realm of embroidered snow?
The Master said, "Winding paths where moss and lichen accumulate time and again; deep within the Snow Hall, the bamboo breeze is clear.
The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Supporting a staff while picking through the falling petals, one follows the path with faith."
As he took a step, he saw the clear blue water. A monk asked, "What about the matter that transcends this? The Master struck him.
He ascended the hall and said, "I, this mountain monk, have a phrase I have long wished to speak to you all. Because worldly affairs were too busy, I never brought it forth.
Today, by chance, there is leisure; why not explain it in detail? Each of you should listen attentively. He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly.

The shade is thick by the courtyard edge; two [people] sit for a long time as if intoxicated. By the embankment, the willows hold pearls and spit forth emerald green. In the pond, the frogs’ drumming resounds like thunder;
beneath the trees, the Chan practitioners nod off to sleep. "A-he-he! Do you understand? Do you understand? He planted his staff on the ground and said:
The sun rises high, casting deep shadows of flowers; the breeze is warm, and the birds' songs shatter [the silence].
The Master asked Shun, "What have you been doing lately? Shun replied, "Above is heaven; below is earth. The Master said:
"Many people will not agree with you," said Shun. Mazu replied, "What benefit is there in requiring them to agree? Mazu then struck him.
Shun said, "Many people will not agree with the Master. Mazu asked, "Why? Shun replied, "Do not corrupt the sons and daughters of others."
The Master said, "Why did Xuansha refuse to acknowledge Lingyun? Shun said, "I urge you to take another cup of wine;
once you have passed the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friends left. The Master nodded his head in approval.
In the spring of the Gui-mao year, he returned once more to his old age to inquire after the plum blossoms. He once said to the assembly, "Time passes swiftly;

you must all urgently attend to the foundation of your feet. On the twenty-seventh day of the first month of winter, he manifested slight illness. By the evening of the thirtieth, he called for an attendant.
He took the medicinal bath and, sitting in the lotus posture, passed away. At that time, the mountain birds cried out in grief, shaking the forest trees.
Yunmen Jibai of Nankang Prefecture informed Chan Master Renxu about his departure; Renxu went to visit Jinming, who drew on the ground with his staff and said:
"Say something toward here. The Master drew a circle with his staff. Ming struck him. The Master shouted. Ming said, "Why shout so recklessly?
The Master shook his sleeves and departed. When he first resided at Wulao Peak on Mount Lu, every time he engaged in discourse with his disciples, none failed to be pleased and convinced.
Later, he moved to Yunmen. One day he said to the assembly: "If you can utter a phrase for turning around..."
Furthermore, there is the "phrase of letting go from the cliff. If one can utter this phrase of letting go, there is also the "final phrase.
Try to convey some news of it; the assembly was at a loss for what to do. The Master said, "If you do not understand, I shall speak for myself.
He then sat upright and recited a verse, after which he cast aside his brush and passed away.
Chan Master Lanruo Zhitian of Chengtian Monastery in Quanzhou, whose courtesy name was Shixian, was the son of the Zheng family of Jinjiang.

Regarding his small instruction given while observing a game of Go, he said: "When a chessman meets its match, one's clumsiness is hard to hide; when a poem reaches the point of being recited repeatedly, only then does its artistry become apparent.
For a monk, carrying his staff and wood wherever he goes and achieving victory through adaptation to circumstances is much like this game of Go; they are indeed similar in their stillness.
Cease. Movement is the deployment of the board’s illumination; these two are a single double-gate, yet they proceed in tandem so that both principle and phenomenon are reached.

Cutting off a corner to fly diagonally is like burying troops to provoke a battle—what prevents striking here while attacking there? Entering directly with a single blade values the breaking of layers.
First ascending the flank to establish a posture, how could one possibly invade the gateway? Relying on a corner to seek survival is to miss the opportunity.
"Several cities have fallen; the three armies have suffered defeat. It was because you delayed for half a moment that you were forced to break through the encirclement.

In the end, you were like one drawing a bow after the enemy has already passed—merely following others up and down. This was certainly a lost strategy. Even if you had been lenient by half a measure, you would still have ended up in second place."

Therefore it is said: "Holding the counting sticks still belongs to the later; winning or losing depends on the first move. Those who wish to understand this must realize the principle of the first move:
unless one breaks through the great iron net, overturns the inverted lotus, and attains mastery over both killing and giving life, one cannot be called a national master.
Even when examined closely, the ultimate standard of a monk’s own station still lacks one move. How so?
This is the ultimate standard for the monk. Before black and white are distinguished, the subtle is difficult to apply; once the patterns appear, it is but a single game of chess.
Only when the nineteen lines are severed across the middle can one sit and enjoy the foundation of peace. At the end of his life, he bathed and passed away while reciting a verse.
Upon cremation, a single sandal remained unburnt and is enshrined to this day. His stupa was built on Mount Qingyuan.
Chan Master Xuezi Jing of Jingming Hermitage at Gaofeng in Huzhou ascended the hall.
He cited the case where Master Zhengjing pointed to a peony flower and asked an attendant, "Do not interpret it as red; do not interpret it as white. How do you interpret its color?
The attendant replied, "The red is beautifully red; the white is beautifully white. Zhengjing said, "You are still turned by colors. The attendant said:
"Set aside the red and the white; I request that the Master speak of something else. Zheng said, "The red is red; the white is white. The Master composed a verse:
"Not red, not white, Set aside these two kinds and do not let it leak out. The cuckoo calls again and again as the sun sets."
The spring wind leaves the branches in disarray, stained with blood.
This is the account of Master Zhain of Xinglong Temple on Mount Lu in Jiangzhou, whose courtesy name was Yun’an and whose secular surname was Li.

He was a native of Sangluo. From birth he possessed innate wisdom and took no pleasure in the studies of the civil service examination system; he served as a *langjiang* by virtue of his family’s hereditary privilege.
Because he was about to violate the law, he was sentenced to execution. His mind was filled with a sense of solemn dread, so he immediately went to Donglin on Mount Konglu to shave his head.

There, while reading the *Record of Peak High* (Gao Feng Lu), he encountered the phrase "dragging a corpse" and felt deep doubt. He traveled extensively to consult various masters, seeking a realization where conduct and understanding were in accord.

Hearing that the elder Jie possessed the spirit of the ancients, he went specifically to his quarters. Upon seeing him, it was as if they shared a karmic affinity from a past life; he thus humbled himself before him.
Ming asked, "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing. What is it? The Master said, "Exposed.
Ming said, "Yesterday someone spoke this way and was given thirty blows and driven out. The Master said, "If you want to strike, strike! Why speak of 'yesterday'?
He struck him immediately as the words left his mouth. Ming held him back, saying, "You blind donkey, making such a mess! The Master prepared to—
As the Master was about to speak further, Ming struck him. As the Master again prepared to speak, Ming struck him once more. The Master then attained sudden and complete realization.

Tianduoyuan composed a verse on this: "When one reaches the point where the mountains end and the waters run dry, the soaring of the Peng bird and the springing of the lion are both too relaxed and too taut."
He took his three-foot-long Dragon Spring Sword and fashioned it into a "Incense for Guiding the Soul and Restoring the Spirit.
Master Yin-zong praised this marvel with a verse: "Having traversed a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags, In the depths of white clouds, I beheld the tracks of the wild sheep."
Turning over, he ascends directly to the highest peak; with lightning and thunder he drives forth the far-flying wild geese.
The Cloud Gate Inscription says: "Shattering it, he brings forth the five-colored marrow of the golden phoenix; Piercing through, he opens the myriad layers of cypress trees in the azure void."
It was simply because the guest did not stay overnight at Longmen; a thunderclap flew forth to send the distant sail away.
The next morning, as Ming entered the room, the Master said, "Yesterday’s public case (*gongan*) was not yet resolved.

He struck a pillar with his palm and said, "You wish to repeat the verse once more. Ming said, "What can be done about this public case? Before the words had even faded, the Master let out a thunderous shout.
Ming also gave a shout. The Master shouted again. Ming said, "After three shouts and four shouts, what then? The Master shouted twice in succession.
Ming said, "To recognize this one shout is a kindness so great it is difficult to repay. The Master prostrated three times, and Ming deeply approved;
he then brought forth the lineage transmission and bestowed it upon him.
Yinzong’s Marvelous Verse says: Suddenly encountering a wine shop, Your cup and my goblet dispel poverty and sorrow.
Hand in hand we enter deep into the peach blossom grove; Who cares whether it is spring or autumn in the human world?
Kim Myeong-uk’s Verse: The sea and sky are vast and wide, a light boat floats upon them; Exhausting every grace, it refuses to rest.
It startles the phoenix perched upon the branches of Cangwu, Surging straight toward the clouds and passing beyond the azure isles.
Shimen Yun’s Verse says: Ruined walls and broken huts, timeless as ever; The four walls are all through, providing no shelter at all.
Suddenly the western wind shakes the cassia seeds, Startling several crows from the eaves.

In the spring of the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era, he returned to reside at Donglin. In the autumn of the Yisi year, he moved to Huagui in Qi, Hubei. In the Jiyou year, he relocated to Biyun on Mount Xiling;
the fourfold assembly flocked there like a river, and all were delighted and convinced by his deliberations on the public cases (gong'an) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Ascending the hall: When all is exhausted and gone, the earth’s axis shifts and the heavens revolve; the dragon roars and the mist rises, the tiger sighs and the wind springs up.
At such a time as this, those who habitually employ their clever maneuvers may, with the single eye of a śramaṇa, seal in place the myriad phenomena of the universe.
Thus they can suck the Western River into their mouths and hide the Northern Dipper within their bodies; with a mere three-inch tortoise-hair brush, they stir and sever the Yellow River.

A single leaf of the chestnut burr splits open the Flower Treasury World; in every instance it appears, in every dharma it is manifest. Cow urine and horse dung shine through the past and illuminate the present;
in every mote of dust there is preaching, in every land there is discourse. Even a white ox and a stray cat roar like thunder and flash like lightning. Thus, the former masters said:
Entering deeply into the principle, one meets the ultimate meaning through non-action. It is further said: "The bright ancient path does not belong to the realm of the mysterious and subtle.

To observe universally with a single thought, all is vast, empty, and still. The patriarchs Xinghua, Fenyang, and our own Yuanhu, having attained this one point, drew the sword from the royal treasury and employed the mechanism of killing and giving life, thereby truly upholding the reputation of the Jibei (Linji) lineage and revealing it to humans and devas.
The True Eye. Today, this mountain monk likewise applies it; without sparing his own private possessions, he lays it all out on the table.
Daring to cast Yunmen’s cake, Zhaozhou’s tea, and Xuefeng’s ball right before you—those who can grasp them will have great cause for enjoyment.
Should there be those of extraordinary caliber, they would further roast the ox of the open field, carve the phoenix of Cangwu, and cleave the bright moon pearl.
Taking that which not even a thousand sages have transmitted—the supreme point beyond—how could they wait for it to be broken bit by bit?
Why then does the iron ox trample through the mysterious passageway, while the rustic elder sings of joy in a time of peace?
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the Xinhai year, he manifested a slight illness to the assembly and remarked, "There is one who will remember this very day next year.
The entire congregation was struck with wonder and amazement. At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is your intention, Master?

The Master replied, "Three hundred and eighty-four days from now, on the first ten days of the seventh month in the Renzi year. He then said to his disciples, "I wish to return to my hometown; it is appropriate [that you prepare]."
"Prepare it quickly. The assembly, thinking he was going as usual, purchased a donkey for him to ride. The Master looked back and laughed, saying, "My journey is not one a donkey can endure.
From then on, he earnestly exhorted the assembly to cultivate purity and cleanliness. On the eighth day of the ninth month...
He entered the city to bid farewell to the assembly. Donors and senior monks from various mountains arrived. On the eleventh day, he returned to the mountain.

On the twelfth day, he ascended the seat to provide instruction, the gist of which was as follows: "After my passing, you are not permitted to hold a formal mourning ceremony or observe the filial rites in the manner of worldly custom, nor are you permitted to collect money for funeral expenses.
You must not construct a stupa. You must cast my remains into the rivers and streams to benefit sentient beings."
Thus, on the fifteenth day at the hour of the Dragon (辰), he bathed, burned incense, sat upright, and passed away while writing a verse.
During the cremation, his remains were recovered; his teeth were white and remained intact, and his prayer beads were divided exactly as before.

The monastics and laypeople of Huang'an prostrated themselves and wept, as if they had lost their own parents. His teacher was Tianqi. On the nineteenth day of the eleventh month of the Xinyou year, [he entered] the world...
His life span was fifty-two years, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was twenty-eight.

When Chan Master Zhendiyan of Ouan and Zhuanan at Taicang happened to read the *Nirvāṇa-samavasaraṇa-parivarta* chapter of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, he encountered the Bodhisattva’s question:

"Now that the four great elements have each departed, where does this illusory body reside? Thereupon, he struck the table and sighed deeply, saying, "Human beings do not understand [the nature of reality]."
This matter is merely a semblance of being a monk; within one's own fundamental portion, it provides no benefit whatsoever. Thereupon, he traveled extensively to seek instruction.

One day, hearing the sound of the wooden board signaling the assembly, he suddenly attained realization. He went to Jinming to visit Master Jie, where he remained in attendance for over a year. Later, he lived in seclusion in Loudong. Due to illness, he retired to Dongguan.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the Ding-si year of the Kangxi era, at the hour of Yin (3–5 a.m.), he requested [to be brought to him].

He wrote a verse with his brush, saying: "Throughout my life I have been solitary; I have kept my door closed and guarded my simplicity. Though my Way has grown cool, I rely on the brilliance of future generations.
With a shout, he threw down his brush and passed away. He was interred at the right side of Lotus Temple in Jinsu Town.
Yuan Yin said, "Sengcan. The Master said, "When the World-Honored One held up the flower, Kāśyapa gave a slight smile.
Tell me, what was he smiling at? Yuan Yin let out a shout. The Master said, "Where does this shout land? Yuan Yin said, "It is not without cause for doubt.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "What about this? Yuan Yin said, "Do not rashly transmit any news. The Master said, "Just now, on the mountain..."
The monk asked, "What is the Way? Yunyan said, "Where is the previous statement? The master said, "This mountain monk is advanced in years.
Yunyan said, "Being advanced in years is quite right," and he then bowed.
Chan Master Miaoyun Zhenxiong of Jinge Temple in the Three Pagodas district of Jiaxing Prefecture was surnamed Xu and was a native of Wuyi, Jinhua.

His father, Zhongfang, served as the Commandant of Denglou. The Master was born within his official residence; even while still in his swaddling clothes, whenever he saw a Buddha or a monk, [he would show signs of reverence].
He was immediately filled with admiration and joy. At the age of nine, he lost his mother.

As the times were fraught with many hardships, Fang sighed and said, "If a great man cannot bring stability to the chaos, it would be better to enter the Empty Gate and pursue the Buddha Vehicle. He then abandoned his official post and followed Huayan, who personally initiated him into the monastic life.
The Master also relied upon Fang for his tonsure and received the full precepts from Lingyin Juede. There, he took up the "Zhuhui" (Cane) kōan and engaged in its investigation.
Without slackening his efforts, he happened to go to North High Peak. Deeply immersed in doubt, he forgot everything else; upon returning, he raised his eyes and saw the moon.

His mind and circumstances became vast and clear of their own accord, and the knot of doubt was instantly released. As he reached his quarters, the assembly reproached him for violating the rules. The Master smiled serenely and said, "If one does not climb high to look out, how can one know the breadth of the vast ocean?
Later, when De Li raised a public case (gong'an) to interrogate him, [the Master] responded with total clarity. Thereupon, he went to pay his respects to [Master] Yan.
The various elders—Muchen Zuoyin, Feiyin, Ruan’an, Fushí, Yulin, Muyun, and Yichu—were such that their sharp spiritual flashes (*jīfēng*) did not yield to those of Wuke;
I have heard this. I also heard that Master Jie’s gate-style was lofty and steep, and his Way was esteemed throughout all quarters.
I therefore went to Jinming. Master Ming asked: "Clouds seal the lion's den; there is no door for facing it or turning away from it. From where do you enter? I replied: "From—"
Yunmen said, "Entering through the gate is not the family treasure. Ming said, "You are a wandering monk; why are you making your living inside the wombs of donkeys and horses?
The Master said, "Today I have personally seen the Abbot. Ming said, "Look at this old monk's eyebrows; how many hairs have fallen out?
The Master said, "They are growing. Ming then struck him. The Master said, "If one does not enter the great waves, how can one..."
Seeing a man playing in the tide, Xuefeng Ming said, "What principle have you seen that you speak thus? The Master brushed out his sleeves and departed. Ming then ordered tea.
Ming picked up a fruit and said, "Is this *amṛta* (clarified butter) or is it poison? The Master replied, "The tongue is in the Master's mouth.
Ming asked, "How do you understand this? The Master gave a shout. Ming placed the fruit before the Master and said, "Try swallowing it."
[The Master] spat it out. The Teacher prostrated and said, "I thank the Abbot for the tea. Ming immediately ordered him to attend the hall and subsequently appointed him as the *Vina* (Rector).
Next, he was promoted to Head of the Monastery (*Jianyuan*). On the New Year’s Day of the *Renzi* year, Ming ascended the hall, held up his whisk, and called to the assembly:
"The World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years; this old monk has opened this hall twenty-five times. At Vulture Peak, he held up a single flower; [now] Jinming raises [his whisk]."

Master Ming raised a fly-whisk and said, "Tell me, is this the same as that, or is it different? Master Shishuang rose from the assembly and bowed, saying, "I am glad that today this old man has finally had a glimpse.
Master Ming held the whisk upright and said, "This very thing extends vertically through the three periods of time and spans horizontally throughout the ten directions.
Tell me, by whose power of grace does it do so? Master Shishuang replied, "Even grinding my bones to powder would not suffice to repay it. Master Ming struck the whisk once. Master Shishuang [bowed].
Having performed his prostrations, he stood according to his rank. That very morning, [the Master] bestowed upon him the lineage descending from the highest source, along with the Dharma verses.
In the *Kāngxī* year *Guǐhài*, he appeared at Dabeisi in Linqing Prefecture. Ascending the hall, the Master gave a shout and said:
"If one speaks of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the mouths of all Buddhas and patriarchs hang upon the wall. Although above it not even a needle may pass... (The text here breaks off).
The Elder also could do nothing but part ways and open a narrow path. He took up his staff, struck it once, and said:
"Is there anyone who disregards their very life who will come forth to meet this staff? A monk asked: "Green grass grows upon the crown of Vairocana."
"A dead snake lies across the feet of Vajrapāṇi. Let us set that aside for a moment; the jade palace is covered in moss. What is the underlying meaning?

The Master said, "White clouds enshroud the green trees; who recognizes the countenance of the Sage Yao? [The student] asked, "Heavenly timing and earthly advantage; the fourfold assembly is in harmony.
How would you express this in a single phrase of celebration? The Master said, "The mountains and rivers are the Emperor’s longevity; the world is the Dharma-King’s body. [The student] asked, "..."
The Li Lake drips with milk, its fragrance transmitted forever; the old shop reopens, the Dharma-transformation renewed. The Master said, "I also require everyone to lend a hand.
[A monk] said, "A single phrase completely transcends all forms; after a thousand years, the Yellow River is clear once more. The Master said, "..."
"What excellent news! [The student] said, "The student has a share in making prostrations. The Master struck him, saying, "Do not pretend.

[The student] asked, "When one brushes aside the weeds and gazes at the wind, and the rubble gives off light—what is the realm of Great Compassion? The Master said, "Clouds sleep upon broken steles; birds roost in the *kāṇḍa* tree.
[The student] said, "Human sages and numinous lands cause white-robed laymen and black-robed monks to gather in crowds. What is the person within the realm? The Master—
[The monk] said, "The eyes are born beneath the brows; the ears rest against the cheeks. [The monk] said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the person and the environment.
As for the matter of fully manifesting the true command, how is it? The Master struck him across the back with his staff. The monk said, "A master of the school—your natural state remains.
The Master said, "Only those on the same path know. He then said, "The bannerpole is raised; the ancient shop is reopened. The treasure storehouse is opened; the [Dharma] is transported..."
This treasure of the renunciant is scattered before all people; let each take as much as they require. If you understand it in this way, you are still somewhat close;
if you do not understand it in this way, the staff will open another path for you. Striking once, he said:

"To shatter the lair of Pāpīyas and manifest the ancestral reputation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must rely on this very thing to grasp the Vajra King’s sword and suspend the numinous [jewel] behind the elbow."
The talisman must be for the right person. Today, this mountain monk, having received the command of the great donors, cannot decline in accordance with the principle.

Cutting through the brambles and stripping away the weeds, I shall carve open the faces of both the living and the Buddha. Tilling the soil and digging through the stones, I shall reveal the natural radiance of the original ground.

Instantly, I shall cause the cold ashes to burst into flame and the withered tree to sprout in spring. The stone lion lets out a roar that startles the green mountains into a sudden awakening; the wooden [man] stands tall at their head.
The horse neighs in the wind; it tramples the Yellow River until it flows backward. Is there anyone who can cast a single glance here? After a long silence, he plants his staff and says:
"Holding the golden whip in hand, I ask the returning traveler: at this late hour of night, who will ride with me across the imperial enclosure?
He then cites Master Jiegan’s ascent to the hall upon taking residence at Jinming: "He broke the meditation hall; heads were covered in dust and faces were smeared with grime."

The Buddha Hall has the forehead of a donkey and the cheeks of a horse; the mountain gate is broken, yet he raises his fists and wields his pestle; the Buddha pavilion is shattered, yet he waits for the moon and sleeps amidst the clouds;
those who recognize him are few. He commands a troop of monks in tattered rags to dwell here, using the broken to break that which is not yet broken.
"Breaking, breaking, not breaking. Not breaking, not breaking the bottom. Its application is infinite; it must be made so that one penetrates in all directions.
If you are one who transcends the school and differs from the common view, this mountain monk can only regard you with special eyes and treat you as one who breaks through what is broken.
Is there anyone among the assembly who can split what cannot be split, who does not break the bottom? If so, come forth! Jinming shall break it through for you."

The Master said: "To turn the sun and moon within the alchemical cauldron, to employ the tongs and hammer beyond the extraordinary, to issue commands to devas and humans, and to weigh the Buddhas and Patriarchs—this old fellow is certainly not lacking in such ability.
Yet, as for upholding the essential principles of the Linji school, that is still not yet achieved.
Had I been there at that time, I would have spread out my sitting cloth, drawn this mark, rolled it into a ball, tossed it behind me, and then opened both [hands]."
The Master said: "I say, 'Yes. Watch how he brings it to a final conclusion. If you all understand it in this way, Dīpaṃkara Buddha will be a fellow-student of yours.
He struck his staff on the ground and said: "Change the bones and wash the entrails, reorganizing from the start; though your whole body is eyes, you must still practice further."
In the summer of the Xinwei year, the local gentry and scholars of Jiahe invited [the Master] to reside at Longyuan in Santan. Ascending the hall, he brandished his whisk and said:

"The hook is cast across the four seas, seeking only the leviathans. Taking his seat and donning his robe, he continued for the sake of those seeking true knowledge; suddenly raising the whisk, he said:
The past has already passed; the future has not yet arrived; it is precisely today that this mountain monk preaches the Dharma.
You must take Great Perfect Enlightenment as your monastery and dwell securely in the Dharma of equality and suchness, preaching so that it manifests before you.

When both the clergy and the laity likewise attain understanding according to the Dharma, then voices will respond to one another and essences will harmonize with one another, causing all demons and outsiders to be utterly extinguished.

The traces universally encompass all Buddhas and sentient beings. Entering into a single mote of dust, they manifest boundless physical forms; within the tip of a single hair, they turn the Great Dharma Wheel.
Mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—sentient and insentient alike—are all contained herein.
Emerging and submerging, he lets out a shout and says: "In the heavens, every star bows toward the North; among men, no water fails to flow toward the East."
A monk asked, "What is the Venerable Immovable One? The Master said, "Born in the hour of the Rabbit; born in the month of the Dog. The verse of the Right Dharma says:
"The silver lamp is overturned, and the great flood submerges the heavens; The sky clears and the sun opens the sea; it is like awakening from a dream."
The mind lingers with regret at the cry of a solitary wild goose; let its sound not startle those sleeping alone.
Lin Guang’s verse says: "As dawn approaches in Fusang, the sun-bird stirs; on the thousand peaks of late autumn, the jade hare rises."
Washing the Milky Way clean is but a single matter; the azure void fills the heavens, scattering jade-like crystals.
Huìyuè’s eulogy says: "The golden crow hastens, the jade hare speeds; from east to west, they turn like a pivot. Radiant and glorious!"
Difficult to describe; its pure radiance can be gathered in the palm. Flying up to the Ruomu tree, it awakens the spring dreams of the human world.

Treading upon and shattering the coral, its reflection ripples across the waters of a thousand rivers. As the green dial of time shifts and passes, one reflects that in every palace within the four gates, spring has arrived at the thirty-sixth degree.
The Verse on the Celestial Breast-Feeding: A pair of rhombus-shaped mirrors reflect one another; The fair lady adorns herself with skill day and night.
In the human world or the heavens above, none can compare; She who could topple a state has no peer in the world.
Tianchi Shan composed this eulogy: "An embroidered mandarin duck is truly remarkable; One flies east, while the other flies west.
Though they once shared a bed, now they sleep alone; The golden needle never again reveals its secret to you."
The Inscription for the Tiangong School states: It does not require fire to be hot; it does not require water to be cool. Morning and evening its mechanism never ceases;
it illuminates clearly, encompassing the eight wildernesses. The wise should not be ignorant of this; those lost in the current merely waste themselves in vain.
Borrowing the shade [of the clouds], it is like the Great Yu; every fragment is a work of art.
A monk asked, "What are the three types of transformation bodies? The Master said, "Do you know how to kill? The monk replied, "In the royal treasury, there is no such blade.
The Master struck him, saying, "You are not one of my kind. A monk asked, "What is the stage of non-retrogression?
The Master said, "The government relies on official documents; private matters rely on contracts. A monk asked, "What is the Patriarch [Dharma]? The Master said, [He]... (text fragmentary).
[The monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Master’s coming from the West? The Master said: "Outside the door, the wind knocks against the bamboo.

[The monk asked: "What does this clarify? The Master said: "In the courtyard, butterflies dance among the flowers. [The monk asked: "I do not understand, Master. The Master said: "The peaches and plums bloom throughout the garden;
the wind carries their fallen petals onto the moss. The monk had no reply. The Master then struck him.
While the Master was at Jinming Temple, the First Abbot, Chū, arrived at dawn and ordered the Master to lead the assembly out to welcome him.
Chū asked, "Fan Li, the lake and sea, moonlight and heaven—why have you been tripped up by the *guansuo* (shackles)? The Master replied, "I am being brought low because of you, Reverend.
Chū raised his staff and said, "Do you recognize this? The Master snatched it away and threw it to the ground. Chū said, "This..."
"You ill-mannered fellow! I shall have my elder brother beat you! The Master said, "One must not rely on power to oppress others," and gave him a slap.
The man initially intended to seize his staff, but the Master simply walked away. When Chujian first met Mingzhao, he said, "This fellow has caused no small amount of trouble for people."
Ming said, "Master, you must not let the thief seize you. Ch'u replied, "I trouble my elder brother to come out to the field for me to clear the air.
Ming looked back at the Master, who performed a prostration and said, "O venerable old monk, please be seated," and immediately served him tea. He then withdrew and went out.
Ch'u looked at Ming and they laughed together, saying, "What a fine disciple!"
A monk asked, "I do not ask about the physical body falling into decay; what is the indestructible Dharma-body?
The Master said, "The eight-armed Nala strikes the Imperial Bell. The monk said, "Please, Master, reveal this clearly to me. The Master said, "A stone man topples the five Mount Sumerus."
Chan Master Tie Rongxuan of Youke Mountain in Pucheng, Jianning Prefecture—also known by the pen-name Ji’ung—ascended the hall and said:
"For over thirty years I have dwelt alone in a cave; The steps are cold, yet I cannot bear the weeds that cling to my skirt. My Chan-mind has already become the snow of midwinter."
"Let him be reborn as a horse or a donkey; why is this so? My back aches from sitting for too long.

He ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master descended from his seat. The administrative officials (zhishi) seized him and asked, "Why did you descend from your seat without uttering a single word?
The Master said, "In the morning I ate two bowls of cold congee, and there is a slight discomfort in my stomach."
"Stop! Wait a moment while I go to the latrine; I shall speak for you. The assembly was at a loss as to what to do.
The Master then returned to his quarters and ascended the hall. "A painting of plum blossoms by a half-open window—do not look upon it with indifference.
A pillow amidst the waves of wind through the pine trees—do not listen to it in confusion. If you, great assembly, wish to know this matter, it is utterly and completely exposed."

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Yesterday, this mountain monk attended a village feast. I bit into a piece of black, shiny grit, and it has been hurting my teeth so much that they still ache this morning.
I cannot speak of yellow or white matters with you brothers. He then descended from his seat.
The monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "If I have a place to stay, I will come and tell the Master.
The Master said, "You are a person who upholds the precepts; why do you not observe the pure regulations? He replied, "Master, please do not charge a person with a crime.
The Master said, "I am not charging you with a crime. An ancient said, 'After eating porridge, wash the bowl and go. What does this mean?"
[The monk] said, "Last night in a dream, someone asked me this question. It happened that I was so overcome by sleep that I did not answer him.
The Master said, "Forget it. A monk asked, "What is the wondrous body? The Master said, "Ditches and pits, mounds and hills; tiles and rubble, thorns and briars."
"What is wondrous function? The Master said, "Striking the void produces sound; striking wood makes no noise.
Chan Master Yuzu Jue of Ganlu Temple in Zhenjiang Prefecture was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Yangzhou.
He received the tonsure at Jianmen on Mount Qingliang in Nanjing and subsequently visited various elders, all of whom marveled at him. Later, he went to visit Jinming, who asked: "All..."
"Set aside for a moment what you have just realized," the Master said. "I shall strike you whether you can speak or not. The Master then gave a shout.
Ming said, "Aside from that shout, try saying something more. The Master replied, "I have come specifically to attend upon you, Venerable Sir.
Ming took up his whisk and struck him, asking, "Is this a reward or a punishment? The Master bowed; Ming struck him again. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and said: "Bring—"
"Offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land. Master Mingdu took the whisk and struck a monk standing nearby, saying, "This is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Mingdu then said, "You must take care of yourself."
The General of the Stone Banner, a Prince of the Second Rank (Huoshuo Efu), invited the Master to ascend the Dharma seat on New Year’s Day.

A monk asked, “The frozen clouds have just unfolded, and the ten thousand mountains reveal their transformations; the sun rises high, and the universe is clear. What is the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year?

The Master said, “A single gust of spring wind has just passed; where would flowers not bloom? [The monk continued,] “Today the General of Annam invites the Master to ascend the seat to offer his auspicious prayers.”

[The Master] extended the phrase. Again, [the student] asked, "How is it? The Master said: "In a hundred years there are thirty-six thousand days; only this year is most auspicious. [The student] said:
"The grace-light of the Dharma-realm shines everywhere, and the colors of heaven and earth turn ever new. [He then asked: "What is the realm of ambrosia?"

The Master said, "The Golden Wheel Ruler governs the three thousand worlds; who is the person of ambrosia? The Master said, "The Jade Calendar proclaims its great mandate, bringing spring to the myriad nations.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then the Dharma transformation is widely spread, and the fourfold assembly shall all equally partake of it. The Master said:
He split the tongue of his *ācārya* and then planted his staff upright, saying: "When mercury falls to the ground, every drop is perfectly round;
when an ancient mirror faces its stand, every speck of dust shines with brilliance. As soon as the spring breeze passes, all things are renewed. One person has cause for celebration."
The myriad people rely upon him. A General who attains Buddhahood on the spot; a General who kills without batting an eye. He who kills without batting an eye attains Buddhahood on the spot.
Like a pearl rolling across a tray, or a tray rolling a pearl. [He] suddenly holds up his staff and says: "Naturally born, jade leaves and golden branches, exquisite;
their brilliance and fragrance have endured for countless years."
In the Jisi year of the Kangxi era, he resided at Kaehwa-sa Temple in the capital. In the first month of summer in the Renshen year, he manifested illness;

sitting in the full lotus posture, he recited a gāthā and passed away. His stūpa was enshrined at the right dragon-side of Ganlu-sa Temple. His worldly age was sixty-one, and his years of monastic seniority were [blank].
Several volumes of his recorded sayings (yulu) have been circulated in the world.

Chan Master Qixian Guangqing of Beiping Muyuan was the son of the Jin family from Shanyin. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. From his youth, he was quick-witted and intelligent.

Once, while visiting a Buddhist monastery, he became inspired by the desire to transcend the mundane world. He received the tonsure at Yunmen and studied the teachings under Sanyi Yu. Later, he went to Tiantong to study under Lin’ye.
Lin asked him, "When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, why did the outsider attain enlightenment? The Master—
Lin said, "To know the sound does not lie in frequent raising [of the staff]. Lin struck him and asked, "Do you still understand where this blow lands?
The Master said, "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to tip. Lin said, "When an ox passes through a window frame, why can its tail not pass through?
The Master said, "Today, Master, you have been caught red-handed by me. Lin said, "This swindler!"
"Vain talk," the Master said, and he shook out his sleeves and departed. Finally, he went to visit Jinming.

Jinming asked, "Setting aside for a moment the matter that the Great Matter is not yet clear, which is like losing one’s parents—why is it that even when the Great Matter is already clear, it is still like losing one’s parents?
The Master replied, "A sorrowful person should not speak of their sorrow to another sorrowful person. Jinming asked, "Where do you apply your mind? The Master said, "Why wash mud with mud?"
Holding up a clod of earth, Ming stretched out one leg and said, "How does my foot compare to a donkey's foot?
The Master bowed and said, "Were it not for the wild geese arriving at night, how could one see the autumn at the sea gate? Ming struck once with his whisk. Yinzhu then spoke in verse:
"Penetrating the layered nets of the teachings, The source of Chan flows through in its subtle pulse. To further clarify the Dharma of the mind, Exert yourself to revitalize the fundamental school."

Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The Dharma is proclaimed at the imperial court; the Way is expounded at Lake Li. As for the upward transmission and upholding [of the truth], how would you speak of it?
The Master said: "One blow leaves a scar. [The monk continued: "The tradition of Huading Peak is established everywhere. As for the Heart Seal of the Patriarchs—"
"How do you instruct? The Master said, "A cast-iron tortoise flies out from the brazier. The monk said, "Great capacity and great function;

when the true command is being exercised, how will you receive a person of transcendent measure? The Master struck him. The monk let out a shout, and the Master struck him back with a succession of blows, then said:
"For over fifty years I have tended a single ox; climbing mountains and wading through waters, I never rested. Now, at this high [age]..."

It is merely a tethering rope for the whip. With its tail drooping and head held high, its nature is already supple. It simply accommodates whatever comes its way; the mountains are vast and the waters are likewise boundless.
What need is there to speak of the plucking of the flower and the subtle smile, or the severing of the arm to find peace of mind?

Why imitate Ciming’s posting of notices in the Sangha Hall, or Dongshan’s pushing back the fruit table? This crew of ancient sages stirs up waves where there is no wind, spreading their influence far and wide.
"Family shame! You are no true men yourselves. Here in the monastery, we have already secured the boundaries; there is no need to further draw snakes or add legs.

You, with eyebrows growing above your eyes and ears hanging down to your cheeks, come here again seeking what bowl? [He] strikes the meditation staff and says: "Each of you, please return to the hall for tea."* *Note: This passage is a classic example of Chan (Zen) rhetoric, using paradoxical language and physical gestures to cut through conceptualization and provoke direct realization.*

In the first month of spring in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill. On the twelfth day of the fourth month, his disciple Yuanjing led the assembly to the abbot’s quarters to request his final instructions.
The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have from the outset never been involved in delusion or enlightenment.

Having suffered from dysentery for three months, I have become so emaciated that my bones are exposed all over my body. If anyone can understand it in this way, they will surely transcend both Buddhas and patriarchs. He spoke again:
The assembly said: "An ancient said, 'When the Dharma-body is ill, the form-body is the Dharma-body; when the form-body is ill, the Dharma-body is the form-body.

Now that the great assembly has asked me about the source of my illness, I, this mountain monk, have searched throughout the entire Dharma-realm for the place where the root of the illness arises, but it is utterly unfindable.
Therefore I say: 'The illness has reached the vital organs; even a divine physician folds his hands in helplessness. He then spoke a verse:
With a great shout, he entered parinirvāṇa in a state of auspicious tranquility. His worldly age was sixty-two, and his years of monastic seniority were forty-one.
Master Zheng Chan of Zhushan Hou’an at Xinghua addressed the assembly. He raised a case: A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the point of intimacy for a student?
Shoushan said, "The five nines end, and once again we meet spring. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is the matter? Shoushan...

[The questioner] said: "Winter has passed and Cold Food Festival is one hundred and five days away. The Master composed a verse: "The spring warmth fills the level plains and the orioles sing clearly;
From this point on, the lutes and songs delight the wayfarers. In contrast, I sigh for those who gallop through the frost; They have failed to appreciate the profound intent of the Lord of the East."
Chan Master Meng’an Jue of Qinglian Temple in Pinghu, whose courtesy name was Yiwèi, was the son of the Fan family of Jiaxing.

He received the tonsure at Jinming Temple and served for many years as the head of the secretariat (ji-shì). Later, he entered the master’s chamber [of his teacher] and subsequently resided at Qinglian Temple, where he engaged in intensive inquiry every day without fail.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the occasion when, on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreat in three different places, causing the Buddha to...
When Kāśyapa was about to strike the gavel to expel [the assembly], as soon as he raised it, he beheld hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs.
Exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not lift the gavel. The World-Honored One then asked, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless.

The Master said: "Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places, thereby disturbing the pure regulations. Kāśyapa struck the gavel intending to expel him, which startled the assembly and agitated the multitude.

When the World-Honored One questioned him, he acted with complacency, causing people to fight one another. Had the true command been put into practice, these three would have deserved to receive blows.
Why? Because they were under the gate of the Blue Lotus."

Master Songxiu Yuan of Xiling Ba’en ascended the hall. Raising the case of Layman Pang, before he had finished speaking, Wang Gonghua stepped forward and asked, "Since he is already a perfected Buddha, why does he need to choose? The Master said, "He drags the plow and pulls the harrow."
Chan Master Zhì of Sùyán in Tàipíng was a native of Máchéng. He ascended the hall and said: "Within the shadows of multicolored clouds, a divine immortal appears;
In hand he holds a red silk fan to shield his face. One must quickly fix one’s gaze upon the immortal; Do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand."
He raised his fan and said, "This is the fan. Now tell me, where is the immortal? He threw down the fan, bowed, and said, "This is the immortal.

Where is the fan? "If you all can fix a single eye upon this point," he said, "you will be able to roam at ease according to your own nature by the waterside or beneath the forest trees. But if you have not yet attained this, bite down firmly."
Bite down with your teeth and go ahead with all your might; naturally, when the water arrives, the channel will be formed.
Take the story of Dongshan’s "Three Pounds of Hemp" as an example; the verse says: "What is the Buddha? Three pounds of hemp. Twist it into a rope to bind the mists and clouds.
If you casually recognize the meaning on the hook's tip, You will laugh the old woman Wang of East Village to death. [End of] Recorded Teachings.
Gang Jueyi traveled through the world.
Chan Master Xuanhui and Chan Master Zhenliang of Yun’an at Puming Temple in Jianning—Zhenliang was the son of the Xie family of Ouning. He ascended the hall and said: "Three pounds of flax."
The dried dung-stick—set that aside for now. As for Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout, let them pass with one stroke.
Do you all still recognize the claws and fangs of the lion, the head and horns of the fierce dragon? To shed the body while sitting amidst a single color is to leave behind a shadow;
not falling into the same wind is to manifest great merit.
Small Sermon: When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. Within the school of the patch-robed monks, there is no need for arduous investigation.
Yet, as the ancient masters said: "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a dog-urine sky.
What matter on this side of reality does this clarify? It was said: "Do not travel the path beneath the mountain," and indeed, one hears the heart-rending cry of a monkey.
The nun Lianhua Ke from Xiuzhou was the youngest daughter of the Tian family of Huai'an. Her father held the rank of *zhishi* (commander) and passed away while serving at the frontier.
When the nun was seven years old, she saw her father’s corpse and sighed with emotion, saying, "What benefit is there in such a human life?

Thereupon, she conceived a resolve to transcend the mundane world; however, she was not yet free to do so. At the age of forty, she went to seek instruction from Chan Master Sanyi at Fanshou. Furthermore...
She went to visit Master Jiegan at Jinming and requested to have her hair shaved. Master Ming refused her request twice or thrice.

The nun became distressed and angry, vomiting blood that filled a basin. Master Ming took pity on her sincerity and granted her the tonsure and ordination, instructing her to contemplate the koan: "All phenomena return to One."
She forgot both sleep and food; before a year had passed, her vital energy was nearly exhausted. One day she saw Ming, who asked, "Where have you returned?

The nun recounted the reason for her state. Ming said, "It is fundamentally already manifest and functioning; why exert so much effort? At these words, the nun’s mind and spirit became calm and settled.
The nun presented this verse: "The entire being is elegant and refined; its meaning is inexhaustible. Majestic and manifest, the Master is revealed alone.
Morning comes, water is changed, incense is burned, and prayers are recited— All is contained within the ordinary activities of daily life. Mingke approved it.
Nun Límínxīn (Lí Mínxīn) of the Jū family was surnamed Yè and was a native of Púzhèn. Having lost her mother at a young age, she invited monks to recite scriptures;

upon seeing painted images of the hells, her heart was immediately moved. She abstained from meat and vowed to renounce the household life. When her father sought to arrange a marriage for her, she died rather than comply.
She subsequently entered a hermitage to shave her head and practiced austerities for several years. She received full ordination at Jīnmíng Temple, where Master Míng instructed her to contemplate...

Regarding the saying, "The matter before one's parents were born," he investigated it for a long time. One day, while ascending a tower, the sound of his foot striking the step triggered an awakening.

He then presented this realization to Chan Master Ming, who subjected him to even more rigorous training. This continued until he uttered the phrase: "From this point on, I have recognized the face of the pre-conception;
from now on, I am a man who stands out from the crowd. One day, while the nun was mending woolen cloth at the home of Scholar Luo Guang, Luo asked her, "How is it?"
This was a phrase that required the exertion of power on that day. The nun made a gesture with her needle as if pricking something.

It happened to be the end of the year; Layman Luo asked, "With what will you pass the year? The nun held up her fist. Luo said, "Is there anything else besides this? The nun replied, "I shall tell the Layman tomorrow morning."
On the day after the full moon of the ninth month in the year of Jiǎyǐn, he bathed, sat upright, recited a gāthā, and passed away.
