The layman Luó Kāilín, a teacher of literature and styled Kōngzhū, was a descendant of the Lí clan. From his youth, when he studied the classics, he was already able to refine his understanding of the ultimate realization of Confucius and Yán Hui;
thus, his spiritual practice was unlike that of others. One day, while accompanying his father, the Duke of Héngyáng, he passed by—
At Jiwai An, he encountered Chan Master Shiche ascending the hall; not believing in the affairs of the Chan school, he treated them with indifference.

During the Bingxu year of the Shunzhi era, his parents passed away one after the other, and he underwent all manner of hardships. His elder brother, Shi Yue’an, constantly inspired him during times of despondency.
He then visited Chan Master Linye of Dongta and subsequently studied under the chief seat Wuer and Feiyin.
The Chan Master Fei spread his two hands wide and asked, "Do you understand? The scholar was at a loss. Fei said, "To miss it right before one's own face.
At this, the scholar gained entry through faith. In the year Wuzi, he went to attend upon Master Jie of Jinming, where he mastered the domestic arts of the well and the mortar.

One evening, during the hall session, the Master raised his incense board and commanded the assembly to offer a response. The scholar stepped forward, seized the incense board, and said, "The handle of the Master’s authority is already in my hands."
The Master held it in his hand and looked at the assembly, saying, "In this entire period, I have found only this common man. The scholar threw down the incense board; the Master approved of him.

The scholar subsequently authored several volumes of commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a manual for visualizing the Buddha in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and collections of *niansong* (verses on cases) from the Chan lineage, all of which circulated in the world.
The layman Xiang Qian, styled Cizan, was the seventh-generation descendant of General Xiang Yi and the son of Jinwu Junqing.
Before his retirement from office, he studied under both Master Boshan and Master Yujisheng, and they both shared kōan-like exchanges with him. Upon resigning from his post, he...
He maintained a relationship as a "foreign friend" with Gu Nanmen Tianjie Sheng and others. Finally, he went to visit Master Jie at Jinming, where their karmic affinity was profound.
He then presented this verse: "Upon merely hearing it mentioned, one should immediately accept it; Why needlessly scar a piece of healthy flesh?
Cast your eyes upon the pivot and first examine the reality: Who does not bear the sun of Fu Sang atop their crown? Master Jie granted him formal approval (*inka*).
Master Shi once raised the koan of Layman Yushan crossing the bridge and falling flat, saying: "Brothers, one eye gazes at the sky, two feet tread upon the earth.
Tell me, where is the bright pearl? After a long silence, he said: "Spring is upon the tips of the grass."
How many descendants of the royal lineage truly understand? There is the *Jiuxin Lu* (Record of Investigating the Mind), which circulates in the world.
Layman Lu Xing, styled Tiaoshi, was a native of Xiushui. Having lost both his parents in childhood, he remained uninvolved with worldly affairs.

He delighted in visiting monastic centers, never tiring of lingering in the company of realized masters. In the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era, he went to Jinming Temple, where Ming instructed him to contemplate:
"All phenomena return to the One. After three years had passed, he happened to read the story of the "Three Blows of the Staff," and it was as if a poor man had found a treasure.
He composed a verse and presented it to Ming. Ming said, "This is merely the work of the conscious mind; you are still halfway there. This is not yet the news of having arrived home.

The Master accepted this with reverence. In the year Gengzi, he went for a second interview. Ming pointed to an ancient pitcher on the seat, and the Master composed a verse that perfectly accorded with Ming’s intention. (1)
There was once a monk who begged for money. A layman sealed up a certain amount and said, "If you can speak the Way, I will give it to you.
The monk said, "I am old. The layman replied, "The four great elements age; how could this [the self] possibly age? The monk pointed to his chest with his hand. The layman said:
"Try picking it up and showing it to me. The monk stepped forward; the Master then struck him with his palm.
The layman Lu Tao, a scholar whose courtesy name was Xuandu, was by nature serene and detached. He had frequently studied the Buddhist scriptures, as if he had practiced them since his youth.
He then visited various masters, including Ming’an, Tiantong, and Pingyang, whose recorded exchanges and witty remarks are engraved in his *Xinglu* (Record of Practice).

In the year Renchen, he went to consult Jinming. Jinming asked, “Have you ever met a true teacher? The Master replied, “I have met six or seven. Jinming said, “Which one among them did you find satisfying?
The Master replied, “If I had found satisfaction, I would not have come here. Jinming laughed and said, “Do not try to deceive this old monk. The Master remained silent.
"Please grant me instruction," he requested. The Master said, "This matter cannot be obtained from without. To clarify the mind-ground, you must examine the *huatou* (critical phrase).
The scholar bowed respectfully and withdrew. One day, while walking, he broke his leg; at that moment, he suddenly realized its essential meaning.

He spoke in verse: "At the crossroads, I struck it directly; In one moment of profuse sweat, the fontanelle opened. The stone man was raised up and laughed aloud; Stretching out my legs was originally..."
He came to stay within the quarters and presented his realization. Mingming deeply approved.

The lay practitioner Zhu Yixian, whose courtesy name was Qinchen, had harbored the aspiration for world-transcending liberation due to the upheaval of the dynastic transition, yet he had not yet realized it.
In the year of Xinmao, he suffered from a blood ailment. He then visited Jinming to seek further instruction and investigate the essential points of the Dharma.
Jinming said, "Layman, look: before a single thought has arisen, from where does this root of illness come?

He was told to look repeatedly in this manner—neither detesting the clamor nor seeking stillness, neither loathing the mundane nor aspiring for the sacred. "The point at which Su Shi and Huang Tingjian gained their strength..."

He transcended this. The officer followed the instructions, and his illness was indeed cured. One night, he raised his head and saw the moonlight shining with brilliant purity; he then attained awakening and composed several verses in succession.
Their gist is as follows: "The five-colored clouds part and the myriad phenomena become clear; The single orb of the mind-moon penetrates through to the bright heavens.
Empty space falls to the ground, leaving no trace; What need is there to use even a single speck of dust for the world? He presented this to Mingming. Mingming—*Mingming*.
He said: "Your bone and spirit are fierce and keen; your will and nature are resolute and daring. You may truly be called 'Zhenyi' (Truly Resolute).
Li Qian, styled Jiaomen, was an expert in the Confucian classics who took pleasure in the study of Buddhism. He once translated the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*).
At the age of twenty-two, he encountered the Chan Master Fushen, who showed him the saying: 'When you do not think of good and do not think of evil, what is that which is your original face?'"
He visited them, and his words were in perfect accord with those of the two masters, Yingning and Sirui.

In the year of Bingwu, he stayed for some time with Kongzhu and Luozizi, and subsequently proceeded to Jinming to visit Master Jie. It happened that the bell was tolling; Master Jie asked, "Is it the bell that rings, or is it the ears that ring?
The scholar replied, "A single string has threaded them all through. Master Jie shouted, "Can you thread this one as well? The scholar prostrated himself.
[The Master] said, "Your kindness is great; it is difficult to repay. During the tea service, the Master asked, "How do you understand the story of Baizhang and the wild fox?
The scholar then overturned his teacup. The Master asked, "As for 'neither falling nor being deluded,' how would you explain that?
The scholar held his teacup upright, facing upward. The Master said, "Setting aside such tricks, try and say a single phrase. The scholar then—
"Hai! Xuedou said. "Why do you shout so recklessly? The monk said, "Preceptor, do not be offended. Xuedou then struck him. The monk bowed.
One day, while attending him, Xuedou asked, "Regarding the old woman of Mount Tai and Zhaozhou—how did he see her through? The monk said, "Old Zhao’s tongue has no bone.
Xuedou nodded in approval and immediately presented this verse: "Zhaozhou bit his tongue and ran away; The old woman was reduced to silence."
Adding soldiers to the hearth; on the day of great peace, victory and defeat are settled. Meritorious deeds are inscribed everywhere upon the annals of history;
casting off one’s hands in Chang’an, there is no need to ask the way. Thus he was named Zhenhong.

The lay practitioner Xu Zhensheng, whose courtesy name was Wusheng, had revered and placed his faith in the Triple Gem since childhood. He took the greatest delight in texts such as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Zhuangzi*, and the *Laozi*.

Upon hearing of Master Jie’s reputation for the Way, he immediately turned to him in faith. Receiving a meditation topic (*huatou*), he applied himself with diligent effort and investigated it for many years.

One day, he entered the inner quarters to request instruction. Master Jie snapped his fan once, and the layman attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse of realization: [Verse omitted per instructions]

Jie approved of this and instructed him on his conduct, emphasizing that he should strive for substance rather than mere formality. In the first month of winter in the year of Xinyou, he was afflicted by a slight illness.
At the moment of his passing, he spoke this verse: "My name is Zhensheng; from where does this sound come? My Dharma-name is Zhenxing; where does this fragrance go now?
People say I am one among the followers of the Buddha—this is truly a grievous injustice. I have read but a few lines of the books of Confucius and Mencius."
"Furthermore, how joyful it is that he does not enter the ranks of the partisan! A-he-he! At midday the sky is clear and the moon is bright;
thus, he has departed in serenity. (Dilu said: "A truly peerless man. According to the *Jinming Jinzu Qinyin Lianfang*, recorded recently by several [masters]).

[The entry for] Xi falsely claims to be a dharma heir of Jinzu. Upon a detailed examination of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) and various other texts, there is no factual evidence to support this; therefore, it is not appropriate to include him within this collection).
Chan Master Chongmo Zhenkai of Baoben in Xiushui was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yongzheng. A native of Huguang, he went to visit Yongzheng, who asked him, "Where have you come from?"
The Master said, "Xin Cheng. Zheng said, "Before you have even set foot [here], I would like to give you a blow.
The Master made a single sweep with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*), whereupon Zheng struck him. After a short while, the Master presented a verse; Zheng took it and asked for more.
The Master said, "I thought there was something else, Master. Zheng deeply approved.

Addressing the assembly, [the Master] recounted the karmic connection of Shishuang’s study under Fenyang, wherein he realized that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary circumstances. The Master offered this verse:
He emptied his belly and poured out his heart to show it to others, yet they failed to realize it; how grievous, how difficult to unfold! One day he was caught in the act—a matter no light;
his eyes encompass heaven and earth, his spirit and bearing fresh and new.
Chan Master Duanyu Zhenzhi of Tui’an at Dongxi was a native of Jiaxing. He studied under Yongzheng and asked about Lingyun’s saying:
"Ever since the first sight of the peach blossoms, until now I have had no further doubts. Why did Xuansha, however, say that he had not yet reached the ultimate?
Yongzheng replied, "The straight does not conceal the crooked. The Master asked, "I wonder, how does one who has reached the bottom utilize this?"
The Master said: "When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. The attendant bowed and served him for twenty years.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the karmic occasion of Xiangyan climbing the tree. The Master offered this verse: "A single stroke fully reveals the upward-moving function;
For a man with no land to call his own, his deeds are truly marvelous. He fears not the eyes of onlookers in the midst of the scene; Possessing a distinct majesty that stirs the four quarters."

In the *Yimao* year of the Kangxi era, while residing at Yongjeongsa, on the twentieth day of the final month of autumn in the *Dingsi* year, he ordered the drum to be beaten to assemble the community.
The Master raised his fist and said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. Each of you must exert yourselves;

do not treat this as trivial. He spoke again: "Throughout my life I have been too lazy to speak; when parting from the assembly, I have no other words. Sit upright and close both eyes; when meeting people, do not err."
[The Master] raised his staff and said, "Tell me, after all, how is it? He let out a shout and then remained silent.
His stupa was enshrined in the Abbot’s quarters. Chan Master Geng Weizhen visited Yongzheng. Yongzheng asked, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens;
after they appeared in the world, why is there no news at all? The Master replied, "He sits and cuts off the tongues of the whole world. Yongzheng [nodded].

[The Master] said, "Not yet. The teacher then presented a verse, saying: "The poisoned sound has not yet been heard before it reaches the ear; The sharp point is concealed within the sleeve—how can it be contended with?
Suddenly emerging in the open light, there is no handle to grasp; It strikes away the very eye of Maheśvara. [The Master] said, "Look straight at this!
That evening, he entered the hall and, citing the teacher’s verse, asked: "This one has a handle; what is it that has no handle?"
Zhaozhou asked, "What is the essential meaning? The Master then gave a shout. Zheng said, "Is there anything else besides this? The Master said, "There is, indeed; it is simply not fit to be cited.
Zheng asked, "Why is it not fit to be cited? The Master said, "For fear of scaring the people of the world to death.
Zheng took up his whisk and struck him. The Master bowed. Zheng struck him again.
Chan Master Hongxing Fayu went to visit Yongzheng. Yongzheng asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Chongde. Yongzheng asked, "Whom have you attended?
The Master replied, "Tiantong, Baoen, and Foyan. Yongzheng asked, "And whom else have you seen?
The Master replied, "Face-to-face with both eyes. Yongzheng held up his fist and said, "Speak a phrase regarding this. The Master said, "To speak it would be to break it."
Zhaozhou said, "It is acceptable. Linji said, "Not yet. Zhaozhou said, "Does the Master wish for me to repeat the verse?
Linji then struck him. Zhaozhou said, "The kindness is too great to repay. Linji struck him again. Zhaozhou bowed. Later, he visited again. Zhaozhou asked, "The wind and rain are pouring down;
it was no easy matter to travel so far. Has the ground beneath your feet ever been soaked? Linji let out a thunderous shout. Zhaozhou said, "You still carry [the traces]."

The mud and water were still there. Master Zheng said, "It is precisely because you, Preceptor, have such a heart of maternal compassion. He struck him right then. The Master prostrated, and Zheng approved.
Chan Master Yuyong went to visit Master Yongzheng and stayed in his service for several years. One day, Zheng asked him, "You have been here continuously for some time."
"How do you conduct yourself? the Master asked. "Putting on clothes and eating food," Xuedou replied. "Is there anything more besides this? Zhengjue asked.
"If there were," the Master said, "it would be a betrayal of the Abbot. "If you say there is nothing," Zhengjue said, "it would also be a betrayal of me, the old monk.
The Master paid his respects with three bows, saying, "Take care. Zhengjue then struck him.

The Senior Monk Eishō Tsūkei visited again. Teishin raised his whisk and said, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs came from the West—was there not already this very message?
The Master then shouted. Teishin asked, "As for the Buddhas appearing in the world and the Patriarchs coming from the West, how about that?
The Master said, "When all sentient beings have been saved. Teishin said, "I see, Preceptor."
Jie asked, "What about you, Master? Zheng immediately shouted. At this, Jie was suddenly enlightened and said, "I thank you for your compassion," and he prostrated himself. Zheng then struck him.
Gaoruo went to visit Master Zheng’an again and consulted Master Yongzheng. Yongzheng asked, "Where have you been hiding yourself all this time?

The Master replied, "I have never concealed anything from the beginning. Yongzheng asked, "In what way is it that you do not conceal anything? The Master said, "The mountains are green and the waters are blue;
the sparrows chirp and the crows caw. Yongzheng asked, "Is this not your original face? The Master said, "Though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon remain the same."
[Zhaozhou] said, "It is the same. Zheng said, "That is not it; speak further. Zhaozhou then shouted.
Zheng struck his *ruyi* (auspicious-gem) staff and said, "Try to say a single phrase here! Zhaozhou bowed. Zheng approved.
The Collection of Droplets of Milk from the Path-Stones, Volume Five (End)
